lessons.title: What Technical Writing Is
lessons.content:
Imagine your cousin from Sylhet is coming to your house in Dhaka for the first time. You send him a message: 'Come to Mirpur, then ask anyone.' He spends two hours wandering around Mirpur 10, calling you every ten minutes. Now imagine you had sent this instead: 'Take the bus to Mirpur 10 circle. Get off at the metro station. Walk north for 3 minutes. Turn left at the green pharmacy. Ours is the yellow building, flat 4B.' He arrives in fifteen minutes and never calls once. Same house, same cousin, same city. The only difference is the writing. That is what this course is about.

What technical writing is: Technical writing is writing that helps a specific reader understand something or do something. The subject is usually technical, like software, machines, data, experiments or procedures, but the real heart of it is the reader. A good technical document is judged by one test: after reading it, can the reader do what they needed to do, correctly, quickly and without asking you? If yes, the writing worked. If the reader is confused, the writing failed, no matter how beautiful the sentences are.

Where you already meet it: You read technical writing every day without noticing. The steps on the bKash screen telling you how to send money. The label on a medicine strip saying 'Take one tablet after meals, twice a day'. The settings page of your phone. The README file on a GitHub project. The lab sheet your teacher gives before an experiment. The error message 'Wrong PIN. You have 2 tries left.' Each of these was written by someone who had to decide what you needed to know, in what order, and in what words.

Technical writing vs creative writing: A short story or a poem wants to make you feel something. It can be mysterious, it can hide the ending, it can use the same word in three different ways for beauty. Technical writing wants you to understand or act, so it does the opposite. It puts the main point first. It uses one word for one thing. It never leaves the reader guessing on purpose. A poem that you have to read five times may be wonderful. A user manual that you have to read five times is broken.

Technical writing vs academic writing: Academic writing, like an essay in a literature class, often shows that the writer has thought deeply and can argue a position. Technical writing overlaps with it, especially in research papers and theses, but its first job is usefulness. A teacher may read your whole essay because grading is their job. A busy engineer reading your report will read the summary, look at one table, and stop. Technical writing is built for readers who are busy and who want to get something done.

The five qualities: Almost every textbook lists the same core qualities, and they are worth remembering. Accurate: every fact, number and step is correct, because a reader will trust it and act on it. Clear: the reader understands it on the first read, with no guessing. Concise: no extra words, but nothing important left out either. Complete: the reader has everything they need, including warnings, units and the expected result. Usable: the reader can find what they need, follow it and come back to it later. Notice that concise and complete pull against each other. Good writers keep both in balance by asking what this particular reader needs.

Accuracy comes first: Of the five, accuracy is the one you can never trade away. Suppose a setup guide says 'Set the voltage to 12 V' when the device needs 5 V. The sentence is short, clear and easy to follow, and it will burn the device. Clear writing that is wrong is worse than messy writing that is right, because the reader follows it confidently. So technical writers check their facts, test their own steps and say honestly when something is uncertain.

Kinds of technical documents: Here is a rough map you will fill in during this course. Documents that inform: reports, lab reports, progress reports, specifications, research papers, definitions and descriptions. Documents that instruct: procedures, user manuals, tutorials, README files, installation guides. Documents that persuade: proposals, recommendation reports, grant applications, a pitch to your manager. Everyday messages: emails, chat messages, meeting notes, bug reports, commit messages. Spoken and visual: presentations, posters, diagrams and slides. Many real documents mix these. A project proposal informs the reader about a problem and then persuades them to fund your solution.

Why engineers must write: Many CSE students think writing is for arts students. In real jobs, software engineers write constantly: design documents before building a feature, pull request descriptions explaining a change, comments in code, tickets describing bugs, emails to clients, documentation for an API, incident reports after something breaks. At university you write lab reports, assignment reports, a project proposal and finally a thesis. A strong coder who cannot explain their work often gets less credit than a slightly weaker coder who can. Clear writing is also clear thinking made visible: when you cannot write a step clearly, it often means you have not fully understood it yet.

Who does this writing: Big software companies employ full-time technical writers, sometimes called documentation engineers, whose whole job is turning what developers know into guides, references and help pages. But most technical writing is done by ordinary engineers, testers, analysts and students as part of their daily work. So you do not need to become a professional writer. You need to become an engineer who writes well enough that people can use your work.

The cost of bad writing: Bad writing is not just ugly, it is expensive. A famous serious example is the Space Shuttle Columbia accident in 2003. During the mission, engineers studied whether a piece of foam that had hit the wing could be dangerous. One of the slides used in the briefings had a reassuring title, while the important warning, that the test data came from foam pieces far smaller than the one that hit the shuttle, was buried in small text lower down. The investigation board that studied the accident criticised how technical information was presented in such slides. Most cases are smaller but still costly: customers who call support because the manual was unclear, a proposal rejected because the reviewer could not find the budget, a teammate who wastes a day because the README skipped one install step.

A worked comparison: Look at these two versions of a lab instruction. Version A: 'The configuration of the router should be done properly with the appropriate settings being applied as necessary.' Version B: 'Set the router IP to 192.168.1.1 and the subnet mask to 255.255.255.0.' Version A has 17 words and tells you nothing you can act on. Version B has only 12 words and tells you exactly what to type. Notice how Version A uses 'should be done', 'appropriate' and 'as necessary', which sound official but carry no information. Most of this course is learning to turn A into B.

The reader is busy, and that changes everything: Readers of technical documents rarely read from start to finish. They skim, they search, they jump to the section they need, they read on a phone while standing in a bus. This one fact explains most of the rules you will learn. Headings exist so people can jump. Summaries come first so people who stop early still get the point. Numbered steps exist so people can keep their place. Tables exist so people can compare at a glance. When a rule in this course seems strange, ask: how does this help a busy reader?

The writing process in one line: Good technical documents are rarely written in one go. Writers plan (who is the reader, what do they need), research (collect the facts), organise (make an outline), draft (write quickly), revise (fix the big picture), edit (fix the sentences) and proofread (fix the typos). You will meet each step in lesson 03. For now, just know that a first draft is supposed to be messy. The quality comes from revising.

Real-life example 1, the bKash help text: Suppose bKash wants to tell users how to set a new PIN. A weak version says: 'In order to facilitate the modification of your Personal Identification Number, kindly navigate to the relevant section of the application.' A strong version says: 'To change your PIN: 1. Open the app. 2. Tap the menu. 3. Tap Change PIN. 4. Enter your old PIN, then your new PIN twice.' The strong version uses everyday words, puts the goal first, gives numbered steps and names the exact buttons. A villager in Kurigram who uses bKash for the first time can follow it. That is the standard to aim for.

Real-life example 2, the group project README: Your team of four builds a library management system for a course project. Only Rafi knows how to run it, because he set it up. The night before the demo, Rafi's laptop dies. If Rafi had written a short README with 'Requirements: Python 3.11 and MySQL. Step 1: create the database with the file setup.sql. Step 2: run pip install -r requirements.txt. Step 3: run python app.py and open localhost:5000', anyone could run the project on another laptop in ten minutes. Without it, the team panics. Technical writing is how knowledge leaves one person's head and becomes useful to everyone.

Common mistakes beginners make: The first mistake is thinking big words sound smart. In technical writing, 'use' beats 'utilise' and 'start' beats 'commence'. The second is writing for yourself instead of the reader, skipping steps that feel obvious to you because you already know them. The third is hiding the main point at the end, like a story. The fourth is never revising: submitting the first draft. The fifth is copying text from the internet without credit, which is plagiarism and is covered in lesson 23. Exams often ask you to define technical writing, list its qualities, compare it with other writing, or rewrite a vague paragraph into a clear one.

How this course is organised: Lessons 02 to 08 build the core skills: knowing your reader, the writing process, clear sentences, precise words, paragraphs, grammar, and conciseness and readability. Lessons 09 and 10 cover how a document looks: layout, figures and tables. Lessons 11 to 17 cover everyday and software documents: emails, definitions, instructions, manuals, README files, API docs and requirements. Lessons 18 to 21 cover reports, proposals, research papers and theses. Lessons 22 and 23 cover citing sources and avoiding plagiarism. Lesson 24 covers presentations and posters, and lesson 25 brings it all together with editing and a capstone project.

Recap: Technical writing helps a specific reader understand or do something. It values accuracy, clarity, conciseness, completeness and usability, with accuracy first. It differs from creative writing because it puts the point first and never makes the reader guess. Engineers write a lot, and bad writing costs time, money and sometimes safety. Every rule ahead comes back to one question: what does this reader need, and how can I make it easy for them?
key_points: Technical writing helps a specific reader understand something or do something; the reader's success is the test.
Core qualities: accurate, clear, concise, complete and usable, with accuracy never traded away.
Unlike creative writing, it puts the main point first, uses one word for one thing and never makes the reader guess.
Documents inform (reports, specs), instruct (manuals, READMEs), persuade (proposals) or are everyday messages (emails, bug reports).
Engineers write constantly: design docs, comments, pull requests, reports, proposals and a thesis.
Readers are busy and skim, which is why headings, summaries first, numbered steps and tables exist.
Bad writing has real costs: support calls, rejected proposals, lost days, and in serious cases safety failures.
lessons.tip: Whenever you finish writing anything, ask one question: could my reader do what they need without calling me? If not, find the spot where they would get stuck and fix that first.
lessons.task: Write directions from the nearest main road to your home for someone who has never been there, in 6 numbered steps or fewer. Give it to a friend or family member and ask them to point out any step where they would have to guess.

quiz.q: What is the main test of a good technical document?
options: The reader can understand or do what they needed without asking the writer
It is longer than five pages
quiz.explain: Technical writing exists to help a specific reader; if the reader succeeds without help, the document worked.

quiz.q: Which quality should never be traded away for the others?
quiz.explain: Clear but wrong writing is dangerous because readers follow it confidently; accuracy comes first.

quiz.q: How does technical writing differ from creative writing?
options: It puts the main point first and uses one word for one thing
It hides the ending to keep the reader interested
It uses as many different words as possible for variety
quiz.explain: Technical writing aims for understanding and action, so it is direct and consistent, not mysterious.

quiz.q: Which sentence is better technical writing for a lab sheet?
options: The configuration of the router should be done properly as necessary.
Appropriate settings must be applied to the router.
Set the router IP to 192.168.1.1 and the subnet mask to 255.255.255.0.
Router configuration is an important step.
quiz.explain: Only this one tells the reader exactly what to do with exact values.

quiz.q: Why do technical documents use headings, summaries first and numbered steps?
options: Because readers are busy, skim and jump to what they need
To make the document look longer
quiz.explain: Most readers skim and search; these features help them find and follow information quickly.

lessons.title: Audience and Purpose
lessons.content:
Suppose your phone's battery drains too fast and you want to explain the problem. To your grandmother you say: 'The phone dies by lunch, even though I charged it at night.' To a friend who studies electrical engineering you say: 'The battery drops about 15 percent per hour on standby, so something is keeping the CPU awake.' To the service centre you write: 'Model X, battery health 78 percent, drains 15 percent per hour on standby since the last system update.' Same problem, three different messages, and each one is right for its listener. Choosing the right message for the right person is the first and most important skill in technical writing.

What audience means: Your audience is the person or group who will read your document. Not people in general, but the actual readers: who they are, what they already know, what they want, and in what situation they will read. The audience decides almost everything else: which words you use, how much background you explain, how long the document is, what goes first, and whether you include formulas, screenshots or both. Writing without knowing your audience is like cooking without knowing who will eat. You might make a very spicy curry for a guest who cannot eat chilli.

What purpose means: Purpose is what you want the reader to know, do or decide after reading. Most technical documents have one of three main purposes. To inform: the reader should understand something, like a report explaining why the server crashed. To instruct: the reader should be able to do something, like a guide for installing software. To persuade: the reader should agree or decide something, like a proposal asking for money for a project. Many documents combine them, but one purpose is usually the boss. If you are not sure what your purpose is, the reader will not be sure either.

The four common reader types: A classic way to think about technical readers is by what they know. Experts know the subject deeply, like a senior engineer or your thesis supervisor. They want precise details, data and method, and they get annoyed by long basic explanations. Technicians are people who build, operate or fix things, like a network technician or a lab assistant. They want clear procedures, exact settings and warnings. Managers and decision makers want the bottom line: what is the problem, what are the options, what does it cost, what do you recommend. They often do not have time for the details. Laypeople, or general readers, have no special knowledge, like a customer using an app. They need everyday words, examples and no jargon. One person can be different types at different times. Your supervisor is an expert in machine learning but may be a layperson in hardware.

Primary, secondary and gatekeeper readers: Real documents often have several readers. The primary reader is the person who will act on the document, for example the manager who approves your project. Secondary readers are others who will read it and be affected, like the finance officer who checks the budget or the technician who will set up the equipment. The gatekeeper is someone who must approve the document before it reaches the primary reader, like your supervisor who checks your proposal before it goes to the department. There may also be future or hidden readers: a new employee who reads your design document two years later, or a lawyer who reads an incident report after a dispute. Writing clearly for them now saves big trouble later.

The reader's context: Besides who the reader is, think about how they will read. Will they read at a desk with time, or on a phone in a bus? Will they read it once, or keep coming back to it while working, like a lab manual next to the equipment? Are they stressed, like someone whose account was just blocked? Is English their second language? Many readers in Bangladesh read English documents comfortably but more slowly than Bangla, so short sentences and common words help them a lot. A reader in a hurry needs the key point in the first line. A reader doing a task needs numbered steps they can follow with one eye on the screen.

The purpose statement: A powerful habit is to write one or two sentences before you start: 'This document is for [reader]. After reading it, they should be able to [know, do or decide something].' For example: 'This guide is for first-year students who have never used Linux. After reading it, they should be able to open a terminal, move between folders and run a C program.' If you cannot fill in this sentence, you are not ready to write yet. The purpose statement also helps you cut: any paragraph that does not help this reader reach this goal is a candidate for deletion.

Topic is not purpose: Beginners often confuse the two. 'Cloud storage' is a topic. 'Help the accounts office decide whether to move its files to cloud storage this year' is a purpose. A topic tells you what you are writing about; a purpose tells you what the writing must achieve, and so what to include and what to leave out. Two documents on the same topic can look completely different because their purposes differ. A history of cloud storage would be interesting but useless to the accounts office, which needs cost, safety and a recommendation. Whenever you get an assignment, turn its topic into a purpose before you start.

Building an audience profile: For bigger documents, make a quick audience profile with a few questions. Who are the readers, and how many types? What do they already know about the subject? What words and terms do they understand? Why are they reading, and what will they do next? What are their attitudes, are they eager, sceptical, worried or forced to read it? How will they read it, on paper, laptop or phone? What could go wrong if they misunderstand? You can answer these in five minutes, and the answers will guide every decision that follows.

Worked example, one topic for three readers: Your team built an attendance app that marks students present using the classroom Wi-Fi. You must write about it for three audiences. For the department head (a manager), the purpose is to persuade: 'The app cuts roll-call time from about 8 minutes to under 1 minute per class and reduces proxy attendance. It costs nothing extra because it uses existing Wi-Fi. We recommend a one-semester trial in two sections.' For the IT officer (a technician), the purpose is to instruct: exact server requirements, the port to open, how to install, how to back up the data. For students (laypeople), the purpose is to instruct simply: 'Connect to the class Wi-Fi, open the app, tap Mark Me Present within the first 10 minutes.' Same app, three documents, three different first sentences.

The curse of knowledge: Once you know something well, it becomes very hard to imagine not knowing it. Psychologists call this the curse of knowledge. It is why experts skip steps, use undefined terms like 'just SSH into the box', and think their explanation is obvious. Your mind fills in the gaps automatically, but the reader's mind cannot. The cure is to test your writing with a real reader from the target audience, or at least to read your document pretending you are that person, asking at every line: would they know this word? Would they know where this button is?

Writing for mixed audiences: Often you cannot choose just one reader. A project report may be read by your supervisor, the external examiner and a future student. The usual solution is layering. Put a short summary at the start that anyone can understand, in plain words, with the main result and recommendation. Then give the main body for the main readers. Then put heavy details, like full data tables, long derivations or code listings, in appendices for the experts who want them. Use headings so each reader can jump to their part. A short glossary helps laypeople without slowing down experts.

Adjusting the level of detail: How do you decide how much to explain? A good rule: explain anything your primary reader probably does not know, and only that. If your reader is a CSE teacher, do not explain what a variable is. If your reader is a shop owner, do not use 'API' without explaining it, or better, avoid it altogether: 'the app talks to the bKash system to check the payment'. When in doubt, a short explanation in brackets helps the beginner and costs the expert only a second.

Tone and attitude: Audience also shapes tone. Writing to your teacher needs respect and formality. Writing to a teammate in chat can be relaxed. Writing to a worried customer needs calm and kindness: 'Your money is safe. The transfer did not go through, so no money was deducted.' Writing to a sceptical reader needs evidence: numbers, tests and sources, not just enthusiasm. Avoid sounding angry, sarcastic or superior, even when the reader made a mistake. A document that makes the reader feel stupid will not be read with goodwill.

Real-life example 1, Pathao and the delivery rider: Imagine Pathao adds a new feature for riders to mark a delivery as complete by taking a photo. The engineering team writes a technical design document for other engineers: database changes, image size limits, API endpoints. But the riders are the real users. Many riders read Bangla more comfortably than English, use budget phones and read while standing next to a bike in traffic. So the rider guide must be in simple Bangla, with three short steps and one picture per step. Same feature, but writing the rider guide like the design document would fail completely.

Real-life example 2, the thesis abstract: Your thesis on detecting rice leaf diseases with deep learning will be read by your supervisor (expert), the external examiner (expert, but busy, reads the abstract first), and maybe an agriculture officer who finds it online (layperson in machine learning, expert in rice). The abstract should be understandable to all three: the problem in plain words (rice leaf diseases reduce yield and are hard to spot early), what you did (trained a model on a few thousand leaf photos), the main result with a number, and why it matters. The method details go in the chapters for the experts.

Common mistakes and exam questions: The most common mistake is writing for yourself, assuming the reader knows what you know. Another is writing for a vague 'everyone', which ends up fitting no one well. Another is choosing the wrong purpose: writing an interesting explanation when the reader needed steps, or giving steps when the manager needed a recommendation. Exams often ask you to define audience analysis, classify readers (expert, technician, manager, layperson), explain primary and secondary readers, write a purpose statement, or rewrite a paragraph for a different audience.

Recap: Know your reader before you write a word. Identify what they know, why they read and how they will read. Decide your purpose: inform, instruct or persuade. Write a purpose statement. Watch out for the curse of knowledge. For mixed audiences, layer the document with a plain summary first and details later. Every later lesson in this course, from sentence style to report structure, is really a way of serving the audience you identify here.
key_points: Audience means the actual readers: what they know, why they read and in what situation they read.
The three main purposes are to inform, to instruct and to persuade; one usually leads.
Common reader types: experts, technicians, managers and laypeople, each needing different detail.
Documents can have primary, secondary, gatekeeper and future readers.
A purpose statement names the reader and what they should know, do or decide after reading.
The curse of knowledge makes writers skip steps; test with a real reader to catch it.
For mixed audiences, layer the document: plain summary first, main body next, heavy detail in appendices.
lessons.tip: Before any document, write one sentence on a sticky note: 'This is for ___, and after reading they should be able to ___.' Keep it in front of you while you write and cut anything that does not serve it.
lessons.task: Pick one thing you know well, such as how to recharge mobile balance or how to submit an assignment on your university portal. Explain it in three short versions: one for your grandparent, one for a classmate, and one for a teacher who needs to approve it. Compare the first sentence of each.

quiz.q: A department head who must approve your project budget is best described as which reader type?
quiz.explain: Decision makers want the problem, options, cost and recommendation, not deep technical detail.

quiz.q: What is a gatekeeper reader?
options: Someone who must approve the document before it reaches the primary reader
The person who will finally act on the document
A reader who only looks at the pictures
Anyone who reads it after ten years
quiz.explain: Gatekeepers, like a supervisor checking a proposal, control whether the document goes forward.

quiz.q: Which is a proper purpose statement?
options: Linux is a very important operating system.
I will write everything I know about Linux.
This guide is for first-year students new to Linux; after reading it they can open a terminal, change folders and run a C program.
quiz.explain: A purpose statement names the reader and what they should be able to do afterwards.

quiz.q: What does the 'curse of knowledge' cause writers to do?
options: Skip steps and use terms the reader does not know
quiz.explain: Knowing a topic well makes it hard to imagine not knowing it, so writers leave gaps the reader cannot fill.

quiz.q: How do you usually handle a report read by experts, managers and general readers together?
options: Write only for the general readers
Layer it: plain summary first, main body next, heavy details in appendices
Make three separate reports with no summary
quiz.explain: Layering lets each reader type find the level of detail they need.

lessons.title: The Writing Process
lessons.content:
Think about how a good cook makes biryani for a wedding. Nobody throws rice, meat and spices into a pot at once and hopes. First the cook decides how many guests are coming. Then buys the ingredients. Then marinates the meat, soaks the rice, fries the onions. Then layers everything and cooks it on low heat. Then tastes it and adjusts the salt. Only then is it served. Writing a good technical document works the same way. It is not one act but a series of steps, and most bad documents come from skipping steps, especially the tasting at the end.

What the writing process is: The writing process is the sequence of activities that turns an idea into a finished document. Different books name the stages slightly differently, but the usual ones are: planning (also called prewriting), researching, organising, drafting, revising, editing and proofreading. The stages are not strictly one after another. You might discover during drafting that you need more research, or realise while revising that the outline was wrong. Good writers move back and forth. But knowing the stages helps you see what kind of work you are doing at each moment, and stops you from trying to do everything at once.

Why one-shot writing fails: Many students sit down the night before a deadline and try to write the final version directly, choosing perfect words, fixing commas and thinking about structure all at the same time. This is like trying to drive, read a map and repair the engine at once. The brain jumps between big decisions (what goes where) and tiny ones (is this spelled right), and does both badly. Separating the stages means that while drafting you only care about getting ideas down, and while editing you only care about sentences. Each job gets your full attention.

Stage 1, planning: Planning answers the questions from lesson 02. Who is the reader? What is the purpose? What does the reader need from this document? What form should it take: an email, a two-page memo, a 30-page report? What is the deadline and are there rules, like a template or a word limit? A five-minute plan can save five hours of writing the wrong thing. For an assignment, read the instructions twice and underline every requirement, such as 'include a flowchart' or 'maximum 1500 words'. Many marks are lost simply because a requirement was missed.

Generating ideas: Once you know the purpose, collect ideas. Brainstorming means writing down every idea quickly without judging, for example a list of everything that could go into a report on campus Wi-Fi problems. Mind mapping means writing the main topic in the middle of a page and drawing branches for subtopics, which helps you see connections. Freewriting means writing nonstop for 10 minutes about the topic, ignoring grammar, to find out what you actually think. Asking questions is very useful for technical topics: the journalist's questions who, what, when, where, why and how, or reader questions like 'What will they ask first?'

Stage 2, researching: Technical writing needs facts, and facts need sources. Research might mean reading documentation, papers or standards, running your own tests and measurements, interviewing users or engineers, or looking at existing documents in your organisation. While researching, take notes carefully. For each note, write where it came from: the URL, book, page or person. This feels slow, but it saves you from two disasters later: not being able to find a source again, and accidentally copying someone's words without credit. Lesson 22 covers citations in detail.

Stage 3, organising and outlining: An outline is the skeleton of the document, a list of headings and points in order. A topic outline uses short phrases, like '2. Causes of slow Wi-Fi: 2.1 Too many users per access point, 2.2 Interference, 2.3 Old routers'. A sentence outline turns each point into a full sentence that states the main claim, like '2.1 Each access point serves about 80 students at peak time, far more than it was designed for.' Sentence outlines take longer but make drafting very fast, because each sentence is already the topic sentence of a paragraph. Common patterns for organising content include chronological (steps in time order), spatial (parts of a machine from top to bottom), general to specific, problem then solution, cause then effect, and comparison. Many technical documents also follow fixed structures, such as the report structure in lesson 18.

Checking the outline: Before drafting, test the outline. Does every section serve the purpose? Is anything missing that the reader needs? Is the order logical for the reader, not just for you? Would a busy reader find the most important point early? Show the outline to your supervisor or teammate now. Changing an outline takes five minutes; changing a finished 20-page draft takes days.

Stage 4, drafting: Drafting means turning the outline into paragraphs. The key rule is speed over perfection. Write the whole thing roughly, even if some sentences are ugly. If you cannot find a word or a number, write a marker like [CHECK] or [NUMBER?] and keep going. You do not have to start at the beginning. Many writers start with the easiest section, often the method or the results, and write the introduction and abstract last, once they know what the document actually says. Stopping to polish every sentence while drafting usually leads to a beautiful first page and no second page.

Stage 5, revising: Revising means re-seeing. You look at the big picture: content, structure and fit to the reader. Is the purpose achieved? Is anything missing, wrong or unnecessary? Are sections in the best order? Does each paragraph have one clear point? Is the main message clear in the first page? Revising may mean moving whole sections, deleting paragraphs you worked hard on, or adding a missing example. It is the stage where the document gets most of its quality, and the one beginners most often skip.

Stage 6, editing: Editing works at the sentence and word level. Are sentences clear and not too long? Is the voice active where possible? Are terms used consistently? Are numbers and units correct? Is the tone right for the reader? Lessons 04 to 08 give you the tools for this stage: plain language, precise words, paragraph flow, grammar and conciseness.

Stage 7, proofreading: Proofreading is the final check for small surface errors: spelling, typos, punctuation, missing words, wrong figure numbers, broken links, formatting slips. It should be done last, because there is no point fixing a typo in a paragraph you will delete during revision. Proofreading tricks: print it or change the font so it looks unfamiliar, read it slowly out loud, read the last sentence first and move backwards so you see words instead of meaning, and check numbers, names and headings separately.

A worked time plan: Suppose you have 10 hours over a week for a lab report. One reasonable split is: planning and research 2 hours (20 percent), outlining 1 hour (10 percent), drafting 3 hours (30 percent), revising and editing 3 hours (30 percent), and proofreading and formatting 1 hour (10 percent). Notice that revising, editing and proofreading together get 4 hours, more than the drafting. That surprises many students, but it matches how experienced writers work. Also notice the gap: if you draft on Monday and revise on Wednesday, you see your own text with fresh eyes and catch far more problems than if you revise immediately.

Writer's block: Sometimes you sit in front of an empty page and nothing comes. Practical cures: lower the bar by telling yourself this is only a rough draft, start with the easiest section, talk the idea out loud to a friend or record yourself explaining it and then type what you said, write the outline as questions and answer each one, or set a timer for 15 minutes and write without stopping. Writer's block is often a sign that the planning is not finished: you do not yet know who the reader is or what you want to say.

Keeping versions: Save versions as you go, either with names like report_v1, report_v2, or better with a tool that keeps history automatically, such as Google Docs version history or Git for text files. Then you can delete boldly during revision, knowing you can recover anything. Never work on the only copy of an important document on one laptop. Your thesis should live in at least two places, for example your laptop and a cloud drive.

Real-life example 1, a semester project report: Nusrat must write a report on her team's flood alert SMS system. Planning: the reader is her course teacher, the purpose is to show what was built and how well it works, the limit is 15 pages. Research: she collects test logs, the system diagram and two papers on flood warnings in Bangladesh. Outline: introduction, system design, implementation, testing, results, limitations, conclusion. Draft: she writes the testing section first because it is the clearest in her head. Revision two days later: she notices the results section has numbers but never says whether 95 percent message delivery is good enough, so she adds a comparison with the requirement. Editing: she cuts three long sentences and fixes inconsistent use of 'alert', 'warning' and 'message'. Proofreading: she finds that Figure 3 is called Figure 4 in the text.

Real-life example 2, a work email that matters: Arif, a junior developer at a Dhaka software company, must ask his team lead to delay a release. He plans first: the reader is busy, the purpose is to get a decision today. He drafts quickly, then revises: his first draft started with a long story about the bug, so he moves the request to the first line ('Can we move the release from Thursday to Sunday?') and puts the reason in two short sentences below. He edits away vague words like 'some issues', replacing them with 'the payment screen crashes on Android 10'. Five minutes of process turned a confusing email into one that gets a quick yes or no.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Starting to write before knowing the reader and purpose. Mixing editing into drafting and never finishing. Skipping revision and only spell-checking. Proofreading on screen right after writing, when your brain still sees what you meant instead of what you typed. Not recording sources during research. Exams often ask you to list and explain the stages of the writing process, to distinguish revising from editing and proofreading, to make an outline for a given topic, or to explain techniques for generating ideas.

Recap: Writing is a process, not a single act: plan, research, organise, draft, revise, edit and proofread. Separate the stages so each gets full attention. Outline before drafting and test the outline early. Draft fast, revise deeply, edit carefully and proofread last. Give revision plenty of time and a fresh pair of eyes. Keep notes of your sources and keep versions of your work. Like the biryani, the quality comes from the steps you do not skip.
key_points: The writing process: plan, research, organise, draft, revise, edit, proofread, moving back and forth when needed.
Separating stages lets you focus: ideas while drafting, sentences while editing.
Brainstorming, mind mapping, freewriting and asking questions help generate content.
Record the source of every note during research to avoid lost sources and accidental plagiarism.
Outlines (topic or sentence) are cheap to change; check them with someone before drafting.
Revising fixes the big picture (content, structure, fit); editing fixes sentences; proofreading fixes surface errors last.
Give revision real time and a break between drafting and revising.
lessons.tip: Draft today, revise tomorrow. Even one night between writing and revising makes your own mistakes jump out at you.
lessons.task: Choose a topic you might write a report on, such as load-shedding in your area or the queue at your university canteen. Spend 10 minutes making a mind map, then turn it into a sentence outline with 5 to 7 points. Show it to a friend and ask which point is unclear.

quiz.q: Which stage focuses on content, structure and fit to the reader?
quiz.explain: Revising is re-seeing the big picture; editing and proofreading handle sentences and surface errors.

quiz.q: Why should proofreading be done last?
options: Because it is the most important stage
Because fixing typos in text you may later delete wastes time
Because spell-checkers only work on finished files
quiz.explain: Revision may cut or rewrite paragraphs, so small fixes are best done at the end.

quiz.q: What is the best attitude while drafting?
options: Write quickly and mark gaps like [CHECK], then keep going
Polish every sentence before writing the next
Avoid outlining so ideas flow freely
quiz.explain: Drafting is for getting ideas down; perfection comes during revising and editing.

quiz.q: A sentence outline differs from a topic outline because it...
options: Uses only one word per heading
States each point as a full sentence making the main claim
quiz.explain: Sentence outlines turn each point into a full claim, which makes drafting faster.

quiz.q: Why should you write down the source of each note during research?
options: To find sources again and avoid accidental plagiarism
So that the abstract is shorter
quiz.explain: Recording sources early makes citing easy and prevents copying words without credit.

lessons.title: Clear Sentences and Plain Language
lessons.content:
Read this sentence from an imaginary office notice: 'Due to the fact that the server was experiencing a high volume of incoming requests from users located in multiple regions, it was decided by the team that an additional instance would be deployed in order to ensure that response times would remain within acceptable limits.' Did you have to read it twice? Most people do. Now read this: 'The server was getting too many requests from users in several regions. To keep response times acceptable, the team added a second server.' Same information. The first version has 46 words in one sentence. The second has 23 words in two sentences, and you understood it in one go. This lesson is about how to write the second kind every time.

What plain language is: Plain language is writing that the intended reader can find, understand and use the first time they read it. It does not mean childish writing, and it does not mean removing technical terms that the reader needs. It means choosing the clearest way to say something for that reader. Governments and organisations around the world have adopted plain language rules for public documents, because unclear forms and letters waste citizens' time and cause mistakes. In technical writing, plain language is simply the default.

Why sentences matter so much: A reader's short-term memory can hold only a few pieces of information at once. While reading a sentence, the reader has to hold the beginning in mind until the verb and the end arrive to complete the meaning. Long sentences with many clauses overload that memory, especially when the main verb comes late. Second-language readers, which includes many readers in Bangladesh reading English, feel this even more. So the shape of your sentences directly controls how hard your document is to read.

Sentence length: A widely used guideline is to keep the average sentence length around 15 to 20 words, and to treat any sentence over about 25 to 30 words as a candidate for splitting. Average matters, not every sentence: a mix of short and medium sentences reads naturally. A worked check: a paragraph has five sentences of 12, 18, 9, 34 and 17 words. Total words = 90, average = 90 / 5 = 18 words, which is fine. But the 34-word sentence is an outlier. Look at it and see if it carries two ideas that could be two sentences. Most word processors and free online tools can show you sentence lengths, so you do not need to count by hand.

One idea per sentence: The easiest way to shorten sentences is to give each one a single main idea. Long sentences usually happen when writers chain ideas with 'and', 'which', 'while' and 'as well as'. Example: 'The app stores the user's location, which is updated every 30 seconds, and sends it to the server, where it is matched with nearby drivers, and the result is shown on the map.' Split it: 'The app records the user's location every 30 seconds. It sends the location to the server. The server finds nearby drivers and shows them on the map.' Each sentence now does one job, and the steps are easier to follow.

Active and passive voice: In the active voice, the subject does the action: 'The program saves the file.' In the passive voice, the subject receives the action: 'The file is saved by the program.' or just 'The file is saved.' Active sentences are usually shorter, clearer and say who does what. Passive sentences can hide the actor, which causes confusion in instructions and reports: 'The password must be reset.' By whom? The user? The admin? Compare 'You must reset your password' or 'The admin resets the password.' Spotting passive voice is easy: look for a form of 'be' (is, are, was, were, been, being) followed by a past participle (saved, sent, reset, decided).

When passive voice is right: Passive is not wrong; it is a tool. Use it when the actor is unknown or unimportant: 'The bridge was built in 1998.' Use it when the thing acted on is the real topic: 'The data was encrypted before upload' in a section about the data. Use it in some scientific method sections where the action matters more than who did it: 'The samples were heated to 80 degrees C.' Some fields and journals prefer the passive in methods, while many modern style guides allow 'We heated the samples'. Check what your teacher or journal expects. The rule is: choose the voice on purpose, and never use the passive to hide responsibility, as in 'Mistakes were made.'

Hidden verbs: A hidden verb, also called a nominalisation, is a verb turned into a noun, usually ending in -tion, -ment, -ance or -ence. 'Decide' becomes 'make a decision'. 'Investigate' becomes 'conduct an investigation'. 'Analyse' becomes 'perform an analysis'. Hidden verbs make sentences longer and weaker. Example: 'The committee made a decision to conduct an investigation into the failure' has 12 words. 'The committee decided to investigate the failure' has 7 words and says the same thing. When you edit, hunt for phrases like 'make a', 'perform a', 'conduct a', 'carry out', 'give consideration to' and turn the noun back into a verb.

Put the subject and verb early: Readers look for who is doing what. If a sentence opens with a long introduction before the subject, the reader waits impatiently. 'After considering the results of the three experiments conducted over the past two months in the network lab under different load conditions, we chose TCP.' The main point arrives at the very end. Better: 'We chose TCP after three experiments in the network lab under different loads.' Also keep the subject and verb close together. 'The router, which was installed last year by the vendor and which has been restarted several times this week, failed' makes the reader carry 'the router' across 17 words before learning what it did.

Use concrete subjects: Sentences are clearer when the subject is a real person or thing: 'The user', 'the server', 'the sensor', 'we'. Sentences starting with 'It is' or 'There are' often waste words. 'There are three files that need to be uploaded' becomes 'Upload three files.' 'It is important to note that the battery must be charged' becomes 'Charge the battery first.' These openers are fine occasionally, but if many of your sentences start that way, you are delaying the point.

State things positively: Negative sentences are harder to process, and double negatives are even harder. 'Do not forget to save' is clearer as 'Remember to save' or simply 'Save your work.' 'The system will not run unless the database is not locked' makes readers stop and work it out. Rewrite as 'The system runs only when the database is unlocked.' Use negatives when you are giving a real prohibition or warning: 'Do not unplug the device during the update' is correct and clear, because the reader needs a firm 'no'.

Address the reader directly: In instructions and user documents, write to the reader as 'you', and use the imperative for commands: 'Tap Send', 'Enter your PIN'. This is shorter and friendlier than 'The user should tap Send'. Many modern documentation style guides, such as those published by large software companies, recommend this second-person style. In formal reports and papers, 'we' is now widely accepted for the authors, though some teachers still prefer an impersonal style. Again, know your reader and follow the expected style.

Untangle noun stacks: Engineers love piling nouns on top of each other: 'user account password reset request form validation error'. Each word modifies the next, and the reader must work backwards to find out what the thing actually is. Is it an error? In what? The form? Which form? Break the stack with a few small words: 'an error in validating the form that users fill in to request a password reset'. Even better, rewrite the whole sentence around a verb: 'If the password reset form has an invalid field, the app shows an error.' A stack of two or three nouns, like 'login page' or 'database server', is fine. Four or more is a warning sign.

Use common words: Prefer the short, common word when it means the same thing. Use instead of utilise, start instead of commence, help instead of facilitate, show instead of demonstrate, buy instead of purchase, enough instead of sufficient, about instead of approximately (unless you need the precise feel), so instead of consequently. This is not about sounding simple; it is about not slowing the reader down with words that add nothing. Keep the technical terms the reader needs, like 'latency' or 'encryption', but drop decorative big words.

A worked rewrite: Original, 34 words: 'It has been observed that the utilisation of the caching mechanism results in a significant improvement in the performance of the application, and it is therefore recommended that it should be enabled by default.' Step 1, find the real subject and verb: caching improves performance. Step 2, replace 'utilisation' and 'improvement' with verbs. Step 3, replace 'significant' with a number if you have one. Step 4, turn the recommendation into a direct statement. Result, 18 words: 'Caching cut average page load time from 2.4 to 0.9 seconds, so we recommend enabling it by default.' Shorter, concrete and actionable.

Real-life example 1, a university notice: A typical notice might read: 'All students are hereby informed that the submission of the registration form must be completed by the concerned students within the stipulated deadline, failing which no consideration will be given.' A plain version: 'Submit your registration form by 15 March. We cannot accept late forms.' The plain version tells students exactly what to do and by when. The original sounds official but forces every student to decode it, and some will misread the deadline.

Real-life example 2, an app error message: A food delivery app shows: 'Transaction processing could not be completed due to an unexpected authentication failure.' A user has no idea what to do. A plain version: 'Payment failed because your card was not verified. Check the card details or try another payment method.' It says what happened, why, and what to do next, in active voice with common words. (HCI, deep-cse-5-5, covers error message design from the interface side.)

Common mistakes and exam questions: Thinking long, complex sentences sound more professional. Overusing the passive, especially in instructions. Burying the main verb inside a hidden-verb phrase. Starting many sentences with 'It is' or 'There are'. Using double negatives. Exams often give a paragraph and ask you to rewrite it in plain language, to change passive sentences to active, to identify nominalisations, or to explain when the passive voice is appropriate.

Recap: Plain language means the reader understands on the first read. Keep sentences around 15 to 20 words on average, one main idea each. Prefer the active voice and use the passive on purpose. Turn hidden verbs back into verbs. Put the subject and verb early and close together. Use concrete subjects, positive statements, 'you' in instructions, and common words. Every one of these changes makes the reader's job easier, which is the whole point.
key_points: Plain language means the intended reader can find, understand and use the text on the first read.
Aim for an average of 15 to 20 words per sentence and split outliers above about 25 to 30.
Give each sentence one main idea; break chains of 'and', 'which' and 'while'.
Prefer active voice; use passive on purpose, when the actor is unknown or unimportant, never to hide responsibility.
Turn hidden verbs (make a decision, conduct an investigation) back into verbs (decide, investigate).
Put the subject and verb early and close together; avoid stacking 'It is' and 'There are' openers.
Use positive statements, 'you' and imperatives in instructions, and common words instead of decorative big ones.
lessons.tip: When you edit, highlight every 'is/are/was/were + -ed' and every '-tion' word. Each one is a place where your sentence might get shorter and clearer.
lessons.task: Find a long official notice or announcement (from your university, a bank SMS, or a utility bill). Rewrite it in plain language with sentences under 20 words. Count the words before and after and see how much shorter it gets without losing information.

quiz.q: Which sentence is in the active voice?
options: The file is saved by the program.
The file has been saved automatically.
quiz.explain: In active voice the subject (the program) does the action (saves).

quiz.q: A paragraph has sentences of 10, 20, 15, 35 and 20 words. What is the average sentence length?
quiz.explain: Total 100 words divided by 5 sentences gives 20 words on average; the 35-word sentence is still worth splitting.

quiz.q: Which is the best rewrite of 'The team made a decision to conduct an analysis of the logs'?
options: The team decided to analyse the logs.
A decision was made by the team to analyse the logs.
An analysis of the logs was decided upon.
The team made the decision of analysing the logs.
quiz.explain: Turning the hidden verbs 'make a decision' and 'conduct an analysis' back into verbs gives the shortest clear version.

quiz.q: When is the passive voice a good choice?
options: When you want to hide who made a mistake
When the actor is unknown or unimportant, as in 'The bridge was built in 1998'
quiz.explain: Passive is useful when the doer does not matter or is unknown, but should never be used to hide responsibility.

quiz.q: Which is the clearest version of 'The system will not run unless the database is not locked'?
options: The system will not run if the database is locked.
The system runs only when the database is unlocked.
Unless locked, the database will not not run the system.
It is not the case that the system runs with a locked database.
quiz.explain: Stating it positively removes the double negative and makes the condition easy to understand.

lessons.title: Precise Words
lessons.content:
Your friend says, 'The internet package is fast, and the download is big, so it will take a little while.' How long is a little while? Ten seconds? Ten minutes? Now your friend says, 'The package is 100 Mbps and the file is 500 MB, so it should take about 40 seconds if the line runs at full speed.' Now you know whether to wait or go and make tea. The first sentence used vague words. The second used precise ones. In technical writing, the reader acts on your words, so vague words are not just weak; they are risky.

What precision means: Precise writing means each word points to exactly one meaning that the reader will understand the same way you do. It covers several habits: using concrete words instead of vague ones, giving numbers with units, using technical terms correctly, defining terms and acronyms, calling the same thing by the same name every time, and avoiding sentences that can be read in two ways. Clear sentences (lesson 04) make text easy to read; precise words make sure that what the reader understands is what you meant.

Concrete vs vague words: Vague words sound like information but give none. Common culprits: fast, slow, big, small, many, few, soon, recently, often, some, several, good, bad, significant, various, appropriate, properly, as needed, etc. Each one makes the reader ask 'How much? Which ones? When exactly?' Replace them with concrete facts. 'The app is slow' becomes 'The home screen takes 6 seconds to load on a 4G connection.' 'Many users complained' becomes '214 users reported the bug in the first week.' 'Restart the server soon' becomes 'Restart the server before 10 pm today.' If you do not know the number, say so honestly ('we have not measured load time yet') rather than hiding the gap behind a vague word.

Numbers and units: A number without a unit is often useless. '500' could be 500 milliseconds or 500 seconds, a big difference if it is a timeout. Always write the unit. Common style rules, following the international SI system: put a space between the number and the unit symbol (5 V, 250 ms, 16 GB); unit symbols are case sensitive (m is metre, M is mega, ms is milliseconds, Ms would be megaseconds); do not add an 's' to symbols for plurals (10 kg, not 10 kgs); and keep the number and its unit on the same line if you can. Be consistent with decimals: write 0.5, not .5, because the lonely dot is easy to miss.

Bits and bytes, a classic trap: In computing, a small letter changes everything. A lowercase b means bit and an uppercase B means byte, and 1 byte = 8 bits. Internet speeds are usually given in megabits per second (Mbps), while file sizes are usually in megabytes (MB). Worked example: a 500 MB file on a 100 Mbps connection. 500 MB = 500 x 8 = 4000 megabits. Time = 4000 / 100 = 40 seconds at full speed, ignoring overhead. If you mistakenly treat both as the same unit, you would predict 5 seconds and be wrong by a factor of 8. Another trap: kilobyte can mean 1000 bytes (kB, decimal) or 1024 bytes. The IEC standard uses KiB, MiB and GiB for the 1024-based units, so 1 KiB = 1024 bytes. When the difference matters, for example in memory sizes, say which one you mean.

Dates and times: '03/04/2025' means 3 April in Bangladesh and the UK but 4 March in the USA. For an international team or a database, that is a real bug waiting to happen. Write the month as a word ('3 April 2025') or use the ISO 8601 format YYYY-MM-DD ('2025-04-03'), which also sorts correctly as text. Give time zones for times: Bangladesh Standard Time is UTC+6, so '10:00 UTC+6' is clear to a colleague abroad. Even the abbreviation BST is ambiguous, because it also stands for British Summer Time. And instead of 'next Friday' in an email that might be read on a Thursday or Saturday, give the date.

Significant digits and honest precision: Precision also means not pretending to be more exact than you are. If you measured response time with a stopwatch, writing '1.2847 seconds' is false precision; your measurement is not that accurate. Write '1.3 seconds' or 'about 1.3 seconds'. Similarly, if 3 out of 7 testers liked a feature, '42.857 percent' looks scientific but hides the tiny sample. Write '3 of 7 testers'. Match the number of digits to how accurate the measurement really is, and give the sample size when you give percentages.

Jargon and technical terms: Jargon is specialised vocabulary of a field: latency, throughput, idempotent, regression, deploy. Jargon is not bad. Among experts, it is precise and saves time: 'the API is idempotent' replaces a whole sentence. It becomes a problem when the reader does not know it. The rule follows from audience analysis: use the terms your reader knows, define the ones they might not know, and replace the ones they do not need with plain words. For a manager, 'the update reduced latency by 40 percent' may need to become 'the update made the app respond 40 percent faster'.

Acronyms and abbreviations: Engineers swim in acronyms: API, SDK, DNS, OTP, SRS, CI/CD. Write the full form the first time you use one, followed by the acronym in brackets: 'Software Requirements Specification (SRS)'. After that, use the acronym. If the document is long or readers jump around, define the acronym again at the start of each chapter or keep a list of abbreviations near the front. Do not invent new acronyms just to save typing; every new acronym is something the reader must remember. And never assume acronyms are universal: OTP means one-time password to a bKash user but could mean something else entirely in another field.

One thing, one name: In creative writing, teachers tell you to vary your words. In technical writing, that habit causes real confusion. If you call something 'user' in section 2, 'customer' in section 3 and 'client' in section 4, a careful reader will wonder if they are three different roles with different permissions. Pick one term for each concept and stick to it. This matters most in requirements and API documents, where 'account' and 'profile' might be different database tables. A glossary at the start or end of a long document, listing each key term and its meaning, keeps you and your team consistent.

Ambiguous pronouns: Words like it, this, that, they and which point back to something. When there are two possible things, the reader may pick the wrong one. 'The app sends the request to the server, and it then checks the token.' What checks the token, the app or the server? Repeat the noun: 'and the server then checks the token.' Be especially careful with a lonely 'this' at the start of a sentence: 'This caused the crash.' This what? The update? The low memory? The setting? Add a noun after it: 'This memory leak caused the crash.'

Misplaced and ambiguous modifiers: The position of a word can change the meaning. 'The script only deletes temporary files on Friday' could mean it deletes only temporary files, or it deletes them only on Friday. Write 'On Fridays, the script deletes only temporary files' or 'The script deletes temporary files only on Fridays', whichever you mean. Another common ambiguity: 'Users with admin rights and testers can delete records.' Can testers delete records only if they also have admin rights? Rewrite as two clear statements, or use a table of who can do what.

Must, should and may: In specifications, a single word decides whether something is required. The internet engineering community standardised these words in RFC 2119: MUST (or SHALL, REQUIRED) means an absolute requirement; MUST NOT means an absolute prohibition; SHOULD (or RECOMMENDED) means there may be valid reasons to ignore it in particular cases, but the consequences must be understood; MAY (or OPTIONAL) means truly optional. Many specifications write these words in capitals and state that they follow RFC 2119. Even outside formal specs, use them carefully: 'The password should be at least 8 characters' and 'The password must be at least 8 characters' lead to different software. Requirements writing is covered further in lesson 17.

Hedging honestly: Sometimes you are not certain, and precision means saying so. Words like may, might, likely, suggests and approximately are called hedges. Used honestly, they show the true strength of your evidence: 'The results suggest that caching reduces load time, but we tested only one server.' Used too much, they make the writing timid and empty: 'It might possibly be somewhat likely that...'. Used too little, they overclaim: 'This proves our method is the best.' Match the strength of the claim to the strength of the evidence. One test proves little; ten repeated tests on different devices justify a firmer claim.

Words to cut or replace: Some words add nothing: very, really, quite, basically, actually, totally, simply. 'Very fast' is still vague; give the number. 'Simply click Install' can make a struggling reader feel stupid; just write 'Click Install'. Also avoid 'etc.' at the end of lists in instructions or requirements, because the reader cannot know what else is included. List everything, or say 'such as' to show the list is just examples.

Real-life example 1, a delivery app status message: A courier app says your parcel will arrive 'soon'. A customer in Chattogram waits all day. A precise message says: 'Your parcel is at the Agrabad hub. Expected delivery: today between 2 pm and 5 pm.' This tells the customer where the parcel is and gives a time window. The company also gets fewer 'where is my parcel?' calls, which saves money.

Real-life example 2, a lab report sentence: A student writes, 'The circuit worked properly and the voltage was good.' The teacher cannot judge anything from this. A precise version: 'The regulator output stayed between 4.95 V and 5.05 V for input voltages from 7 V to 12 V, within the expected 5 V plus or minus 2 percent.' Now the teacher can see exactly what was measured and compare it with the specification. Precision turns opinion into evidence.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Using vague adjectives instead of numbers. Forgetting units, or mixing bits and bytes. Defining an acronym after already using it many times. Switching names for the same thing. Starting sentences with an unclear 'this'. Writing 'should' when you mean 'must'. Exams often ask you to identify vague words in a paragraph and make them precise, to explain why consistent terminology matters, to define jargon for a lay reader, or to explain the difference between must, should and may.

Recap: Precise words mean one clear meaning for every reader. Replace vague words with concrete facts and numbers. Always give units, and watch bit versus byte. Match your digits and hedges to your real evidence. Use jargon only when the reader knows it, define acronyms on first use, and use one name for one thing. Fix ambiguous pronouns and modifiers. Use must, should and may deliberately. Precision is how your reader ends up with exactly the picture that is in your head.
key_points: Precise writing gives every word one meaning that the reader understands the same way you do.
Replace vague words (fast, many, soon, significant) with concrete facts and numbers; admit unknowns honestly.
Always give units with a space (5 V, 250 ms); b is bit, B is byte, and 1 byte = 8 bits.
Do not claim false precision; match digits to measurement accuracy and give sample sizes with percentages.
Define acronyms on first use, use jargon only for readers who know it, and keep one name for one thing.
Fix ambiguous pronouns (it, this) and misplaced modifiers (only) by repeating the noun or moving the word.
Use MUST, SHOULD and MAY deliberately as defined in RFC 2119, and hedge claims to match the evidence.
lessons.tip: After drafting, search your document for 'fast', 'slow', 'many', 'some', 'soon', 'significant' and 'etc.'. Each hit is a place to add a number, a name or a full list.
lessons.task: Check your internet package speed and pick a file or video you want to download. Calculate how long it should take at full speed (convert MB to megabits by multiplying by 8). Then download it and compare. Write two precise sentences explaining the difference.

quiz.q: How long does a 500 MB file take on a 100 Mbps connection at full speed, ignoring overhead?
quiz.explain: 500 MB x 8 = 4000 megabits; 4000 / 100 Mbps = 40 seconds.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid calling the same thing 'user', 'customer' and 'client' in one document?
options: Readers may think they are different roles
It makes the document too short
quiz.explain: In technical writing, different words suggest different things, so varying terms creates confusion.

quiz.q: According to RFC 2119, what does SHOULD mean?
options: Recommended, but there may be valid reasons to ignore it if consequences are understood
quiz.explain: SHOULD is a strong recommendation, weaker than MUST and stronger than MAY.

quiz.q: Which sentence avoids an ambiguous pronoun?
options: The app sends the request to the server, and it then checks the token.
The app sends the request to the server, and the server then checks the token.
It was then checked by it.
quiz.explain: Repeating 'the server' removes any doubt about what checks the token.

quiz.q: A student timed a response with a stopwatch. Which way of reporting it is most honest?
quiz.explain: A stopwatch is not accurate to a ten-thousandth of a second, so extra digits would be false precision; vague words give no information.

lessons.title: Paragraphs, Flow and Lists
lessons.content:
Imagine a train from Dhaka to Chattogram. Each carriage is separate, but they are joined by strong couplings, and they all run on the same track in the same direction. A good document works like that train. Each paragraph is a carriage carrying one load. Transitions are the couplings that join them. The purpose of the document is the track. If carriages are overloaded, uncoupled or pointing in different directions, the train does not arrive. This lesson is about building paragraphs that carry one load each, joining them smoothly, and knowing when to switch from paragraphs to lists.

What a paragraph is: A paragraph is a group of sentences about one main idea. Visually, it is a block of text separated by white space. That white space tells the reader 'a new idea starts here', so it is a promise. If one paragraph mixes three ideas, you break that promise and the reader loses track. If one idea is chopped into many tiny paragraphs, the reader cannot see what belongs together. In technical documents, paragraphs are usually short: often 3 to 6 sentences, rarely more than about 150 words. On a phone screen, a 250-word paragraph looks like a wall.

The topic sentence: Most good technical paragraphs begin with a topic sentence, a sentence that states the main point of the paragraph. The other sentences then support it with explanation, evidence, examples or details. Why put it first? Because busy readers skim by reading the first sentence of each paragraph. If your topic sentences are good, a reader can understand the whole document by reading only them. Example topic sentence: 'The new caching layer reduced server load by about a third.' Supporting sentences then give the numbers, explain how it was measured and mention a limitation. The reader knows from the first line what the paragraph is for.

A worked test, the skim test: Take a page you wrote and copy only the first sentence of each paragraph into a list. Read the list. Does it make a sensible summary of the page? If one entry is something like 'In addition to this, there are other aspects too', that paragraph has no clear point. Rewrite its first sentence to state the point, or merge the paragraph with another. This five-minute test catches more structural problems than reading the page three times.

Unity and length: Unity means every sentence in the paragraph supports its main idea. When editing, ask of each sentence: does this belong to this paragraph's point? If not, move it or delete it. If a paragraph has grown to two different points, split it, giving each its own topic sentence. If two short paragraphs make the same point, merge them. Paragraph length is a signal, not a rule: a one-sentence paragraph can be fine for emphasis or a short transition, but many one-sentence paragraphs in a row make the document feel like a list without bullet marks.

Coherence, old before new: A paragraph is coherent when each sentence connects smoothly to the next. A powerful technique is the old-to-new pattern: begin each sentence with something the reader already knows (from the previous sentence) and end it with the new information. Example of poor flow: 'The system uses a message queue. Orders from the website are stored temporarily by it. Lost orders during peak traffic were the reason we added it.' Better: 'The system uses a message queue. The queue stores orders from the website temporarily. We added it because orders were being lost during peak traffic.' Each sentence starts with what was just mentioned (the queue, it) and adds something new at the end, where English readers naturally expect emphasis.

Transitions: Transitions are words and phrases that show how ideas relate. They are signposts for the reader. To add: also, in addition, furthermore. To contrast: however, but, on the other hand, in contrast. To show cause and effect: because, so, therefore, as a result. To give an example: for example, for instance, such as. To show sequence: first, next, then, finally, after that. To summarise: in short, overall, to sum up. Use them when the relationship is not obvious, but do not paste 'Furthermore' or 'Moreover' at the start of every sentence. If every sentence has a heavy transition, they stop meaning anything.

Repetition and pointing words: Coherence also comes from repeating key terms (remember, one name for one thing from lesson 05) and from careful use of pointing words like this, these, such and that. 'This approach' or 'These results' at the start of a sentence connect it strongly to the last one, as long as it is clear what 'this' refers to. Repetition of key nouns is not bad style in technical writing; it is glue.

Opening and closing paragraphs: Paragraphs also have special jobs at the edges of a section. An opening paragraph tells the reader what the section covers and why, sometimes previewing its parts: 'This section explains the three causes of slow Wi-Fi we found: overloaded access points, interference and old routers.' Now the reader has a map. A closing paragraph, when a section is long, pulls the points together and links forward: 'Of the three causes, overloaded access points matter most, so section 4 focuses on adding capacity.' Short sections do not need either. Long ones feel lost without them.

Parallel structure: Parallelism means expressing similar ideas in the same grammatical form. It makes lists and comparisons easy to read. Not parallel: 'The app lets users track parcels, payment of bills, and to chat with support.' Parallel: 'The app lets users track parcels, pay bills and chat with support.' All three items are now verbs in the same form. Parallelism matters most in lists, headings and steps. If one heading is 'Installing the app', the next should be 'Configuring the app', not 'Configuration' or 'How to configure'.

When to use lists: Lists are excellent for some content and terrible for other content. Use a numbered list when order matters: steps in a procedure, ranked items, stages in a process. Use a bulleted list when order does not matter: features, requirements, items to bring, options. Lists help readers scan, see how many items there are and check items off. A good guideline is to use a list when you have three or more parallel items that the reader may want to scan or act on.

When not to use lists: Lists remove the connecting words that show relationships: because, so, but, unless. A bulleted list of five facts cannot say that the second causes the third or that the fourth only applies when the first is true. Reasoning, arguments, explanations and trade-offs belong in paragraphs. Slides and reports made entirely of bullets often hide weak thinking, because the writer never had to connect the points. A useful check: if your list items start with words like 'but', 'because' or 'however', they want to be a paragraph.

Writing good lists: Introduce the list with a sentence that tells the reader what the list is, often ending with a colon: 'Before the lab, bring the following:'. Keep items parallel. Keep items short; if an item needs several sentences, consider subheadings instead. Keep lists to a manageable length; a list of 20 bullets is hard to use, so group items under subheadings. Be consistent with punctuation: either all items are full sentences ending with full stops, or all are fragments, usually without full stops. Avoid deep nesting; two levels is normally the maximum readers can follow.

BLUF and the inverted pyramid: BLUF stands for Bottom Line Up Front, a style used widely in military and business writing: put your conclusion or request in the first sentence. Journalists use a similar idea called the inverted pyramid: the most important information first, then supporting details, then background. Both fit technical readers, who may stop reading at any point. Compare a status update that starts with 'On Monday we began testing, and on Tuesday we found some issues, and after investigation...' with one that starts 'The release is delayed by two days because of a login bug; the fix is ready and being tested.' The second gives the bottom line in one sentence. Details can follow for those who want them.

Worked paragraph rebuild: Original paragraph: 'There were various issues during testing. Some testers used old phones. The login screen was found to be slow by users. Also the colours were liked. In addition, it took 7 seconds to load on a Symphony phone with 2 GB RAM. The team will look into this.' Problems: no topic sentence, a stray point about colours, passive voice, a vague 'this'. Rebuild: 'Testing showed that the login screen is too slow on low-end phones. On a Symphony phone with 2 GB of RAM, it took 7 seconds to load, compared with under 2 seconds on newer phones. Most of our users in rural areas use similar low-end devices. The team will profile the login screen this week to find what causes the delay.' The colour feedback moves to a separate paragraph about visual design, where it belongs.

Real-life example 1, a Teams or Slack update: Rumana, a tester at a fintech startup in Dhaka, posts a daily update. Her old style was one long paragraph mixing yesterday's work, blockers and plans. Her new style: a first line with the bottom line ('Blocked: cannot test bill payment until the sandbox API key is renewed'), then three short bulleted sections: done, doing next, blockers. Her team lead says he now reads her updates in 15 seconds and acts on the blocker immediately. The list fits because the items are separate; the bottom line fits because the reader needs the most urgent fact first.

Real-life example 2, the discussion section of a lab report: Tanvir's first draft of a discussion section was a bulleted list: '- Throughput was lower than expected - Packet loss happened - The switch was old - Results differ from theory'. His teacher wrote: 'How are these connected?' He rewrote it as a paragraph: 'Throughput was 18 percent lower than the theoretical value. The main reason appears to be packet loss at the switch, which was an older model that dropped packets when its buffer filled. When we repeated the test with a newer switch, the gap fell to 5 percent.' The paragraph shows cause and effect, which the list could not.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Paragraphs without topic sentences. Paragraphs that mix several points. Walls of text with no breaks, especially on screens. Overusing bullets for reasoning. Non-parallel lists and headings. Hiding the conclusion at the end of a status message. Exams often ask you to identify the topic sentence of a paragraph, to reorganise a jumbled paragraph, to convert a paragraph into a parallel list or a list into a coherent paragraph, or to explain BLUF and the inverted pyramid.

Recap: One paragraph, one idea, usually led by a topic sentence. Test your structure by reading only the first sentences. Keep unity by moving or deleting sentences that do not belong. Build flow with old-to-new order, clear transitions and repeated key terms. Use parallel structure in lists and headings. Use numbered lists for order, bullets for unordered items, and paragraphs for reasoning. Put the bottom line up front. Like the train, each carriage carries one load, and all of them move in the same direction.
