key_points: A paragraph carries one main idea, usually stated in a topic sentence at the start.
The skim test: read only the first sentence of each paragraph; together they should summarise the page.
Unity means every sentence supports the paragraph's point; move or delete sentences that do not.
Old-to-new order and well-chosen transitions make sentences flow; repeated key terms act as glue.
Parallel structure (same grammatical form) is essential in lists, headings and steps.
Use numbered lists for order, bulleted lists for unordered items, and paragraphs for reasoning and cause-effect.
BLUF and the inverted pyramid put the most important point first, because readers may stop at any time.
lessons.tip: Before submitting any report, do the skim test: paste the first sentence of every paragraph into a new page. If that page does not read like a sensible summary, fix the topic sentences first.
lessons.task: Take a paragraph from one of your old assignments. Underline the topic sentence (or write one if it is missing), cross out any sentence that does not support it, and check that each sentence starts with something mentioned in the sentence before. Compare the before and after with a friend.

quiz.q: Where does a topic sentence usually go in a technical paragraph?
options: At the start, stating the paragraph's main point
At the very end, as a surprise
In the middle, hidden among details
quiz.explain: Readers skim first sentences, so leading with the main point helps them understand quickly.

quiz.q: Which list is parallel?
options: Track parcels, payment of bills, to chat with support
Track parcels, pay bills, chat with support
Parcels tracking, to pay bills, chatting
quiz.explain: All three items use the same verb form, which makes the list easy to read.

quiz.q: When is a paragraph better than a bulleted list?
options: When you need to show cause and effect or reasoning
When you list items to bring to a lab
When steps must be done in order
quiz.explain: Lists drop connecting words like because and so; reasoning needs paragraphs.

quiz.q: What does BLUF stand for?
quiz.explain: BLUF means stating the conclusion or request in the first sentence.

quiz.q: In the old-to-new pattern, where does new information usually go in a sentence?
quiz.explain: Sentences start with known information that links to the previous sentence and end with the new information.

lessons.title: Grammar and Punctuation for Engineers
lessons.content:
Look at this sign at an imaginary software firm: 'Lets eat, team!' Now add one apostrophe: 'Let's eat, team!' Now remove the comma: 'Let's eat team!' The last one suggests something rather alarming. Grammar and punctuation look like small details, but they change meaning. In code, a missing semicolon stops the program from compiling. In writing, a missing comma does not stop anything; the reader just silently understands something you did not mean. This lesson covers the grammar and punctuation errors that most often hurt technical documents, especially those written by Bangladeshi students writing in English.

Why grammar matters in technical writing: There are two reasons. First, meaning: some errors create ambiguity or say the wrong thing, which can cause real mistakes. Second, trust: readers judge your competence from your writing. A proposal full of basic errors makes the reviewer wonder whether your code and calculations are just as careless. That may not be fair, but it happens. You do not need perfect, literary English. You need correct, clear, consistent English. Most of the errors that matter come from a short list, which you can learn and check.

Subject-verb agreement: The verb must match its subject in number. 'The server is down' (one server), 'The servers are down' (many). The mistakes happen when words come between the subject and verb: 'The list of failed tests are attached' is wrong, because the subject is 'list', not 'tests'. Correct: 'The list of failed tests is attached.' Another trap is the word 'data'. Traditionally it is plural (one datum, many data), so some scientific journals write 'the data are'. In everyday computing usage, 'the data is' is widely accepted as a mass noun. Either is acceptable in most places; pick one and stay consistent, and follow your journal or teacher's preference.

Articles a, an and the: Bangla has no direct equivalents of English articles, so they are one of the hardest parts of English for Bangladeshi writers. The basic rules: use 'a' or 'an' for a singular countable thing mentioned for the first time or not specific: 'We built an app.' Use 'the' for something specific that the reader can identify: 'The app runs on Android.' (the one we just mentioned). Countable singular nouns almost always need an article or another determiner: not 'Server crashed', but 'The server crashed'. Uncountable nouns like information, software, equipment, advice and feedback do not take 'a' and have no plural: not 'a software' or 'softwares', but 'a piece of software' or 'software tools'; not 'informations', but 'information'.

A or an goes by sound: The choice between 'a' and 'an' depends on the sound of the next word, not its first letter. 'An hour' (silent h), 'a university' (starts with a 'yoo' sound), 'an MBA' (starts with an 'em' sound), 'a URL' (starts with a 'yoo' sound), 'an HTTP request' (starts with an 'aitch' sound). For acronyms, it depends on how people say them: 'an SQL query' if you say 'ess-queue-ell', 'a SQL query' if you say 'sequel'. Either is fine; just be consistent in one document.

Tense in technical documents: Use the past tense for what you did and what happened: 'We trained the model for 50 epochs. Accuracy reached 91 percent.' Use the present tense for facts that are generally true, for what your document contains, and for what figures show: 'TCP guarantees in-order delivery.' 'Figure 3 shows the training loss.' 'This report describes the system.' Use the future tense for plans: 'The next version will support Bangla.' A common mistake is mixing tenses randomly within a section, for example 'We collect the data, then we trained the model, and the results will be shown in Table 2.' Pick the tense by what the sentence is about.

Run-on sentences and comma splices: A comma splice joins two complete sentences with only a comma: 'The test failed, we fixed the bug.' A run-on joins them with nothing at all: 'The test failed we fixed the bug.' Both are errors. Fix them in one of four ways: a full stop ('The test failed. We fixed the bug.'), a semicolon ('The test failed; we fixed the bug.'), a joining word ('The test failed, so we fixed the bug.'), or by making one part dependent ('After the test failed, we fixed the bug.'). Watch especially for 'however' between two sentences: 'The code compiles, however it crashes' is a comma splice. Correct: 'The code compiles; however, it crashes.' or 'The code compiles. However, it crashes.'

Apostrophes: its and it's: 'It's' always means 'it is' or 'it has': 'It's running.' 'Its' is possessive, like 'his' or 'her': 'The app saves its settings.' A trick: if you can replace the word with 'it is', use 'it's'. Apostrophes also show possession for nouns: 'the user's password' (one user), 'the users' passwords' (many users). Apostrophes are not used for plurals: write 'APIs', '1990s' and 'PDFs', not 'API's', '1990's' or 'PDF's'.

Dangling modifiers: A modifier is a phrase that describes something. It dangles when the thing it describes is missing from the sentence. 'After running the test, the results were saved to a file.' Who ran the test? The sentence grammatically says the results ran the test. Fix: 'After running the test, we saved the results to a file.' Another example: 'Using a faster algorithm, the processing time dropped by half.' The processing time did not use the algorithm. Fix: 'Using a faster algorithm, we halved the processing time.' or 'With a faster algorithm, processing time dropped by half.' Dangling modifiers often come with the passive voice, which is another reason to prefer active.

Colons and semicolons: A colon introduces something that explains or lists what came before: 'The app needs three permissions: camera, location and storage.' The part before a colon should normally be a complete sentence, so avoid 'The permissions are: camera, location and storage.' A semicolon joins two closely related complete sentences: 'Version 1 used polling; version 2 uses push notifications.' Semicolons can also separate list items that already contain commas: 'We tested in Dhaka, Bangladesh; Kolkata, India; and Kathmandu, Nepal.' If you are unsure about a semicolon, a full stop is almost always safe.

Commas that matter: Commas after introductory phrases help readers: 'If the battery is low, the app pauses syncing.' Commas around extra information that could be removed: 'The router, which we bought in 2020, failed.' (we have one router) versus 'The router that we bought in 2020 failed.' (identifies which router among several). The serial or Oxford comma before 'and' in a list of three or more, as in 'red, green, and blue', is a style choice; some style guides require it and others do not. What matters is consistency and avoiding ambiguity.

Capitalisation and names: Capitalise proper nouns and product names exactly as their owners write them: JavaScript, GitHub, iOS, macOS, MySQL, PostgreSQL, bKash, YouTube. Do not capitalise ordinary technical words just because they feel important: write 'the database server' and 'machine learning', not 'the Database Server' and 'Machine Learning', unless they start a sentence or are part of a title. In headings, choose either sentence case ('Setting up the database') or title case ('Setting Up the Database') and use it everywhere.

Hyphens in compound words: When two words together describe a following noun, they are usually hyphenated: 'a real-time system', 'a well-known method', 'a 5-second delay', 'a two-factor login'. After the noun, the hyphen is usually dropped: 'The system works in real time.' 'The method is well known.' Do not hyphenate adverbs ending in -ly: 'a highly available service', not 'a highly-available service'.

Common Bangladeshi English slips: Some patterns come from translating Bangla directly or from habits common in South Asian English. 'Discuss about the problem' should be 'discuss the problem', because discuss already means talk about. 'Return back' and 'repeat again' are redundant: 'return' and 'repeat' are enough. 'Cope up with' should be 'cope with'. 'Revert' in formal international English means to go back to a previous state, so 'Please revert by Friday' confuses many readers; write 'Please reply by Friday'. 'Myself Rafi' as an introduction should be 'I am Rafi' or 'My name is Rafi'. 'I have a doubt' (meaning a question) should be 'I have a question'. 'Do the needful' is vague; say exactly what you need. 'Prepone' is not understood outside South Asia; write 'bring forward' or 'move earlier'.

e.g. and i.e.: These two Latin abbreviations are often mixed up. 'e.g.' means for example: 'Use a browser, e.g. Chrome or Firefox' (others are fine too). 'i.e.' means that is, or in other words: 'Use the latest version, i.e. 3.2' (only that one). If you are not sure, write 'for example' or 'that is' in full, which is often clearer anyway.

Tools and checking: Spell-checkers in word processors catch many typos but not wrong words that are real words, like 'form' instead of 'from' or 'there' instead of 'their'. Grammar checkers such as the ones built into editors, Grammarly or LanguageTool catch many agreement, article and comma problems, but they also make wrong suggestions, especially with technical terms. Treat them as a helpful second reader, not as a judge. Reading aloud catches missing words and run-ons. Keeping a personal list of your own common mistakes and searching for them before submitting is one of the most effective habits.

Real-life example 1, a job application email: Sadia applies for an internship at a software company in Dhaka. Her draft says: 'Myself Sadia, I have completed my BSc in CSE, i am interested to join your esteemed organization, kindly revert.' A recruiter scanning 200 emails may skip it. Her revised version: 'Dear Hiring Team, I am Sadia Rahman, a final-year CSE student at XYZ University. I am applying for the Android Developer Intern position. My CV and GitHub link are attached. I would be glad to discuss how I can contribute. Thank you for your time.' Correct capitals, no comma splices, clear request, and no unusual phrases.

Real-life example 2, a bug report: A tester writes: 'Login not working, its showing error, user enter correct password but its not work.' The developer cannot tell what exactly happens. Rewritten: 'Login fails with a correct password. Steps: enter a valid phone number and password, tap Log In. Expected: home screen opens. Actual: the error Invalid credentials appears. It happens on Android 12 but not on Android 14.' Grammar is not just decoration here; fixing 'its' and adding articles and verbs turned a vague complaint into a report someone can act on. (Lesson 11 covers bug reports further.)

Common mistakes and exam questions: The errors that appear most in student reports are missing or wrong articles, uncountable nouns made plural (softwares, informations, equipments), its versus it's, comma splices, tense mixing, dangling modifiers and South Asian phrases like 'discuss about'. Exams often give sentences to correct, ask you to choose a or an, ask about tense use in reports, or ask you to punctuate a paragraph correctly.

Recap: Correct grammar protects meaning and builds trust. Match subjects and verbs. Learn the article rules and the uncountable nouns. Choose tense by what each sentence describes. Fix comma splices with a full stop, semicolon or joining word. Know its from it's, and never use apostrophes for plurals. Make sure modifiers have something to modify. Use colons, semicolons, capitals and hyphens consistently. Watch for the common Bangladeshi English slips. Use tools, but stay the final judge.
key_points: Grammar errors can change meaning and reduce the reader's trust in your technical work.
Subjects and verbs must agree, even with words between them (the list of tests is attached).
Articles: a/an for first mention or non-specific, the for specific; a or an depends on the sound (an hour, a URL).
Uncountable nouns (software, information, equipment, feedback) have no 'a' and no plural.
Use past tense for what you did, present for general facts and what figures show, future for plans.
Fix comma splices with a full stop, semicolon, joining word or dependent clause; its is possessive, it's is it is.
Avoid common slips: discuss about, return back, cope up, revert (for reply), Myself Rafi, softwares.
lessons.tip: Keep a personal 'my mistakes' list. Every time a teacher or tool corrects you, add it. Before submitting anything, search your document for the items on that list.
lessons.task: Take one page of a recent report or long email you wrote. Search it for: its/it's, 'discuss about', 'softwares' or 'informations', ', however', and sentences without an article before a singular noun. Correct each one and count how many you found.

quiz.q: Which sentence is correct?
options: The list of failed tests are attached.
The list of failed tests is attached.
The list of failed tests were attached.
The lists of failed test is attached.
quiz.explain: The subject is 'list' (singular), so the verb is 'is'; 'of failed tests' does not change it.

quiz.q: Which uses the article correctly?
quiz.explain: The choice depends on sound: HTTP starts with the 'aitch' vowel sound, so 'an'.

quiz.q: Which sentence has a dangling modifier?
options: After running the test, the results were saved to a file.
After running the test, we saved the results to a file.
We ran the test and saved the results.
The results were saved after we ran the test.
quiz.explain: The sentence implies the results ran the test, because the person who ran it is missing.

quiz.q: How should 'The code compiles, however it crashes' be fixed?
options: The code compiles however, it crashes.
The code compiles, however, it crashes.
The code compiles; however, it crashes.
The code compiles however it crashes.
quiz.explain: Two complete sentences joined by 'however' need a semicolon (or a full stop) before it.

quiz.q: What is the best replacement for 'Please revert by Friday' for an international reader?
options: Please discuss about it by Friday.
Please do the needful by Friday.
quiz.explain: In international English, revert means go back to a previous state; 'reply' is clear to everyone.

lessons.title: Conciseness and Readability
lessons.content:
Think of a Dhaka rickshaw at rush hour. Every extra bag you put on it slows it down, and if you pile on too much, it barely moves. Words in a sentence work the same way. Each word that carries no meaning is an extra bag the reader has to pull. This lesson is about two connected ideas: conciseness, which means removing every word that does not do a job, and readability, which means measuring roughly how hard a text is to read. Both serve the same busy reader you met in lesson 01.

What conciseness is: Concise writing says everything the reader needs in as few words as possible. Notice both halves. Concise does not mean short at any cost. A two-line installation guide that skips a required step is short but not concise; it is incomplete. A twenty-page guide where every sentence is needed is concise even though it is long. Conciseness is about the ratio of useful words to total words. The goal is a document where nothing can be removed without the reader losing something.

Why wordiness happens: Writers add extra words for several reasons. Some think long phrases sound more formal or intelligent. Some are unsure of their point and circle around it. Some copy the style of old official documents. Some write while thinking and never go back to trim. And sometimes the writer is trying to reach a word count. Whatever the reason, the reader pays: more time, more effort and a higher chance of missing the key information buried among filler.

Wordy phrases and their short forms: Many common phrases have a one-word equivalent. In order to becomes to. Due to the fact that becomes because. At this point in time becomes now. In the event that becomes if. Has the ability to becomes can. For the purpose of becomes for or to. In spite of the fact that becomes although. With regard to becomes about. A large number of becomes many (or better, the actual number). It is possible that becomes may. Make an attempt to becomes try to. Prior to becomes before. Learn to spot these, because they appear constantly in student reports and office emails.

Redundant pairs and repeated meaning: Some phrases say the same thing twice. Past history (history is already past), future plans, end result, basic fundamentals, completely finished, each and every, final outcome, true facts, advance planning, revert back, repeat again, close proximity, ATM machine (the M already means machine), PIN number (the N already means number). Cut the extra word. Also watch for sentences that restate the previous sentence in different words: 'The system is very slow. It does not perform quickly.' The second sentence adds nothing.

Empty openers and filler: Some sentence openings and phrases carry no content. It is important to note that. It should be mentioned that. As we all know. Needless to say. In this day and age. Basically. As a matter of fact. It goes without saying. If something is important, the reader will see it from what you say; you do not need to announce it. If it goes without saying, do not say it. Deleting these phrases rarely loses anything.

A worked cut: Original, 36 words: 'In order to ensure that the system is able to handle a large number of users at the same time, it is necessary for us to make a decision regarding the purchase of an additional server.' Step by step: 'In order to ensure that the system is able to handle' becomes 'To handle'. 'A large number of users at the same time' becomes 'many users at once'. 'It is necessary for us to make a decision regarding the purchase of' becomes 'we need to decide whether to buy'. 'An additional server' becomes 'another server'. Result, 15 words: 'To handle many users at once, we need to decide whether to buy another server.' That is 21 words, or about 58 percent, removed with no loss of meaning. If you know the number of users, replace 'many' with it and the sentence becomes precise as well as concise.

When longer is better: Do not cut words that help the reader. Definitions for a lay reader, an example after an abstract idea, a warning before a dangerous step, a transition that shows cause and effect, units, and context needed to understand a number all add length but also add value. Telegraphic writing that drops articles and verbs, like 'Server restart req. ASAP, pls chk logs', saves the writer time but may cost the reader more. Clarity first; conciseness serves clarity, not the other way round.

What readability is: Readability is how easy a text is to read and understand. Many things affect it: word familiarity, sentence length, structure, layout, the reader's background and their motivation. Since the 1940s, researchers have built readability formulas that estimate difficulty from simple counts, mainly sentence length and word length. They cannot measure meaning, but they give a quick warning when text is getting heavy. Many word processors and online tools calculate them automatically.

Flesch Reading Ease: Rudolf Flesch's formula gives a score, usually between 0 and 100, where higher means easier: Reading Ease = 206.835 minus 1.015 times (words divided by sentences) minus 84.6 times (syllables divided by words). Roughly, scores of 60 to 70 are plain English that most adults read easily, 30 to 50 is difficult (typical of academic text), and below 30 is very difficult. Very simple text can score above 100, and very dense text can go below zero.

Flesch-Kincaid Grade Level: A related formula estimates the US school grade needed to understand the text: Grade = 0.39 times (words divided by sentences) plus 11.8 times (syllables divided by words) minus 15.59. A grade of 8 means a typical 13- to 14-year-old student could read it. Many plain-language guides suggest aiming around grade 8 to 10 for general audiences. Technical documents for experts can be higher, but lower is usually kinder.

Gunning Fog Index: Robert Gunning's index also estimates years of schooling: Fog = 0.4 times ((words divided by sentences) plus 100 times (complex words divided by words)), where complex words have three or more syllables. Gunning's rules do not count proper names, compound words made of short words, or words that reach three syllables only through endings like -ed or -es.

Worked example, easy text: 'The app sends a code to your phone. Type the code to log in. If the code does not arrive within two minutes, tap Resend.' Count: 3 sentences, 25 words and 29 syllables. Words per sentence = 25 / 3, about 8.33. Syllables per word = 29 / 25 = 1.16. Reading Ease = 206.835 minus 1.015 times 8.33 minus 84.6 times 1.16, which is about 100, the very easy end of the scale. Flesch-Kincaid grade = 0.39 times 8.33 plus 11.8 times 1.16 minus 15.59, about 1.3. Anyone can follow it.

Worked example, hard text: 'Authentication necessitates the utilisation of a verification code transmitted to the registered mobile device.' Count: 1 sentence, 14 words, 35 syllables (authentication 5, necessitates 4, utilisation 5, verification 5, transmitted 3, registered 3, mobile 2, device 2, and six one-syllable words). Syllables per word = 35 / 14 = 2.5. Reading Ease = 206.835 minus 1.015 times 14 minus 84.6 times 2.5, about minus 19, below zero. Flesch-Kincaid grade is about 19.4, beyond a university degree. For Fog, there are 5 complex words (transmitted is not counted because it reaches three syllables only by adding -ed), so Fog = 0.4 times (14 + 100 times 5 / 14), about 19.9. Same message as the easy text, but the scores warn you clearly that it is heavy.

What the formulas miss: Readability formulas are rough tools. They do not know whether your sentences make sense, whether the order is logical, whether terms are defined, or whether the reader already knows the topic. 'Eat the cat ran fast red' scores as very easy. A necessary technical term like 'encryption' raises the score even if the reader knows it well. Short choppy sentences can score well but feel robotic. So use the scores as smoke detectors: a very high grade level tells you to look for long sentences and heavy words, but the real test is still a human reader from your audience.

Readability for Bangla readers and second-language readers: The classic formulas were designed for English and English-speaking readers. Researchers have proposed readability measures for Bangla text, but they are less standard. The general principles still hold: shorter sentences, familiar words, clear structure and good layout help. For readers reading English as a second language, common words matter even more than for native readers, because a rare word may stop them completely. When writing for a broad Bangladeshi audience, such as a government service app, consider offering both Bangla and English, and test both with real users.

Real-life example 1, a bank SMS: A bank sends: 'Dear Valued Customer, this is to inform you that your account has been debited with an amount of BDT 5,000.00 on account of ATM cash withdrawal at the ATM booth located at Dhanmondi.' Cut version: 'BDT 5,000 withdrawn from your account at the Dhanmondi ATM on 12 May, 3:15 pm. Not you? Call 16xxx.' Shorter, adds the date and time the customer needs, and gives an action for fraud. Short SMS messages also cost less and fit on one screen.

Real-life example 2, a thesis introduction paragraph: Imran's thesis introduction scored grade 21 on a Flesch-Kincaid checker. Looking closer, he found sentences averaging 38 words and many hidden verbs. He split long sentences, replaced phrases like 'with the objective of facilitating the enhancement of' with 'to improve', and kept the necessary terms like 'convolutional neural network'. The grade dropped to about 14, still academic, as expected for a thesis, but his supervisor said it finally read smoothly. The formula did not fix the writing; it pointed to where the problems were.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Padding to reach a word count. Thinking formal means wordy. Cutting so much that the text becomes telegraphic or loses required detail. Trusting readability scores blindly, or ignoring them completely. Exams often give a wordy paragraph to make concise, ask you to list wordy phrases and replacements, ask you to calculate a Flesch Reading Ease or Fog index from given counts, or ask about the limitations of readability formulas.

Recap: Concise writing removes every word that does no job, while keeping everything the reader needs. Replace wordy phrases, cut redundant pairs and empty openers, and keep words that add clarity. Readability formulas such as Flesch Reading Ease, Flesch-Kincaid and Gunning Fog estimate difficulty from sentence and word length. Use them as warning lights, not as judges, and always test with real readers. Like the rickshaw, your sentence moves fastest when it carries only what is needed.
key_points: Concise means everything the reader needs in as few words as possible, not short at any cost.
Replace wordy phrases (in order to, due to the fact that, at this point in time) with short forms (to, because, now).
Cut redundant pairs (past history, PIN number, end result) and empty openers (it is important to note that).
Keep words that help: definitions, examples, warnings, units, transitions and context.
Flesch Reading Ease = 206.835 - 1.015(words/sentences) - 84.6(syllables/words); higher means easier.
Flesch-Kincaid Grade = 0.39(words/sentences) + 11.8(syllables/words) - 15.59; Fog = 0.4(words/sentences + 100 x complex/words).
Formulas only count length; they cannot judge meaning, order or the reader's background, so test with real readers.
lessons.tip: Paste your next report into any free readability checker. Do not chase a number; instead, look at the sentences it marks as hardest and fix those few first.
lessons.task: Write a 100-word paragraph explaining what your final year project or a favourite app does. Then cut it to 60 words without losing any fact. Count words, sentences and syllables in both versions and calculate the Flesch Reading Ease for each.

quiz.q: What is the concise form of 'due to the fact that'?
options: in view of the fact that
quiz.explain: 'Because' says the same thing in one word.

quiz.q: Which phrase is redundant?
quiz.explain: The N in PIN already stands for number, so 'PIN number' repeats it.

quiz.q: A text has 100 words, 5 sentences and 140 syllables. What is its Flesch Reading Ease, approximately?
What is a key limitation of readability formulas?
options: They always give the same score
They count length but cannot judge meaning, logic or the reader's knowledge
quiz.explain: Formulas use counts like sentence length and syllables, so nonsense can score as easy.

quiz.q: Which situation shows that longer can be better?
options: Adding 'It is important to note that' before a sentence
Adding a definition of 'API' for a shop owner reading the guide
quiz.explain: A definition for a reader who needs it adds real value, unlike filler phrases.

lessons.title: Document Design and Layout
lessons.content:
Imagine two shops in New Market selling exactly the same clothes. In the first, everything is piled in one huge heap on the floor. In the second, shirts are on one rack, trousers on another, sizes are labelled and there is space to walk. Both shops have the same products, but you will find your shirt in the second shop in two minutes and give up on the first. Document design is the second shop. The words are the products; the layout decides whether the reader can find and use them.

What document design is: Document design is the visual arrangement of a document: headings, spacing, fonts, alignment, lists, emphasis, page size, colours and the placement of figures and tables. Its job is not decoration. Its job is to show the structure of the content, to help readers find what they need and to make reading comfortable. A well-designed page lets a reader understand the organisation of a document before reading a single full sentence.

How people actually read: Readers of technical documents scan before they read. Eye-tracking studies on web pages by the Nielsen Norman Group found a common pattern they called the F-pattern: readers read across the top, then partway across a little lower, then scan down the left side looking for something interesting. Not every reader follows this exactly, but the lesson is clear: readers look at the top, at headings and at the left edge. So put important words at the start of headings and paragraphs, where the scanning eye lands.

Headings: Headings are the most powerful design tool in technical writing. They work like signboards on a highway. Good headings are informative: 'Installing Python on Windows' tells you more than 'Installation' and far more than 'Section 2'. They are short, usually under about eight words. They are parallel within a level, as you learned in lesson 06. And they are frequent enough that readers never face more than about a page or a screen of text without one.

Heading hierarchy and numbering: Long documents need levels of headings: level 1 for chapters or major sections, level 2 for subsections, level 3 for smaller parts. Each level should look clearly different, usually by size and weight, with higher levels larger and bolder. Try not to go deeper than three levels; deeper hierarchies confuse readers. Many technical reports and theses use decimal numbering: 1, 1.1, 1.1.1. Numbers make cross-references easy ('see section 3.2') and show the hierarchy clearly. Do not create a single subsection under a section: if you have 2.1, you should have at least 2.2, because dividing something into one part is not really dividing it.

Navigation aids: Long documents need ways for readers to know where they are. A table of contents at the start lists headings with page numbers. Running headers or footers repeat the document or chapter title on every page. Page numbers let people say 'see page 14' in a meeting. Cross-references ('see Table 3' or 'see section 4.2') guide readers to related parts, and in digital documents they should be clickable links. A list of figures, a list of tables and an index help in very long documents such as theses and manuals. For online documentation, a search box and a sidebar menu do the same job.

White space: White space, also called negative space, is the empty area on a page: margins, space between paragraphs, space around headings, figures and lists. Beginners often see empty space as wasted paper and try to fill it. In reality, white space groups related items and separates unrelated ones, gives the eyes a rest and makes the page look approachable. A heading should sit closer to the paragraph below it than to the paragraph above, so readers see which text it belongs to. Dense pages with tiny margins look hard before the reader starts.

Typefaces: A typeface is a design of letters, like Times New Roman, Arial, Calibri, Georgia or SolaimanLipi for Bangla. Serif typefaces have small strokes at the ends of letters (Times New Roman, Georgia); sans-serif typefaces do not (Arial, Calibri, Helvetica). Traditionally, serif fonts were used for printed body text and sans-serif for headings and screens, though modern high-resolution screens make both readable. Practical rules: use one or two typefaces in a document, not five. Use a monospaced font such as Consolas or Courier for code, so characters line up. For Bangla, choose a Unicode font that renders conjuncts (juktakkhor) correctly, and test it on the devices your readers use. (HCI, deep-cse-5-5, covers Bangla font rendering on screens.)

Size and spacing: For printed body text, about 10 to 12 points is common; many university templates specify 12 point. On screens, body text around 16 pixels is a common default for web pages. Line spacing (leading) of about 1.2 to 1.5 times the font size makes text comfortable; many thesis templates require 1.5 or double spacing. Headings are larger, but do not make every heading huge; clear steps in size, such as 16, 14 and 12 points, are enough.

Line length: Very long lines tire readers, because the eye has to travel far and may lose its place returning to the next line. Very short lines break the reading rhythm. A widely used typographic guideline is about 45 to 75 characters per line for body text, with around 66 often cited as comfortable. This is one reason why newspapers use columns and why well-designed web pages do not let text stretch across a wide monitor.

Alignment: Left-aligned text with a ragged right edge is usually the easiest to read, because spacing between words stays even. Fully justified text, where both edges are straight, looks neat in print, but in narrow columns or without good hyphenation it creates uneven gaps called rivers. Centred text is fine for titles but hard to read for paragraphs, because each line starts at a different place. Many university thesis templates require justified text; if so, follow the template and turn on automatic hyphenation if possible.

Emphasis: Bold, italics, underline, capitals and colour draw attention, so use them rarely, or they stop working. Bold is good for key terms when first defined, for warnings and for interface labels in instructions ('Tap Save'). Italics are traditionally used for titles of books and for occasional emphasis. Avoid underlining in documents that will be read on screens, because underlined text looks like a link. Avoid long passages in capitals; they are harder to read because all words have the same rectangular shape. If everything is emphasised, nothing is.

Templates and styles: Most word processors and tools like LaTeX let you define styles: Heading 1, Heading 2, Body Text, Caption, Code. Use them instead of manually making text bigger and bolder. Styles keep formatting consistent, let you change all headings at once, and allow the software to generate an automatic table of contents and a navigation pane. Many universities provide thesis templates with styles already defined. Using them from day one saves days of reformatting at the end.

Chunking and callouts: Chunking means breaking content into small, separate pieces that a reader can take in one at a time: short paragraphs, lists, tables, steps and boxes. Callout boxes, sometimes shaded or bordered, set apart special information such as a note, a tip, a warning or a summary of key points. They work because they look different from the main text, so use them only for information that truly needs to stand out. A page with six coloured boxes looks like a noticeboard, and the reader stops trusting that boxes mean something important.

Paper versus screen: Documents are increasingly read on screens, often on phones. Designing for screens means shorter paragraphs, headings that work as links, no tiny fonts, layouts that reflow to narrow widths, and avoiding scanned PDFs that cannot be searched or zoomed well. If a document will be printed, check page breaks so that a heading never sits alone at the bottom of a page and a table is not split awkwardly. Ask how your reader will most likely read it, and design for that first.

Accessibility basics: Accessible documents can be used by people with different abilities, including low vision, colour blindness and those using screen readers. Use real heading styles, not just bold text, because screen readers use headings to navigate. Give images alternative text describing what they show. Do not rely on colour alone: 'the failed tests are in red' is useless to a reader who cannot distinguish red from green; add a label or symbol too. Use enough contrast between text and background. The Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) recommend a contrast ratio of at least 4.5 to 1 for normal body text at the AA level.

Worked contrast check: Contrast ratio is calculated from the relative luminance of the two colours, giving a value from 1 to 1 (same colour) up to 21 to 1 (black on white). Light grey text #AAAAAA on white gives about 2.3 to 1, well below 4.5, so it is too faint for body text, though designers often use it for 'subtle' notes. Grey #767676 on white gives about 4.54 to 1, just passing, while the very similar #777777 gives about 4.48 to 1 and just fails. You do not need to compute this by hand; free contrast checkers do it, but you should check rather than guess.

Real-life example 1, a lab manual: The networking lab at a Dhaka university used a 20-page manual typed as continuous text in one font size. Students kept missing steps. A teaching assistant redesigned it: numbered headings for each experiment (Experiment 3: Configuring VLANs), a short Objectives box at the start, numbered steps with commands in a monospaced font, bold warnings before any step that could disconnect the lab network, and white space between steps. The content barely changed, but questions during lab sessions dropped sharply because students could find their place.

Real-life example 2, a government service notice online: Imagine a notice explaining how to apply for a trade licence online, posted as a scanned image of a printed page. It cannot be searched, a screen reader cannot read it, the text is tiny on phones and the steps are buried in one long paragraph. A redesigned version as a real web page uses a clear title, short sections with headings (Who can apply, Documents you need, Steps, Fees, Contact), numbered steps, readable Bangla Unicode text with good contrast, and works on a phone. Same information, far more usable.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Walls of text without headings. Vague headings like 'Introduction 2' or 'Other things'. Too many fonts and colours. Manual formatting instead of styles, leading to inconsistent headings. Centred or fully justified paragraphs in narrow columns. Low-contrast grey text. Using colour alone to carry meaning. Exams often ask you to explain principles of document design, the role of headings and white space, serif versus sans-serif, why line length matters, or to redesign a poorly formatted page.

Recap: Document design shows the structure of your content and helps busy readers scan and find. Use informative, parallel, numbered headings with at most about three levels. Use white space generously to group and separate. Choose one or two readable typefaces, sensible sizes and line spacing, and lines of about 45 to 75 characters. Prefer left alignment, use emphasis rarely, build documents with styles and templates, and design for accessibility with real headings, alt text, no colour-only meaning and enough contrast. Like the well-organised shop, a well-designed document lets readers find what they came for.
key_points: Document design arranges headings, spacing, fonts and emphasis to show structure and help readers find things.
Readers scan the top, headings and left edge first, so put key words at the start of headings and paragraphs.
Headings should be informative, short, parallel and numbered (1, 1.1, 1.1.1), with at most about three levels.
White space groups related items and separates unrelated ones; it is not wasted space.
Use one or two typefaces, monospace for code, about 45 to 75 characters per line, and mostly left alignment.
Use emphasis rarely, and build documents with styles and templates rather than manual formatting.
Accessibility: real heading styles, alt text, no meaning by colour alone, and contrast of at least 4.5:1 for body text.
lessons.tip: Before writing a long report, set up your Heading 1, Heading 2, Body and Caption styles in the template. Then you never format by hand, and your table of contents builds itself.
lessons.task: Take one page of a lab sheet, notice or old assignment that looks crowded. Redesign it on paper or in a word processor: add informative headings, break paragraphs, number steps and add white space. Ask a friend which version they could find information in faster.

quiz.q: Which heading is most informative?
quiz.explain: It tells the reader exactly what the section covers, so they can decide quickly whether to read it.

quiz.q: What is a commonly recommended line length for body text?
options: As wide as the screen allows
quiz.explain: Lines of roughly 45 to 75 characters are comfortable; very long or very short lines tire readers.

quiz.q: Why should you use heading styles instead of just making text bold and large?
options: Bold text is not allowed in reports
Styles change the language of the text
Styles keep formatting consistent, build tables of contents and help screen readers navigate
quiz.explain: Real heading styles carry structure that software and assistive tools can use.

quiz.q: According to WCAG AA, what is the minimum contrast ratio for normal body text?
quiz.explain: WCAG AA requires at least 4.5:1 for normal-size text.

quiz.q: Why should you not say only 'the failed tests are shown in red'?
options: Red is never used in technical documents
Readers with colour blindness may not tell red from other colours, so add labels or symbols
quiz.explain: Meaning should not rely on colour alone; labels or symbols make it accessible.

lessons.title: Figures and Tables
lessons.content:
Try describing the Dhaka metro rail route in words only: 'The line starts at Uttara North, then goes to Uttara Centre, then Uttara South, then Pallabi...' By the fifth station, your listener is lost. Now show them the route map on the station wall: a coloured line with dots and names. They understand it in seconds. Some information is naturally visual or naturally tabular, and forcing it into paragraphs makes the reader work much harder. This lesson is about choosing between text, tables, charts and diagrams, and making each one clear and honest.

What figures and tables are: In technical documents, a table arranges information in rows and columns. Everything else that is visual, such as charts, graphs, diagrams, flowcharts, photographs, screenshots, maps and drawings, is usually called a figure. Figures and tables are not decorations added to make the document look scientific. They are part of the content and must earn their place by helping the reader understand something faster or better than words alone.

Choosing text, table, chart or diagram: Use text for a few numbers or a simple point: 'Response time fell from 2.4 to 0.9 seconds' needs no chart. Use a table when the reader needs exact values or must compare several items across several properties, such as specifications of four laptops. Use a chart when the shape of the data matters more than exact values: a trend over time, a comparison of sizes, a relationship between two variables. Use a diagram to show structure or process: system architecture, network topology, a flowchart of an algorithm, the parts of a device. A useful question: what do I want the reader to notice? Exact numbers suggest a table; a pattern suggests a chart; how parts connect suggests a diagram.

Designing tables: A good table has a numbered caption, clear column headings with units ('Latency (ms)', not just 'Latency'), and a logical row order, for example sorted by value or grouped by category. Align numbers on the right or on the decimal point so they can be compared at a glance, and use the same number of decimal places in a column. Keep lines minimal: a few horizontal rules at the top, below the header and at the bottom are often enough; a full grid of heavy lines makes tables look busy. If a table is long, consider whether the reader needs all the rows or whether a summary plus an appendix would serve them better.

Bar charts: Bar charts compare quantities across categories: number of complaints per district, sales per month, accuracy of five models. Bars should start at zero, because readers judge bars by their length. Sort bars by value unless the categories have a natural order (like months). Horizontal bars work well when category names are long. Avoid 3D bars; the extra depth makes values harder to read and adds nothing.

Line charts: Line charts show how something changes over a continuous variable, most often time: daily active users over a year, temperature through a day, training loss over epochs. The horizontal axis is usually time. Lines suggest continuity, so do not connect categories that have no order. Unlike bar charts, line charts do not always need to start at zero, because the reader is looking at change and shape, but say clearly where the axis starts and do not exaggerate small changes. Use a few lines at most; a chart with eight overlapping lines in similar colours is unreadable.

Scatter plots and pie charts: Scatter plots show the relationship between two numeric variables, one point per item, for example file size against upload time for 200 uploads. They reveal patterns like a rising trend or clusters, and outliers. Pie charts show parts of a whole, but people judge angles and areas poorly, so pies work only with a few slices (around five or fewer) that add up to 100 percent and differ clearly. If you want readers to compare slices precisely, a bar chart is almost always better.

Showing spread and uncertainty: An average alone can hide a lot. If two versions of an app both average 1.5 seconds to load, but one ranges from 1.4 to 1.6 seconds and the other from 0.5 to 6 seconds, users experience them very differently. Charts can show this with error bars (a line above and below each bar or point showing, for example, the standard deviation or a confidence interval), with box plots that show the median, quartiles and outliers, or simply by plotting all the individual points when there are not too many. Whatever you show, say in the caption what the error bars mean and how many measurements each value is based on, for example 'Mean of 30 runs; bars show one standard deviation'.

Labels and units: Every chart needs a title or caption saying what it shows, labelled axes with units ('Download speed (Mbps)', 'Time (days)'), readable tick marks and a legend if there is more than one data series. Better still, label lines directly at their ends instead of using a separate legend, so readers do not have to look back and forth. Use fonts large enough to read when the figure is printed at its final size; many student reports shrink screenshots of charts until the axis labels become unreadable.

Captions and numbering: Number figures and tables separately and in order of appearance: Figure 1, Figure 2, and Table 1, Table 2. In many technical styles, including IEEE, table captions go above the table and figure captions go below the figure. A caption should be informative: 'Figure 3: Average page load time before and after caching, measured over 1,000 requests' says much more than 'Figure 3: Results'. If you use a figure from another source, credit it in the caption and cite it in the references, as lesson 22 explains.

Referring to figures in the text: Every figure and table must be mentioned in the text, ideally before it appears, and the text should tell the reader what to notice: 'As Figure 3 shows, caching cut load time by more than half.' Do not just write 'See Figure 3' and leave the reader to guess the point. Place figures and tables close to where they are discussed. A figure that is never mentioned in the text is a sign that it either does not belong or that the discussion is missing.

Honest visuals, the truncated axis: The most common way charts mislead is a bar chart whose vertical axis does not start at zero. Worked example: two internet providers have average speeds of 48 Mbps and 52 Mbps. If the axis starts at 45, the bars have heights of 3 and 7 units, so the second bar looks about 2.33 times as tall. The real ratio is 52 divided by 48, about 1.08, meaning only 8.3 percent faster. Edward Tufte called the ratio between the size of an effect shown in a graphic and its size in the data the lie factor. Here the graphic shows a 133 percent difference (from 3 to 7) for an 8.3 percent difference in data, a lie factor of 16. A responsible writer starts the bars at zero, or uses a dot or line chart and clearly marks where the axis begins.

Other ways to mislead: Using area or volume to show a one-dimensional quantity: doubling both the width and height of an icon to show doubled sales makes it look four times bigger. Choosing a convenient time window that hides an inconvenient trend. Using different scales on two charts placed side by side. Removing outliers or failed test runs without saying so. Showing averages without spread when the variation is large. Even when not intentional, these mistakes damage trust. Honest figures show the data fairly, state their limits and let readers judge.

Diagrams and screenshots: Diagrams such as architecture diagrams, network diagrams and flowcharts should use consistent shapes and arrows, with a short legend if shapes mean different things. Keep them simple: show the components and connections relevant to the point, not every detail of the system. Standard notations such as UML or standard flowchart symbols help technical readers (Software Engineering, deep-cse-4-4, covers UML). Screenshots are excellent in user documentation, but crop them to the relevant part, highlight the button or field you refer to, hide personal data such as phone numbers or balances, and update them when the interface changes.

Colour in figures: Use colour to group or highlight, not to decorate. Choose colours that remain distinguishable for colour-blind readers; avoid relying on red versus green alone, and consider varying shape or line style too. Check that the figure still works when printed in black and white, since many reports are still printed. Keep colour meaning consistent across all figures: if the old system is grey and the new system is blue in Figure 2, keep that in Figure 5.

Real-life example 1, a dengue report: Suppose a student project analyses weekly dengue hospital admissions in Dhaka over a year. A table of 52 weekly numbers is hard to read; the reader cannot see the seasonal peak. A line chart with weeks on the horizontal axis and admissions on the vertical axis shows the monsoon rise and fall at a glance. A caption states the data source and the period. A short sentence in the text points out the key pattern: admissions rise sharply after the start of the monsoon and peak several weeks later. The exact weekly numbers go in an appendix table for readers who need them.

Real-life example 2, comparing cloud plans: A startup in Chattogram must choose between three hosting plans. The writer first tried a paragraph listing prices, storage, bandwidth and support for each, and the manager got confused. A table with plans as columns and properties as rows, units in the row labels and the recommended plan highlighted with a bold heading and a short note made the comparison instant. A bar chart would have been the wrong choice here because the manager needed exact values across several properties.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Charts used where one sentence would do. Missing axis labels or units. Unreadable small fonts. Bar charts not starting at zero. Pie charts with ten slices. 3D effects. Figures never mentioned in the text, or mentioned with no explanation. Uncredited figures copied from the internet. Exams often ask you to choose the best visual for given data, to list the elements of a good table or graph, to spot what is misleading in a chart, or to explain caption and numbering conventions.

Recap: Use figures and tables when they help the reader more than words. Tables give exact values and comparisons; bar charts compare categories; line charts show change over time; scatter plots show relationships; pies show a few parts of a whole; diagrams show structure and process. Label everything with units, number and caption every visual, refer to it in the text and say what to notice. Keep visuals honest: start bars at zero, avoid distorted areas and selective data, and credit your sources. Like the metro map, a good visual turns a confusing description into instant understanding.
key_points: Tables give exact values and multi-property comparisons; figures (charts, diagrams, screenshots) show patterns and structure.
Choose by what the reader should notice: exact numbers (table), pattern (chart), how parts connect (diagram).
Bar charts compare categories and must start at zero; line charts show change over time; scatter plots show relationships.
Pie charts only for a few parts of a whole; avoid 3D effects.
Label axes with units, number figures and tables separately, and write informative captions (IEEE: table caption above, figure caption below).
Mention every figure in the text and say what to notice.
Truncated axes, distorted areas and selective data mislead; Tufte's lie factor compares the effect shown to the effect in the data.
lessons.tip: For every figure, write one sentence that starts with 'This figure shows that...'. If you cannot finish it, the figure has no clear point yet.
lessons.task: Record something simple for one week, such as daily minutes spent on your phone or daily load-shedding hours. Present it once as a table and once as a chart with proper title, axis labels, units and caption. Decide which one makes the pattern clearer and write one sentence explaining why.

quiz.q: Which visual is best for showing daily active users over a year?
quiz.explain: Line charts show change over a continuous variable like time.

quiz.q: Two providers average 48 and 52 Mbps. A bar chart's axis starts at 45. Roughly how many times taller does the second bar look?
quiz.explain: Bar heights are 3 and 7 units above 45, so 7/3 is about 2.33, even though the real difference is only about 8 percent.

quiz.q: In IEEE style, where do figure captions usually go?
options: At the end of the document
quiz.explain: In IEEE style, figure captions go below figures and table captions go above tables.

quiz.q: When is a table better than a chart?
options: When you want to show a trend at a glance
When there are only two numbers
When you want a decorative page
When the reader needs exact values across several properties
quiz.explain: Tables let readers look up and compare exact values, like plan prices and limits.

quiz.q: What is wrong with writing only 'See Figure 3' in the text?
options: It does not tell the reader what to notice in the figure
The figure number must be in words
quiz.explain: Good text points out the key pattern, such as 'Figure 3 shows that caching cut load time by more than half'.

lessons.title: Emails and Workplace Messages
lessons.content:
Your teacher receives 60 emails a day. One of them has the subject 'Hi' and begins: 'Sir, I am a student of yours, I have a problem, please help.' Another has the subject 'CSE 3201 Section B: request to resubmit Lab 4 by Sunday' and begins: 'Dear Sir, could I resubmit Lab 4 by Sunday 14 April? My file was corrupted during upload on Thursday; I have attached the error screenshot.' Which one gets a quick, helpful answer? Emails and chat messages are the technical writing you will do most often in your life, probably several times a day. Each one is small, but together they decide how people see you at university and at work.

What workplace messages are: Workplace messages include emails, chat messages on tools like Slack, Microsoft Teams or WhatsApp groups, short memos, meeting notes, bug reports and status updates. They share a few features: they are short, the reader is busy and reading many others, and the reader usually needs to do something: answer, decide, fix, attend or approve. So everything you learned about audience, purpose, plain language and BLUF applies here in a concentrated form.

The subject line: The subject line is the headline that decides whether, when and how carefully your email gets opened. A good subject line is specific and tells the reader what the email is about and, ideally, what you need. Weak: 'Hello', 'Problem', 'Urgent!!!', 'Assignment'. Strong: 'CSE 3201 Lab 4: request to resubmit by 14 April', 'Server outage 10:15-10:40 today: cause and fix', 'Approval needed: BDT 25,000 for test devices by Thursday'. Some teams use prefixes like [Action], [FYI] or [Decision needed]. Keep subject lines to roughly ten words so they are not cut off on phones.

Bottom line up front: Start the body with your main point or request, not with background. A busy reader should know within the first two lines what you want. Then give only the context needed to act. Compare: 'I was working on the module last week and found that when users have a slow connection, the image upload sometimes fails, and after investigating...' with 'Can we raise the upload timeout from 10 to 30 seconds? On slow connections, about 1 in 8 image uploads fail at 10 seconds.' The second version asks first and supports the request with one precise fact.

One clear ask: Many emails fail because the request is vague or hidden. Make the action explicit: what exactly you need, from whom, and by when. 'Let me know your thoughts' is vague. 'Please confirm by Wednesday 5 pm whether we can use Lab 3 on Saturday' is clear. If you have several requests, number them so the reader can answer each one: '1. Can we use Lab 3? 2. Can we keep the projector until 6 pm?' If an email has two unrelated topics, consider sending two emails with separate subject lines, so each can be answered and found later.

Structure of a good email: A simple pattern works for most emails: a greeting; the main point or request in the first sentence or two; necessary details or context in short paragraphs or a short list; the next step or deadline; a polite closing and your name, with role or student ID if the reader might not know you. Keep paragraphs short, two to four sentences, because many emails are read on phones. Mention attachments in the text ('I have attached the error screenshot') and check that they are actually attached before sending.

Tone and politeness: Email has no facial expression or tone of voice, so messages can sound colder or angrier than you intended. Be polite but not grovelling. 'Could you please...' and 'Thank you for your help' are good; long chains of 'kindly', 'humbly' and 'esteemed' are unnecessary and can sound unnatural to international readers. Avoid all capitals (it reads as shouting), many exclamation marks, sarcasm and blame. If you are upset, write the draft, wait an hour, and reread it before sending. Match the formality to the relationship: a first email to a teacher or a client is more formal than a message to a teammate.

Worked example, emailing a teacher: A weak email: Subject: 'Sir'. Body: 'Sir I could not attend the quiz due to some problem. Please give me another chance. Rahim.' Problems: no course, no section, no ID, vague reason, no proposed solution. A better email: Subject: 'CSE 2105 Section A: missed Quiz 2 on 3 March (medical)'. Body: 'Dear Dr. Hasan, I missed Quiz 2 on 3 March because I was admitted to hospital with dengue from 2 to 5 March. I have attached the discharge certificate. Would it be possible to take a make-up quiz, or should I follow another process? I am available any day next week after 2 pm. Thank you for considering my request. Best regards, Rahim Uddin, ID 2021-1-60-045'. The teacher can act immediately without asking anything.

Memos and formal letters: A memo is a short internal document, traditionally with To, From, Date and Subject lines at the top, used for announcements, policies and short reports inside an organisation. Today most memos travel as emails, but the structure is the same: purpose first, then details, then action required. Formal letters, still used for official applications, recommendation requests and communication with government offices in Bangladesh, follow a fixed layout with sender address, date, recipient address, subject, salutation, body and signature. The writing advice does not change: state the purpose in the first paragraph and keep the body short and specific.

To, Cc, Bcc and reply-all: Put people who must act in the To field. Use Cc (carbon copy) for people who need to be informed but not act, such as your supervisor on an email to a vendor. Use Bcc (blind carbon copy) when sending to many people who should not see each other's addresses, such as an announcement to all workshop participants; this protects their privacy. Use reply-all only when everyone on the thread needs your reply. A 'Thanks!' sent to 80 people wastes 80 people's attention.

Follow-ups: Sometimes you get no answer. Wait a reasonable time, perhaps two or three working days for a non-urgent email, then reply to your own email so the history stays together: 'Dear Sir, I am following up on my request below about the make-up quiz. Please let me know if you need any other documents.' Do not send the same email five times in a day, and do not switch to calling the teacher's personal phone unless they have invited it.

Chat messages: Chat is faster and more informal than email, but clarity still matters. Do not send 'Hi' and wait for a reply before asking your question; send the full question in one message so the other person can answer when they see it. Use threads to keep conversations on topic. Put the important part first: 'Blocked: staging server is down since 11:00, cannot test payments' is better than six messages building up to it. Remember that chat messages in work tools are often stored and searchable, so write as if your manager might read them later.

Safety and privacy in messages: Never send passwords, OTPs or full card numbers by email or chat; legitimate services do not ask for them, and messages can be forwarded or leaked. Check the To field before sending, because email programs autocomplete names and a confidential file can easily go to the wrong 'Rahman'. Be careful with large attachments and sensitive data; share them through your organisation's approved storage with access control instead. And remember that anything you write in a work message may be read by others later, including in disputes.

Asking a good technical question: When you ask a teammate, a teacher or an online forum for help with a bug, a good question saves everyone time. Include: what you are trying to do; what you expected to happen; what actually happened, including the exact error message (copied as text, not a blurry photo of the screen); what you have already tried; and the relevant environment details such as language version, operating system and library versions. If possible, share a minimal reproducible example: the smallest piece of code that still shows the problem. Often, while building that minimal example, you find the bug yourself.

Bug reports: A bug report is a structured message for developers. A typical format: a short, specific title ('Login fails with correct password on Android 12'); steps to reproduce, numbered; expected result; actual result; environment (device, OS version, app version); frequency (every time, or 3 out of 10 tries); and evidence such as screenshots or logs. One bug per report. Avoid emotion and blame ('This stupid login is broken again') and stick to observable facts. Software Testing and QA (deep-cse-5-8) covers bug tracking in depth.

Meeting notes and action items: After a meeting, someone should send short notes: date, attendees, decisions made, and action items. Each action item needs three parts: the action, the owner, and the deadline. 'Fix the login bug' is weak. 'Nadia: fix the Android 12 login bug and deploy to staging by Tuesday 16 April' is strong. Without an owner and a deadline, actions tend to be forgotten, and everyone remembers the meeting differently. Notes do not need to record who said every sentence; they record what was decided and who does what next.

Real-life example 1, a client update at a Dhaka software firm: A project manager must tell a garments factory client that a feature will be late. Her first draft opens with three paragraphs about technical difficulties. She rewrites it: subject 'Inventory module: delivery moves from 10 May to 20 May'. First line: the new date and the reason in one sentence. Then what is already working, what the client can use now, and what she needs from them (sample data by 5 May). The client replies within an hour, accepting the new date. Clarity and honesty in a difficult message preserved trust.

Real-life example 2, the WhatsApp group project: Four students share a group chat for their database course project. Messages like 'kal meet?' and 'ki obostha' lead to confusion about who is doing what. One member starts posting a short weekly summary: decisions (we use MySQL, not MongoDB), tasks with owners and dates (Tania: ER diagram by Sunday; Joy: login page by Tuesday), and open questions. Within a week, the project runs more smoothly. The summary is a tiny technical document doing a big job.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Vague subject lines. Burying the request at the end. No deadline or owner. Too informal or too flowery for the reader. Reply-all abuse. Sending 'Hi' and waiting. Bug reports with no steps or versions. Exams often ask you to write an email or memo for a scenario, to improve a poorly written email, to list the parts of a good bug report, or to explain Cc, Bcc and professional email etiquette.

Recap: Workplace messages are short documents for busy readers who need to act. Write specific subject lines. Put the main point or request first. Make one clear ask with a deadline. Use a simple structure, short paragraphs and a polite, natural tone. Use To, Cc, Bcc and reply-all carefully. Follow up patiently. In chat, send complete messages. Ask technical questions with expected and actual results, exact errors and what you tried. End meetings with decisions and action items that have owners and deadlines. Done well, your messages make people want to work with you.
key_points: Workplace messages are short documents for busy readers who usually need to act.
Subject lines should be specific (course, topic, request, date), roughly ten words or fewer.
Put the main point or request first (BLUF), make one clear ask, and give a deadline.
Be polite and natural; avoid all caps, sarcasm and excessive 'kindly' or 'esteemed'.
Use To for people who act, Cc to inform, Bcc to protect addresses, and reply-all only when everyone needs it.
Good technical questions and bug reports give steps, expected vs actual results, exact errors, environment and what you tried.
Meeting notes record decisions and action items, each with an owner and a deadline.
lessons.tip: Before you press Send, read only the subject line and the first two sentences. If the reader would not know what you want from those alone, rewrite the opening.
lessons.task: Write an email to a course teacher asking to change your lab group, using a specific subject line, a request in the first sentence, the reason in one or two sentences, and your ID. Then rewrite one recent WhatsApp or Messenger question you sent so it could be answered without any follow-up questions.

quiz.q: Which subject line is best?
options: CSE 3201 Lab 4: request to resubmit by 14 April
quiz.explain: It names the course, the topic, the request and the date, so the reader knows what to expect.

quiz.q: Where should the main request usually go in a workplace email?
options: In the first one or two sentences
At the very end, after the background
quiz.explain: Bottom line up front lets busy readers see immediately what you need.

quiz.q: When should you use Bcc?
options: To hide that your manager is reading
For people who must act on the email
When sending to many people who should not see each other's addresses
quiz.explain: Bcc protects recipients' privacy, for example in announcements to a large group.

quiz.q: What makes an action item complete in meeting notes?
options: It is written in capital letters
It has an action, an owner and a deadline
quiz.explain: Without an owner and a deadline, action items tend to be forgotten.

quiz.q: Which belongs in a good bug report?
options: Steps to reproduce, expected result, actual result and environment details
Several unrelated bugs in one report
quiz.explain: These details let a developer reproduce and fix the problem; one bug per report keeps it trackable.

lessons.title: Definitions and Descriptions
lessons.content:
Your little cousin asks, 'What is a router?' If you say 'It's a networking device', she is no wiser; a phone is also a networking device. If you say 'It's the box with blinking lights that gives us Wi-Fi', she now knows which object you mean, but not what it does. If you say 'A router is a networking device that forwards data between different networks, for example between your home Wi-Fi and the internet', she has a real definition. Defining terms and describing objects and processes are basic building blocks of technical writing. Reports, manuals, specifications and theses are full of them, and a weak definition can confuse an entire document.

Why definitions matter: Readers cannot understand a sentence if they do not understand its key words. In technical fields, everyday words often have special meanings: 'bug', 'cache', 'thread', 'shell', 'cookie'. Other terms are completely new to lay readers: 'latency', 'encryption', 'API'. And sometimes even experts disagree about where a term's boundaries lie: what exactly counts as a 'user', a 'transaction' or an 'active account' in your system? A clear definition fixes the meaning for this document, so writer and reader are talking about the same thing.

Parenthetical definitions: The lightest kind of definition is a short explanation in brackets or after a comma, right where the term first appears. 'The app uses two-factor authentication (a second check, such as a code sent to your phone, in addition to your password).' 'Latency, the time a request takes to travel to the server and back, rose to 300 ms.' Parenthetical definitions are ideal when most readers know the term but some may not; they help beginners without slowing experts much.

Sentence definitions: A formal sentence definition has three parts: the term, the class (the general group it belongs to) and the distinguishing features (what makes it different from other members of that class). This pattern goes back to classical logic, where it was called genus and differentia. Example: 'A router (term) is a networking device (class) that forwards data packets between different networks (distinguishing features).' 'A compiler (term) is a program (class) that translates source code written in a high-level language into machine code before the program runs (distinguishing features).' The last part, 'before the program runs', separates a compiler from an interpreter.

Worked check of a sentence definition: Test your definition with two questions. First, is the class right and not too broad? 'A router is a thing that...' fails because 'thing' tells the reader nothing. Second, do the distinguishing features exclude everything else in the class? 'A router is a networking device that connects computers' fails, because a switch also connects computers. Add the real difference: routers forward between different networks using network addresses such as IP addresses, while a switch connects devices within the same local network. Also avoid circular definitions that use the term to define itself: 'Encryption is the process of encrypting data' teaches nothing. Write instead: 'Encryption is the process of converting readable data into a scrambled form that only someone with the right key can turn back into readable data.'

Extended definitions: Sometimes a sentence is not enough, especially for important or complex terms in a report or for lay readers. An extended definition starts with a sentence definition and then develops it with one or more methods: examples ('Popular cloud services include Google Drive and Dropbox'); comparison and contrast ('Unlike RAM, storage keeps data when the power is off'); analogy ('A firewall is like the security guard at a building's gate, checking who may enter'); negation, saying what it is not ('Machine learning is not a program that thinks like a human; it is a method for finding patterns in data'); parts ('A URL has a scheme, a domain and a path'); process ('Here is what happens when you type a URL'); history or origin of the word; and visuals such as a diagram. A good extended definition may be one paragraph or a full section.

Operational definitions: In reports and research, you often need to define a term by how it is measured or decided in your project. This is an operational definition. 'Active user' could mean many things; your report might say 'In this report, an active user is someone who opened the app at least once in the past 30 days.' 'Slow page' might mean 'a page that takes more than 3 seconds to fully load on a 4G connection, measured by our test script'. Operational definitions make results repeatable and comparable. Without them, two teams may report very different numbers about the 'same' thing.

Where to put definitions: Define a term the first time it appears. For a document with many terms, add a glossary, an alphabetical list of terms and definitions, usually at the start of a specification or the end of a manual or thesis. In a report for mixed readers, put essential definitions in the text and optional ones in the glossary. Do not define terms your readers obviously know; defining 'computer' for software engineers wastes their time and can feel insulting.

What a technical description is: A technical description explains what something is like: its parts, appearance, function or how it works. There are two main kinds. A mechanism description describes an object or system: a device, a machine, a piece of software, a network setup. A process description explains how something happens, step by step: how a payment is processed, how rain forms, how a compiler works. Descriptions inform; they do not ask the reader to do anything. That is the key difference from instructions (lesson 13), which tell the reader what to do.

Mechanism descriptions: A classic structure has three parts. Introduction: define the object, state its purpose, give an overall picture (size, shape, main material or platform), and list its main parts. Part-by-part description: describe each part in a logical order, such as top to bottom, outside to inside, or the order in which data flows; for each part say what it is, what it looks like or what it is made of, and what it does. Conclusion: explain how the parts work together in one cycle of operation, and perhaps mention variations or limitations. A labelled diagram is almost always helpful.

Worked mechanism description, a home Wi-Fi router: Introduction: 'A home Wi-Fi router is a small networking device that connects the devices in a home to each other and to the internet. A typical one is about the size of a book, with external antennas, indicator lights and several ports at the back. Its main parts are the WAN port, the LAN ports, the wireless radio with antennas, and the processor with memory and firmware.' Part by part: 'The WAN port connects to the internet provider's line. The LAN ports connect wired devices such as a desktop computer. The wireless radio sends and receives data over Wi-Fi, often on the 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz bands. The processor runs the firmware, which decides where each packet should go.' Conclusion: 'When a phone requests a web page, the request travels over Wi-Fi to the router, the router forwards it through the WAN port to the internet, and the reply returns the same way to the phone.'

Process descriptions: A process description also has three parts. Introduction: name the process, explain its purpose and when or where it happens, and give an overview of the main stages. Step-by-step description: describe each stage in chronological order, explaining what happens, what causes it, and what each stage produces for the next. Conclusion: summarise the process, the result and perhaps how long it takes or what can go wrong. Process descriptions use the third person and present tense ('the server checks the code'), not imperatives ('check the code'), because the reader is learning how it works, not doing it.

Worked process description, OTP login: 'One-time password (OTP) login lets a user prove they own a phone number without remembering a password. The process has four stages. First, the user enters their phone number, and the app sends it to the server. Second, the server generates a random code, typically six digits, stores it with an expiry time of a few minutes, and sends it to the phone by SMS. Third, the user types the code into the app, which sends it back to the server. Fourth, the server compares the code with the stored one; if it matches and has not expired, the server marks the user as logged in and deletes the code so it cannot be reused. If the code is wrong or expired, the login fails and the user can request a new code.' Notice the overview, the numbered stages and the explanation of what happens on failure.

Real-life example 1, a glossary for a hospital app: A team building an appointment app for a hospital in Rajshahi writes a requirements document read by doctors, administrators and developers. Words like 'appointment', 'visit', 'slot' and 'booking' were being used loosely, causing arguments about features.
