They wrote a glossary: 'Slot: a 15-minute time period in a doctor's schedule that can hold one appointment. Appointment: a slot reserved for a specific patient. Visit: an appointment that the patient actually attended.' With these operational definitions, reports like 'number of visits per day' meant the same thing to everyone.

Real-life example 2, explaining mobile banking to new users: An NGO training programme in a rural area needs to explain to farmers what a mobile financial service account is. A dictionary-style sentence definition alone did not work. The trainers used an extended definition: a simple sentence definition, an analogy ('it is like a small bank account that lives inside your phone number'), a negation ('you do not need a smartphone; a basic phone works with a menu code'), and a process description of sending money, with pictures. The farmers understood not only the term but how to use the service safely.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Circular definitions. Classes that are too broad ('a thing', 'a process'). Distinguishing features that do not distinguish. Defining terms too late, after using them many times. Mixing instructions into a description. Describing parts in random order. Exams often ask you to write a sentence definition and identify its parts, to expand a definition using specific methods, to write a mechanism or process description of a familiar object, or to explain the difference between a description and instructions.

Recap: Definitions fix the meaning of key terms for your reader. Use parenthetical definitions for quick help, sentence definitions (term, class, distinguishing features) for precision, extended definitions for important or difficult terms, and operational definitions for anything you measure. Avoid circular and overbroad definitions, and use a glossary for many terms. Mechanism descriptions explain what something is and its parts; process descriptions explain how something happens in stages. Both follow an introduction, a detailed middle and a conclusion. With good definitions and descriptions, your cousin finally knows what a router is.
key_points: Definitions fix the meaning of key terms so writer and reader mean the same thing.
Parenthetical definitions give quick help in brackets where a term first appears.
A sentence definition has term + class + distinguishing features; avoid circular or too-broad definitions.
Extended definitions add examples, comparison, analogy, negation, parts, process, history or visuals.
Operational definitions say how a term is measured in your project (e.g. active user = opened the app in the past 30 days).
Mechanism descriptions: introduction with purpose and main parts, part-by-part detail, then how the parts work together.
Process descriptions explain stages in time order in third person present tense; instructions instead tell the reader what to do.
lessons.tip: Test every sentence definition by asking: could anything else in the same class fit these features? If yes, add the feature that rules it out.
lessons.task: Write a sentence definition and a five-sentence extended definition of a term from your course (for example cache, compiler or firewall) for a reader who is not a CSE student. Then write a short process description of something you know well, like how a bKash Send Money transaction goes from your phone to the receiver.

quiz.q: What are the three parts of a formal sentence definition?
quiz.explain: A sentence definition places the term in a class and then states what makes it different from others in that class.

quiz.q: Why is 'A router is a networking device that connects computers' a weak definition?
options: Its distinguishing feature also fits other devices such as switches
quiz.explain: Good distinguishing features exclude other members of the class; routers forward between different networks.

quiz.q: Which is an operational definition?
options: A user is a person who uses something.
In this report, an active user is someone who opened the app at least once in the past 30 days.
Users are very important for apps.
A user is like a customer in a shop.
quiz.explain: It defines the term by exactly how it is measured in the project, making results repeatable.

quiz.q: How does a process description differ from instructions?
options: Process descriptions use numbered steps; instructions never do
A process description explains how something happens, while instructions tell the reader what to do
quiz.explain: Descriptions inform in third person; instructions use imperatives for the reader to act.

quiz.q: What usually comes in the introduction of a mechanism description?
options: The definition, purpose, overall picture and list of main parts
Only the price of the device
quiz.explain: The introduction orients the reader before the part-by-part description.

lessons.title: Instructions and Procedures
lessons.content:
Remember assembling a new table fan or a ready-made shelf? The box contains 14 pieces, 20 screws of three sizes and a folded sheet of instructions. Step 4 says 'Attach part C to part B' but the picture shows the part upside down, and the screws are not named. Two hours later, you have one screw left over and the shelf wobbles. Bad instructions waste time, cause damage and sometimes cause injuries. Good instructions are almost invisible: you just follow them and the thing works. Instructions are probably the most common kind of technical document, and writing them well is a precise skill.

What instructions are: Instructions tell a reader how to carry out a task, step by step. They are action-oriented: the reader reads a step, does it, checks the result, and moves to the next. Installation guides, lab procedures, setup guides for an app, standard operating procedures (SOPs) in a company, recipe-like steps in a README and the steps on a bKash screen are all instructions. Their single goal is that the reader completes the task correctly and safely, ideally on the first attempt.

When you need written instructions: Write instructions when a task has several steps, when steps must happen in a specific order, when mistakes are costly or dangerous, when many people must do the task the same way, or when the task is done rarely so nobody remembers it. Examples: setting up the lab network, restoring a database backup, onboarding a new team member, a monthly server patch. If a task has one obvious step, a sentence is enough; a full procedure would be overkill.

Analysing the task first: Before writing, do the task yourself and record every action, including the ones that feel too obvious to mention. Note what the reader must have before starting, where decisions happen ('if you see X, do Y'), what can go wrong, and what the screen or device shows after each step. Then think about the reader: is this someone who has never used a terminal, or a system administrator? For a beginner, 'open a terminal' needs its own explanation; for an administrator it does not.

Structure of a set of instructions: A complete set of instructions usually has: a specific title that names the task ('Installing Python 3 on Windows 11', not 'Python'); a short introduction saying what the task achieves, who it is for and roughly how long it takes; prerequisites, meaning what the reader needs first, such as software versions, accounts, permissions, tools or materials; any safety warnings that apply to the whole task; the numbered steps; the expected final result, so the reader knows they succeeded; and troubleshooting for common problems. Short instructions can drop some parts, but the steps, prerequisites and expected result are almost always needed.

Writing each step: Use the imperative mood, starting with a verb: 'Click Save', 'Enter your phone number', 'Connect the blue cable to port 1'. Put one main action in each step. 'Open the app, log in, go to Settings and turn on notifications' is four steps disguised as one; split it so the reader can keep their place. If a step needs context, put the purpose or condition first: 'To save your changes, click Save' or 'If the green light is off, press the reset button', so the reader knows why or when before acting. Name interface elements exactly as they appear, and highlight them consistently, for example in bold.

Numbering and sub-steps: Number steps when order matters, which is almost always in instructions. Keep the number of top-level steps manageable; if a procedure has 30 steps, group them into stages with headings, such as 'Part A: Prepare the server' and 'Part B: Install the database', each with its own numbered steps. Use sub-steps (a, b, c) for small actions inside a step, but avoid going deeper than one sub-level. Use bullets, not numbers, for options where any one will do: 'Choose one of the following: a USB cable, or Wi-Fi'.

Decisions and branches: Real tasks often branch: Windows users do one thing, Mac users another; if the device shows a red light, the reader must take a different path. Handle branches clearly. For a short branch, use a conditional step: 'If you use Windows, open Command Prompt. If you use macOS, open Terminal.' For long branches, split the instructions into separate sections ('On Windows', 'On macOS') and tell readers at the start which section to follow. For complex decisions, a small table or flowchart works better than nested 'if' sentences. Never make the reader read both paths in full only to discover half of it does not apply.

Showing results and feedback: After important steps, tell the reader what they should see: 'Click Install. A progress bar appears; installation takes about 2 minutes.' 'Run python --version. The terminal shows Python 3.12 or later.' This feedback lets readers confirm they are on track and notice immediately if something went wrong, instead of discovering at step 15 that step 3 failed.

Safety notices: When a step can hurt people, damage equipment or lose data, warn the reader before the step, not after it. Many industries use standard signal words, following standards such as ANSI Z535 in the United States: DANGER for a hazard that will cause death or serious injury if not avoided; WARNING for a hazard that could cause death or serious injury; CAUTION for a hazard that could cause minor or moderate injury; and NOTICE for information about damage to equipment or property, not injury. In software documentation, the most common is a warning about data loss: 'Warning: This command deletes all records in the table. Back up the database first.' Make notices visually distinct, state the hazard, the consequence and how to avoid it, and do not overuse them, or readers will start ignoring them.

Notes and tips: Not every extra piece of information is a warning. Use a 'Note' for helpful information that does not affect safety ('Note: The menu may be named Preferences on older versions') and a 'Tip' for shortcuts or better ways. Keep them short and place them where they are needed. If a note is essential for success, it is probably part of the step itself.

Screenshots and diagrams: Visuals help, especially for software and assembly tasks. A screenshot next to a step shows the reader exactly where to click. Crop it to the relevant part, highlight the important element with a box or arrow, and make sure it matches the current version of the software. For physical tasks, simple line drawings often work better than photos because they remove clutter. Always put the visual next to the step it supports, and never make the visual the only place where essential information appears, because some readers cannot see images and screenshots go out of date.

Troubleshooting: A troubleshooting section anticipates common problems. A table with three columns works well: Problem (what the reader sees), Possible cause, and Solution. For example: 'Problem: pip is not recognised. Cause: Python was installed without adding it to PATH. Solution: rerun the installer and tick Add Python to PATH.' Collect troubleshooting items by watching real users try the instructions and by checking support questions.

Keeping instructions current: Instructions go out of date quickly. A new app version moves a button, a menu gets renamed, a command gains a new option. Outdated instructions are often worse than none, because readers trust them and get stuck. Put a 'last updated' date and the software version the instructions apply to at the top. Assign someone to own each important procedure, and update it whenever the product changes. In software teams, keeping instructions in the same repository as the code (the docs-as-code idea in lesson 15) makes it easier to update both together.

Testing instructions with real users: Instructions are not finished until someone from the target audience has followed them without your help. Sit beside them, give them only the document, and stay silent. Note where they hesitate, misread, skip or ask questions. Each of those moments is a defect in the writing, not in the user. Usability testing, which HCI (deep-cse-5-5) covers in detail, applies directly here. Even one or two test users usually reveal the worst problems.

Worked example, rewriting a lab instruction: Original: 'Next the IP of the PC must be configured properly and the connection to the router should be checked using ping, also make sure the cable is connected.' Rewritten: '1. Connect the PC to port 1 of the router with an Ethernet cable. 2. Open Network Settings on the PC. 3. Set the IP address to 192.168.1.10 and the subnet mask to 255.255.255.0. 4. Open a terminal and run: ping 192.168.1.1. You should see four replies. If you see Request timed out, check that the cable is firmly connected at both ends.' The order now matches the real order (the cable comes first), each step has one action, values are exact, and the expected result and a fix are given.

Real-life example 1, a mobile recharge guide for elderly users: A telecom company wants older customers in Sylhet to recharge their own balance. Its first guide used English menu names, small fonts and long sentences. The redesigned guide is in Bangla with large text, one step per line, a picture of the exact screen for each step, and a final line saying what SMS they will receive when it works. A note tells them what to do if the SMS does not arrive within 5 minutes. The number of calls to the help line about recharging drops noticeably.

Real-life example 2, a deployment runbook: A software team in Dhaka writes a runbook for deploying its app on Thursday nights. Before, only one senior developer could deploy, and every deployment caused a few minutes of panic. The runbook lists prerequisites (access to the server, latest backup confirmed), numbered steps with exact commands, the expected output after each command, a warning before the database migration step, and a rollback procedure if something fails. Now any trained team member can deploy, and the senior developer can take a holiday.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Steps in the wrong order. Several actions in one step. Missing prerequisites. Warnings placed after the dangerous step. Vague verbs like 'configure properly' or 'set up as needed'. Screenshots that do not match the current interface. Never testing the instructions with a real user. Exams often ask you to list the parts of a set of instructions, to rewrite poor instructions, to explain the levels of safety notices, or to write instructions for a simple task like changing a password or making a cup of tea.

Recap: Instructions help a reader complete a task correctly and safely. Analyse the task by doing it yourself. Give a specific title, introduction, prerequisites, numbered steps, expected result and troubleshooting. Write each step in the imperative with one action, put conditions and purposes first, and show what the reader should see. Place safety notices before the hazard using clear signal words. Use visuals next to their steps. Then test with real users and fix every point where they stumble. When instructions are good, nobody notices them; the fan simply works.
key_points: Instructions tell a reader how to complete a task step by step; success on the first attempt is the goal.
Analyse the task by doing it yourself and recording every action, decision and result.
Typical structure: specific title, introduction, prerequisites, numbered steps, expected result, troubleshooting.
Write steps in the imperative, one action per step, with conditions or purposes before the action.
Tell readers what they should see after important steps so they can confirm progress.
Put safety notices before the hazard; signal words: DANGER, WARNING, CAUTION, NOTICE (property damage).
Test instructions with real users from the target audience and fix every hesitation or mistake.
lessons.tip: Hand your instructions to a friend and watch them follow it in silence. Every time they pause or ask 'what now?', you have found a step to rewrite.
lessons.task: Write instructions for changing the Wi-Fi password on your home router or for setting a new screen lock on a phone. Include a title, prerequisites, numbered steps with one action each, what the reader should see, and one troubleshooting tip. Test it on a family member.

quiz.q: Which is the best-written step?
options: The settings should be changed appropriately.
Open the app, log in, go to Settings and turn on notifications.
Notifications can be turned on in Settings if desired by the user.
quiz.explain: It uses the imperative, has one action and names the interface element exactly.

quiz.q: Where should a warning about data loss appear?
options: Before the step that can cause it
After the step that can cause it
quiz.explain: Readers must see the hazard before they act, or the warning is useless.

quiz.q: In standard safety signal words, which is used for damage to equipment or property but not injury?
quiz.explain: NOTICE covers property or equipment damage; the others relate to injury of different severity.

quiz.q: Why should instructions tell the reader what they should see after a step?
options: So the reader can confirm progress and notice problems early
quiz.explain: Feedback lets the reader detect a failed step immediately rather than many steps later.

quiz.q: What is the best way to find problems in a set of instructions?
options: Read them again yourself many times
Watch real users from the target audience follow them without help
quiz.explain: Writers know the task too well; only real users reveal where the instructions fail.

lessons.title: User Manuals and Help Documentation
lessons.content:
Think about a large library like the one at Dhaka University. Some visitors want a guided tour on their first day. Some want to find one specific book right now. Some want to look up a fact in an encyclopedia. Some want to sit and understand a difficult idea deeply. A good library serves all four, with different spaces for each. User documentation for software is the same. A single long manual that tries to serve everyone in one sequence of chapters usually serves nobody well. This lesson is about how modern user documentation is organised, and how to write each part.

What user documentation is: User documentation is everything written to help people use a product: user manuals, getting-started guides, online help, tutorials, FAQs, tooltips, troubleshooting pages, release notes and in-app messages. It is different from developer documentation (READMEs, API references and design documents, covered in lessons 15 and 16), which helps people build or change the product. The user's goal is not to read documentation; it is to get their work done. Documentation succeeds when it gets them back to their work quickly.

How users actually use help: Studies of users and the experience of support teams show a consistent pattern: most users do not read manuals from start to finish before using a product. They start using it, get stuck, and then look for help about one specific problem, often by searching. Many skim, try something, and come back. This is sometimes called the paradox of the active user: people are eager to act and reluctant to read, even when reading first would save time. Good documentation accepts this and is built for searching, scanning and jumping in at any point.

The Diataxis framework: A widely used way to organise documentation is the Diataxis framework, developed by Daniele Procida. It divides documentation into four kinds based on what the reader needs. Tutorials are learning-oriented: they take a beginner by the hand through a complete small project so they gain confidence ('Build your first to-do list app'). How-to guides are task-oriented: they help a user who already knows the basics achieve a specific goal ('How to export your data to Excel'). Reference is information-oriented: it describes the product accurately and completely, like a dictionary ('List of all settings and what they do'). Explanation is understanding-oriented: it discusses concepts, background and reasons ('Why your data syncs only on Wi-Fi'). Mixing these kinds in one page usually makes each one worse.

Why separating the four kinds helps: A tutorial interrupted by long explanations loses the beginner's momentum. A reference page full of chatty tutorial steps becomes hard to scan for the one fact the expert wants. A how-to guide that tries to teach all the concepts becomes too long for the user who just wants to finish the task. When each page has one job, writers know what to include and readers know what to expect. In practice, pages link to each other: a how-to guide can link to the explanation for those who want to know why.

Task-based topics: Within how-to guides, organise around user tasks, not around the product's menus or the internal architecture. Users think 'I want to send money to my brother', not 'I want to learn about the Transaction module'. So titles should be tasks, often starting with a verb or 'How to': 'Send money to another account', 'Change your PIN', 'Download a statement'. Each topic should be self-contained enough to be useful when reached directly from a search, with links to prerequisite topics rather than assuming the user read the previous chapter.

Minimalism: In the late 1980s, John Carroll and colleagues studied how people learned to use computers and found that shorter, action-focused manuals worked better than long, systematic ones. His book The Nurnberg Funnel (1990) described this approach, known as minimalism. Its main ideas: let users act quickly on real tasks instead of reading long introductions; anchor the documentation in tasks users actually want to do; support users in recognising and recovering from errors, because errors are normal; and keep text short, so users can read to do, read to learn or read to find. Minimalism does not mean leaving out necessary information; it means removing everything that does not help the user act.

The classic manual structure: Some products, especially hardware, medical devices and software delivered to organisations, still need a complete printed or PDF manual. A typical structure is: title page with product name and version; table of contents; safety information and conventions (what bold text or a warning icon means); an introduction to the product and its main parts; getting started; task-based chapters; reference chapters; troubleshooting; glossary; and an index. Even inside a single manual, the four kinds of documentation can live in separate chapters, so readers still know where to look.

Getting-started guides: The getting-started guide is often the most read piece of documentation, because every new user meets it. It should get the user to a first success within minutes: install or sign up, do one meaningful thing, see a result. It should not list every feature. A good pattern is: what you need before you start; three to seven steps to the first useful result; what to do next, with links to tutorials and how-to guides. If your product's first success takes 40 steps, the product may need simplifying, not just the guide.

Reference documentation: Reference material must be accurate, complete and consistent. Every setting, field, command or error code should appear, described in the same structure: name, what it does, possible values, default value, and an example. Reference is read by lookup, so use tables, consistent headings and alphabetical or logical order. It can be dry; that is fine. Its virtue is that the user can trust it. Reference is often generated partly from the product itself, such as a list of configuration options, which helps keep it accurate.

FAQs and troubleshooting: Frequently asked questions pages are useful when they really collect frequent questions, drawn from support tickets, search logs and user feedback. They become useless when filled with invented questions that are really marketing ('Why is our app the best?'). Write each question in the user's words and answer it directly in the first sentence. Troubleshooting pages organise problems by symptom, because users know what they see, not what caused it: 'The app says No internet connection even though Wi-Fi is on', followed by possible causes and fixes in order from most likely to least likely.

Error messages as documentation: For many users, the error message is the only documentation they ever read. A good error message says what happened, why if known, and what the user can do next, in plain words, without blaming the user. 'Payment failed: the receiver's number is not registered. Check the number and try again.' is documentation in one line. HCI (deep-cse-5-5) covers error message design in the interface; technical writers often help write and review these messages, and link them to help pages for more detail.

Release notes: Release notes tell users what changed in a new version. Users want to know: what is new that I can use, what was fixed that may have bothered me, and what changed that might affect how I work. Write them for users, not for developers: 'You can now pay electricity bills from the home screen' instead of 'Implemented BillPayService v2 integration'. Group changes into categories like New, Improved and Fixed, and highlight anything that requires the user to act, such as updating settings. Developer-facing changelogs are covered in lesson 16.

Measuring whether documentation works: You can measure documentation, not just hope it helps. Useful signals include: which help pages are viewed most; which searches return no results (these reveal missing topics or wrong words); answers to a 'Was this page helpful?' button; how many support tickets ask questions already answered in the docs, which suggests those pages are hard to find or unclear; and how long new users take to reach their first success. Each signal points to a specific page to improve.

Localisation for Bangladeshi users: Many products in Bangladesh need documentation in Bangla as well as English. Localisation is more than translation. It includes using natural, everyday Bangla rather than stiff literal translation of English sentences; keeping product terms consistent across the app and the help pages (if the button says 'টাকা পাঠান', the help page should not call it 'Send Money' in Bangla text); using local examples, dates, currency (BDT, Taka) and phone number formats; and choosing fonts that render Bangla conjuncts correctly. It also helps to write the English source simply, with short sentences and no idioms, because simple English translates more accurately.

Real-life example 1, a school management app: A Dhaka startup sells an app that schools use to publish results and notices. Its original help was one 60-page PDF manual organised by menu. Teachers rarely opened it and called support instead. The team rebuilt the help: a five-step getting-started guide for new schools; how-to pages titled by task ('Publish exam results', 'Send a notice to one class'); a reference page for every setting; a troubleshooting page built from the 20 most common support calls; and short Bangla versions of the most used tasks. Support calls about basic tasks fell, and teachers began to share links to specific help pages with each other.

Real-life example 2, a farmer advisory app: An app that gives crop advice to farmers sends tips by voice and text. Many users have limited literacy. The documentation team uses minimalism to the extreme: each help item is one short Bangla sentence, a picture and a short voice recording. Help is placed exactly where needed, such as a small question mark next to the field asking for land area, explaining whether to enter bigha or decimal. This shows that documentation does not have to be a manual; it can be embedded in the product where users need it.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Organising help by the product's internal structure instead of user tasks. Mixing tutorial, how-to, reference and explanation on one page. Long introductions before any action. FAQs full of marketing. Release notes written in developer jargon. Translating word for word without localising. Exams often ask you to list types of user documentation, to explain minimalism or the four kinds of documentation, to outline a user manual for a given product, or to rewrite a help topic in task-based form.

Recap: User documentation helps people get their work done and get back to it. Users skim, search and jump in, so build documentation for that. Separate tutorials, how-to guides, reference and explanation, as the Diataxis framework suggests. Organise how-to topics by user tasks, keep them self-contained and title them with verbs. Apply minimalism: action first, real tasks, error recovery, short text. Give new users a fast getting-started path, keep reference accurate, base FAQs and troubleshooting on real questions, write error messages and release notes for users, and localise thoughtfully for Bangla readers. Like a good library, good documentation has the right space for every kind of visitor.
key_points: User documentation helps people use a product and get back to their work; it differs from developer documentation.
Most users skim, search and jump in rather than reading manuals from start to finish.
Diataxis separates tutorials (learning), how-to guides (tasks), reference (information) and explanation (understanding).
Organise how-to topics by user tasks with verb-based titles, each usable on its own from a search.
Minimalism (Carroll): act quickly on real tasks, support error recovery, keep text short.
Getting-started guides lead to a first success within minutes; reference must be accurate, complete and consistent.
Base FAQs and troubleshooting on real questions, write release notes for users, and localise Bangla documentation naturally.
lessons.tip: Before writing any help page, decide which of the four kinds it is: tutorial, how-to, reference or explanation. If you cannot pick one, you are probably trying to write two pages at once.
lessons.task: Pick an app you use daily, such as a ride-sharing or food delivery app. List five real tasks a new user would want to do, write how-to titles for them starting with a verb, and write one complete how-to page for the hardest task in under 150 words.

quiz.q: In the Diataxis framework, which kind of documentation is task-oriented for a user who knows the basics?
quiz.explain: How-to guides help users achieve a specific goal; tutorials are for learning as a beginner.

quiz.q: What is a key idea of minimalism in documentation?
options: Let users act quickly on real tasks and support recovery from errors
Write one long manual in strict order
quiz.explain: Carroll's minimalism focuses on action, real tasks, error recovery and short text.

quiz.q: Which is the best title for a how-to help topic?
quiz.explain: Users search by task, so titles should name the task, usually starting with a verb.

quiz.q: How should troubleshooting pages usually be organised?
options: By the developer who wrote the code
Alphabetically by internal error code only
By symptom, meaning what the user sees
quiz.explain: Users know what they see, not the cause, so organising by symptom helps them find the fix.

quiz.q: Which release note is written for users?
options: You can now pay electricity bills from the home screen
quiz.explain: User-facing release notes describe what users can now do, in plain language.

lessons.title: README Files and Code Comments
lessons.content:
Imagine you inherit a house from a relative. You get the keys, but no one tells you where the main electric switch is, which tap leaks, or why one door must never be locked from inside. You will figure it out eventually, after a few accidents. Software projects are the same. Code tells the computer what to do, but it rarely tells a human why it was written this way, how to run it, or what will break if you change something. README files, comments, docstrings and commit messages are the notes that the previous owner leaves for the next one. Often the next owner is you, six months later, having forgotten everything.

What developer documentation is: Developer documentation helps people who build, run, change or use code: teammates, new contributors, other developers calling your library, your future self, and your teachers when they grade a project. It lives close to the code: a README at the top of the repository, comments and docstrings in the source files, commit messages in version control, and more formal documents such as API references and design documents (lesson 16). The reader is technical but not inside your head.

What a README is for: A README is the front door of a project. It is usually the first file anyone opens, and on platforms like GitHub and GitLab it is displayed automatically on the project's main page. In about a minute, it should answer: What is this project? Is it useful to me? How do I get it running? Where do I go next? A project without a README, or with a README that just says 'My project', forces every visitor to read the code to find out basic facts.

Sections of a good README: A practical README usually contains: the project name and a one or two sentence description of what it does and for whom; optionally a screenshot or short example of it working; requirements (language version, database, operating system); installation steps, numbered, with exact commands; usage, showing the most common way to run or use it, with a small example and its output; configuration, such as environment variables or settings files; how to run the tests; project structure, if it is not obvious; how to contribute, or a link to a CONTRIBUTING file; the licence; and contact or maintainers. Small student projects do not need every section, but name, description, requirements, installation and usage are almost always needed.

Worked README for a student project: 'Bus Seat Booker. A web app that lets students book seats on university buses and shows live seat availability. Requirements: Python 3.11, PostgreSQL 15. Installation: 1. Clone the repository. 2. Run pip install -r requirements.txt. 3. Create a database named busbooker. 4. Copy .env.example to .env and set DATABASE_URL. 5. Run python manage.py migrate. Usage: run python manage.py runserver and open http://localhost:8000. Log in with the demo account shown in .env.example. Tests: run pytest. Team: Nadia (backend), Arif (frontend), Joy (database). Licence: MIT.' A teammate or teacher can run this project in ten minutes without asking anyone.

Other files around the README: Larger projects add a few standard files next to the README. A LICENSE file states the legal terms for using the code; common open-source licences include MIT, Apache 2.0 and the GNU GPL, and without a licence others have no clear permission to reuse your code. A CONTRIBUTING file explains how to report bugs, set up a development environment, follow the coding style and submit changes. A CHANGELOG records changes between versions (lesson 16). An example configuration file such as .env.example shows which settings are needed without exposing real passwords or keys, which must never be committed to the repository.

Markdown basics: Most README files are written in Markdown, a lightweight formatting language created by John Gruber, with input from Aaron Swartz, in 2004. Markdown uses plain text symbols that are readable even before rendering: a line starting with # is a heading (## for a second-level heading); a line starting with - or * is a bullet; 1. starts a numbered list; text between single asterisks is italic and between double asterisks is bold; text in backticks is inline code; a block of lines between triple backticks is a code block; and [text](link) creates a link. Because it is plain text, Markdown works well with version control: changes show up clearly line by line.

Why comments matter, and what they are for: Code says what the program does. Good comments say what the code cannot say: why it does it this way, what assumption it makes, what limitation or trap exists, and where to find more detail. The most important rule: comment the why, not the what. A comment like '// add 1 to i' above 'i = i + 1' adds nothing; anyone who can read code sees that. A comment like '// Retry up to 3 times because the payment gateway sometimes drops the first request after idle periods' explains a decision that would otherwise look strange and might be removed by a future developer.

Good and bad comments: Useful comments include: the reason for a non-obvious decision; a warning ('Do not change this order; the bank API requires amount before account'); a reference to a bug ticket, specification or algorithm source; an explanation of a complex regular expression or formula; and TODO notes with enough context to act on, ideally with a ticket number. Harmful or useless comments include: restating the code; commented-out blocks of old code left 'just in case' (version control already keeps history); comments that are no longer true because the code changed; and long changelogs at the top of files. A wrong comment is worse than no comment, because readers trust it.

Naming as documentation: Often the best way to avoid a comment is to make the code explain itself through names. Compare 'int d; // elapsed time in days' with 'int elapsedDays;'. Compare 'if (u.s == 3)' with 'if (user.status == Status.BLOCKED)'. Good names for variables, functions and classes are a form of technical writing: precise, consistent and in the reader's vocabulary. Extracting a complicated condition into a well-named function such as isEligibleForRefund() documents the rule better than a comment would.

Docstrings and API comments: Many languages have a standard way to document functions, classes and modules in the code itself: docstrings in Python (described in PEP 257), Javadoc comments in Java, KDoc in Kotlin, JSDoc in JavaScript and dartdoc comments in Dart. They are written right above or inside the function and can be extracted by tools to generate reference documentation. A good docstring states what the function does in one sentence, describes each parameter and the return value, lists errors or exceptions it may raise, and may include a short example. Example: 'Calculate the delivery fee for an order. Args: distance_km (float): distance from the restaurant, must be non-negative. Returns: int, the fee in taka. Raises: ValueError if distance_km is negative.'

Commit messages: Every commit in version control should explain the change for someone reading the history later. A widely followed convention: a short summary line of around 50 characters, written in the imperative mood ('Fix crash when phone number has spaces', not 'Fixed stuff' or 'changes'); then a blank line; then, if needed, a body explaining why the change was made and anything a reviewer should know. Some teams follow structured formats such as Conventional Commits, with prefixes like feat: and fix:. Messages like 'update', 'final', 'final2' or 'asdf' make the project history useless when you later need to find when and why a bug was introduced.

Pull request descriptions: When you ask teammates to review and merge code, the pull request description is a small technical document. It should say what the change does, why it is needed (link the issue or ticket), how it was tested, and anything the reviewer should look at closely, such as a risky migration. Screenshots help for user interface changes. A good description shortens review time and reduces misunderstandings.

Docs-as-code: Docs-as-code is the practice of treating documentation like code: writing it in plain-text formats such as Markdown, storing it in the same version control repository as the code, reviewing changes to it through pull requests, and building and publishing it automatically. The big advantage is that code and documentation change together: when a developer changes how a feature works, the reviewer can ask in the same pull request for the docs to be updated. This reduces the most common documentation problem: docs that silently go out of date.

Real-life example 1, the thesis code handover: Sabbir's thesis trained a model to detect fake news in Bangla. After he graduated, his supervisor gave the code to a new student, Mim. There was no README, the data paths were hard-coded to Sabbir's laptop, and comments said things like '# temp fix'. Mim spent three weeks just getting the code to run. When Mim finished her own work, she wrote a README with requirements, the exact dataset version and where to download it, how to train and evaluate, the expected accuracy, and known issues. The next student got the project running in an afternoon.

Real-life example 2, an open-source Bangla library: A developer in Dhaka publishes a small library that converts English digits to Bangla digits and formats Taka amounts. Its README shows the install command, a three-line example with output, and a table of supported functions. Each function has a docstring with an example. Within a few months, other developers use it in their apps and send improvements, partly because they could understand it within a minute of opening the page. Good documentation is often the difference between code that is reused and code that is ignored.

Common mistakes and exam questions: No README, or a README with only the project name. Installation steps that skip a requirement. Comments that repeat the code or have become false. Commented-out code left in the repository. Cryptic names that need comments to explain them. Commit messages like 'update'. Exams and viva questions may ask what a README should contain, the difference between good and bad comments, how to write a commit message, what docstrings are, or why documentation should live with the code.

Recap: Developer documentation helps others, and your future self, understand, run and change code. A README is the front door: what the project is, requirements, installation, usage, tests, contribution and licence. Write it in Markdown. Comment the why, not the what; delete false comments and dead code; let clear names do much of the explaining. Use docstrings for functions and classes. Write commit messages and pull request descriptions that explain what changed and why. Keep docs next to the code so they change together. Like the notes in an inherited house, good developer docs prevent accidents for whoever comes next.
key_points: Developer documentation (README, comments, docstrings, commit messages) helps people build, run and change code.
A README is the project's front door: description, requirements, installation, usage, tests, contribution, licence.
Markdown is a plain-text formatting language (# headings, - bullets, backticks for code) that works well with version control.
Comment the why, not the what; remove false comments and commented-out code.
Clear names for variables and functions are documentation and often remove the need for comments.
Docstrings (e.g. Python PEP 257, Javadoc) describe purpose, parameters, return values, errors and examples.
Commit messages: short imperative summary, blank line, body explaining why; docs-as-code keeps docs and code changing together.
lessons.tip: Before you push any project, clone it into a fresh folder and follow only your README to run it. Every extra step you needed is a line missing from the README.
lessons.task: Write a README for one of your course projects with a description, requirements, numbered installation steps, a usage example and the team members. Then find three comments in your code that only repeat what the code does and replace them with comments that explain why, or delete them.

quiz.q: Which comment is most useful?
options: // Retry up to 3 times because the payment gateway sometimes drops the first request after idle periods
quiz.explain: It explains why the code exists, which the code itself cannot show.

quiz.q: Which sections are almost always needed in a README?
options: Name, description, requirements, installation and usage
A list of every function's internal variables
The full history of every commit
quiz.explain: These let a new reader understand the project and get it running.

quiz.q: Which is the best commit message summary line?
options: Fix crash when phone number has spaces
quiz.explain: It is short, specific and in the imperative mood, so the history explains itself.

quiz.q: What is docs-as-code?
options: Printing code and binding it as a manual
Keeping documentation in plain text in the same repository and review process as the code
quiz.explain: Docs-as-code lets code and documentation be reviewed and updated together.

quiz.q: Why should commented-out blocks of old code usually be deleted?
options: Version control already keeps the history, and dead code confuses readers
quiz.explain: Old code can be recovered from version control; leaving it in the file only adds noise.

lessons.title: API and Design Documentation
lessons.content:
Think of a restaurant menu. You do not need to know how the kitchen works, which cook is on duty or where the rice is stored. The menu tells you what you can order, what each item includes, how much it costs and sometimes how long it takes. If the menu says 'Chicken biryani, BDT 280, serves one' and that is what arrives, you trust the restaurant. An API, or application programming interface, is a menu for software: it lists what other programs can ask for and what they will get back. API documentation is the written menu. If it is wrong or missing, developers cannot order, or they order the wrong thing and the integration breaks.

What API documentation is: API documentation explains how to use an interface that a program exposes to other programs. This might be a web API that a mobile app calls over HTTP, a library of functions in a programming language, or an interface of an operating system or device. Its readers are developers, often from other teams or other companies, who want to integrate quickly and correctly. They are technical, impatient and practical: they want to copy an example, change two values and see it work.

The parts of good API documentation: Strong API documentation usually has: an overview of what the API does and its main concepts; a getting-started or quickstart guide that leads to a first successful call in minutes; authentication instructions, explaining how to get and send keys or tokens; a reference for every endpoint or function; error documentation; information about limits, such as rate limits and maximum sizes; versioning and changelog; and often tutorials or how-to guides for common tasks. These map neatly onto the four kinds of documentation from lesson 14: tutorials, how-to guides, reference and explanation.

Documenting an endpoint: For each endpoint of a web API, the reference should give: the method and path, for example POST /v1/orders; a one-sentence description of what it does; authentication required; path, query and body parameters, each with name, type, whether required, allowed values, default and a description; an example request; an example response with its status code; possible error responses; and notes such as idempotency or rate limits. Consistency matters more than style: if every endpoint follows the same layout, developers learn where to look.

Worked endpoint reference: 'POST /v1/orders. Creates a food order for the logged-in customer. Authentication: Bearer token in the Authorization header. Body parameters: restaurant_id (string, required): the restaurant's ID. items (array, required): each item has menu_item_id (string) and quantity (integer, 1 to 20). delivery_address_id (string, required). note (string, optional, up to 200 characters). Example request body: restaurant_id r_102, items: menu_item_id m_7 with quantity 2, delivery_address_id a_55. Response 201 Created: returns the order with order_id, status pending and total_bdt 560. Errors: 400 Bad Request if quantity is outside 1 to 20; 401 Unauthorized if the token is missing or expired; 404 Not Found if the restaurant does not exist; 409 Conflict if the restaurant is closed.' A developer can now write the call without guessing.

Writing descriptions that help: Each description should say what the endpoint or parameter means for the caller, not repeat its name. 'user_id: the user ID' adds nothing. 'user_id: the ID of the customer placing the order, as returned by POST /v1/users' tells the developer where the value comes from. Start endpoint descriptions with a verb ('Creates', 'Returns', 'Cancels'), mention side effects such as sending an SMS or charging a card, and state units and formats for every value: money in paisa or taka, times in UTC ISO 8601, distances in metres.

Examples first: Developers often skip descriptions and jump straight to examples. So make examples complete, realistic and correct: a full request with headers and body, and the full response, not fragments. Use realistic values rather than 'foo' and 'bar', so readers understand what each field means. Show examples in the languages your users actually use, such as a curl command plus examples in JavaScript, Python or Kotlin. Test every example; a broken example damages trust in the whole documentation. Many teams run their documentation examples automatically as tests.

Documenting errors: Errors are where developers spend most of their debugging time, so document them carefully. For a web API, list the HTTP status codes used and what they mean in your API: 200 OK, 201 Created, 400 Bad Request, 401 Unauthorized, 403 Forbidden, 404 Not Found, 409 Conflict, 429 Too Many Requests, 500 Internal Server Error. Give each specific error a stable code and a clear message in the response body, for example error code ORDER_QUANTITY_INVALID with the message 'quantity must be between 1 and 20'. Explain what the client should do: fix the request, refresh the token, wait and retry, or contact support.

Limits and a worked rate-limit example: Developers must plan around limits, so state them precisely. Suppose the docs say 'Each API key may make 60 requests per minute; extra requests receive 429 Too Many Requests with a Retry-After header in seconds.' A developer who must sync 300 products, one request each, can now calculate that it will take at least 300 / 60 = 5 minutes, and design a queue instead of firing all 300 calls at once and failing. Also document pagination ('results are returned 50 per page; use the next_cursor value to get the next page'), maximum body sizes and timeouts.

OpenAPI and generated reference: Many web APIs describe their endpoints in a machine-readable format called the OpenAPI Specification, formerly known as Swagger. An OpenAPI file, written in YAML or JSON, lists every path, method, parameter, request body, response and error. Tools can turn it into interactive reference pages where developers can try calls in the browser, and can generate client code. This keeps the reference consistent and close to the real API. But generated reference is only a skeleton: humans still need to write good descriptions, examples, getting-started guides and explanations of concepts.

Versioning and semantic versioning: APIs change, and changes can break the programs that depend on them. Documentation must say which version it describes and how versions change. A widely used scheme for libraries is Semantic Versioning, which numbers versions as MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH. Increase PATCH for backward-compatible bug fixes (2.3.1 to 2.3.2), MINOR for new backward-compatible features (2.3.2 to 2.4.0), and MAJOR for incompatible changes that may break existing users (2.4.0 to 3.0.0). Web APIs often put a major version in the path, such as /v1/ and /v2/. When something will be removed, mark it as deprecated in the docs first, with a date and the replacement to use.

Changelogs: A changelog is a file or page listing notable changes in each version, newest first, for developers who depend on the project. A popular convention, Keep a Changelog, groups changes under Added, Changed, Deprecated, Removed, Fixed and Security, with the version number and release date as a heading. Example entry: '2.4.0 (2025-03-10). Added: note field on orders. Deprecated: delivery_time parameter; use delivery_window instead, removal planned in 3.0.0. Fixed: total_bdt was rounded incorrectly for orders over BDT 10,000.' A changelog is written for humans; it is not a dump of commit messages.

Design documents: A design document, sometimes called a technical design doc or RFC inside companies, describes how a team plans to build something before building it. Typical sections: context and problem; goals and non-goals (what this design will deliberately not solve); the proposed design with diagrams, data models and APIs; alternatives considered and why they were rejected; trade-offs, risks and open questions; testing, rollout and monitoring plans. Writing it forces the author to think clearly, and sharing it lets teammates find problems while changes are still cheap. Software Engineering (deep-cse-4-4) and System Design (deep-cse-6-13) cover the engineering content; here the focus is writing it clearly.

Architecture decision records: An ADR is a short document that records one important architectural decision. The idea was popularised by Michael Nygard in 2011. A typical ADR has a title, a status (proposed, accepted, superseded), the context (the situation and forces), the decision itself, and the consequences, good and bad. Example: 'ADR 7: Use PostgreSQL for the order service. Context: we need transactions and complex queries; the team knows SQL. Decision: use PostgreSQL. Consequences: strong consistency and mature tools; we must manage schema migrations carefully.' A folder of ADRs answers the question every new team member asks: why did we build it this way?

Keeping documentation fresh: Outdated API docs are a common and serious problem. Practices that help: keep docs in the same repository as the code (docs-as-code, lesson 15); require documentation updates in the same pull request as API changes; generate reference from the code or OpenAPI file; test examples automatically; show the last-updated date and version on each page; and give readers an easy way to report errors. Assign ownership: documentation that belongs to everyone is maintained by no one.

Real-life example 1, a payment gateway integration: A Bangladeshi e-commerce startup integrates an online payment gateway. The gateway's documentation offers a sandbox with test credentials, a quickstart showing the full payment flow in five steps, an endpoint reference, and a page listing every error code with a suggested action. The startup's developer finishes the integration in two days. With another provider whose documentation consisted of an outdated PDF with no examples, a similar integration had taken two weeks and several support calls. For API providers, documentation quality directly affects how many developers adopt them.

Real-life example 2, the internal design doc: A team at a Dhaka ride-sharing company plans to change how fares are calculated during rain. Before coding, the lead writes a six-page design doc: the problem (riders complain fares jump unpredictably), goals (fares shown upfront, capped surge), non-goals (no change to driver payouts in this phase), the proposed algorithm, two alternatives, and the rollout plan in one city first. Reviewers spot that the cap would conflict with an existing promotion system. Fixing that in the document takes an hour; fixing it after launch would have taken weeks and angry customers.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Reference without examples, or with untested examples. Missing authentication steps. Errors undocumented or documented only as 'an error occurred'. No version information. Breaking changes without deprecation notice. Changelogs that are just commit logs. Design docs written after the code, only to satisfy a process. Exams may ask what API documentation should contain, to document a given endpoint, to explain semantic versioning, to describe the sections of a design document, or to explain what an ADR is.

Recap: API documentation is the menu that lets developers use your software correctly. Provide an overview, quickstart, authentication, a consistent reference for every endpoint with parameters, examples and errors, and limits. Put tested, realistic examples first. Use OpenAPI to generate and check reference, but write the human parts. Version clearly with semantic versioning, deprecate before removing, and keep a human-readable changelog. Write design docs and ADRs to think before building and to record why. Keep everything fresh by tying documentation changes to code changes. Like a reliable menu, good API documentation earns trust with every correct order.
key_points: API documentation is the menu that tells developers what they can request and what they will get back.
Good API docs include overview, quickstart, authentication, endpoint reference, errors, limits, versioning and changelog.
Each endpoint: method and path, description, auth, parameters (type, required, values), example request and response, errors.
Put complete, realistic, tested examples first; developers often read examples before descriptions.
OpenAPI files describe web APIs in machine-readable form and can generate interactive reference, but humans write explanations.
Semantic versioning: MAJOR for breaking changes, MINOR for new compatible features, PATCH for compatible fixes; deprecate before removing.
Design docs (goals, non-goals, design, alternatives, risks) and ADRs (context, decision, consequences) record how and why systems are built.
lessons.tip: When you document an endpoint, copy your own example request into a terminal and run it exactly as written. If it fails, the documentation is wrong, not the reader.
lessons.task: Pick a simple feature, such as 'add a book to a library system'. Write a reference entry for a POST endpoint that does it: method and path, description, parameters with types, an example request, an example response with status code, and at least three error cases. Then write a three-line changelog entry for adding it.

quiz.q: Under semantic versioning, what kind of change moves version 2.4.0 to 3.0.0?
options: An incompatible change that may break existing users
quiz.explain: The MAJOR number increases for breaking changes.

quiz.q: Which HTTP status code fits a request with a missing or expired token?
quiz.explain: 401 indicates the request lacks valid authentication.

quiz.q: What is the OpenAPI Specification used for?
options: Describing web APIs in a machine-readable format that tools can use
quiz.explain: OpenAPI files describe paths, parameters and responses, and tools generate reference and client code from them.

quiz.q: Which sections are typical of an architecture decision record (ADR)?
options: Title, status, context, decision and consequences
quiz.explain: ADRs capture one decision with its context and consequences.

quiz.q: In a design document, what are 'non-goals'?
options: Goals the team failed to reach
Things the design deliberately will not solve
quiz.explain: Stating non-goals sets clear boundaries and prevents scope confusion.

lessons.title: Requirements and Specifications Language
lessons.content:
A tailor in Gulistan is asked to make 'a nice shirt, not too tight'. The customer comes back and is unhappy: the shirt is too loose, and 'nice' meant a different collar. Now imagine the customer had said: 'Chest 40 inches, sleeve 24 inches, regular fit, button-down collar, white cotton.' The tailor can make exactly that, and both can check the result with a measuring tape. Software requirements work the same way. Vague requirements lead to arguments, rework and failed projects. Precise, testable requirements let developers build the right thing and testers check it. This lesson is about the language of requirements: how to write each sentence so that it means one thing and can be verified.

Where this fits: Software Engineering (deep-cse-4-4, lesson 08) covers requirements engineering: functional and non-functional requirements, the Software Requirements Specification (SRS) structure, elicitation and validation. System Analysis and Design (deep-cse-4-6) covers how requirements are gathered and analysed. Here we focus on the writing: the sentences, words and patterns that make requirements clear. Quick recap: a functional requirement says what the system must do ('The system shall send an OTP to the user's phone'); a non-functional requirement says how well or under what constraints ('OTP delivery shall take less than 10 seconds for 95 percent of requests').

Why requirement wording matters so much: Requirements are a kind of contract between clients, users, developers and testers. Each group reads them differently, often months apart, and with different interests. A developer may read 'fast' as 2 seconds, the client as instant, and the tester has no way to check either. Studies and industry experience have long shown that errors introduced in requirements are among the most expensive to fix, because they are discovered late, after design, code and tests have been built on them. A clear sentence written in week one can save months later.

Qualities of a good requirement: Standards such as ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148 list qualities of well-formed requirements. The most important for writers are: necessary (it describes something truly needed); unambiguous (it can be read only one way); complete (it contains all needed information, including conditions and units); singular or atomic (it states one requirement, not several joined by 'and'); feasible (it can be achieved with the available technology, time and budget); verifiable (there is a practical way to test or inspect that it is met); and consistent (it does not contradict other requirements). If you remember just one, remember verifiable: if nobody can test it, it is not yet a requirement.

Shall, must, should and may: Many requirement documents use 'shall' for mandatory requirements. Some modern guides prefer 'must', because 'shall' is old-fashioned in everyday English. Either works if the document says clearly which word marks a requirement and uses it consistently. 'Should' marks a recommendation or desirable feature, and 'may' marks an option. Avoid 'will' for requirements, because it can be read as a prediction ('the system will be fast') rather than an obligation. As lesson 05 explained, RFC 2119 gives standard meanings for MUST, SHOULD and MAY, and many specifications refer to it.

Words that cause ambiguity: Some words almost guarantee an unclear requirement: fast, quick, efficient, user-friendly, easy, intuitive, flexible, robust, secure, reliable, adequate, minimal, maximal, as appropriate, if possible, etc., and/or, and so on, support (as in 'support many users'). Each should be replaced by a measurable statement or removed. 'User-friendly' might become 'A first-time user shall be able to complete a money transfer within 2 minutes without help, in usability tests with at least 5 participants.' Pronouns like 'it' and 'this' and words like 'all' and 'any' also need checking: 'all users' might include administrators you did not intend.

One requirement per sentence: A requirement such as 'The system shall allow users to register and log in and shall send a welcome email' contains three requirements. If registration works but the email fails, has the requirement passed or failed? Split it into three numbered requirements, each testable on its own. Similarly, avoid 'and/or', which hides two different meanings, and avoid escape clauses like 'unless technically difficult', which make the requirement impossible to enforce.

State the need, not the design: A requirement should usually say what the system must achieve, not how to build it. 'The system shall store data in MySQL' fixes a design choice that may not matter to the client and blocks better options. 'The system shall keep each order record for at least 5 years and return any record within 3 seconds' states the real need and leaves the design to the engineers. Design constraints are sometimes genuine, for example 'must run on the university's existing Oracle server', and then they belong in a separate constraints section with the reason written down, so that later readers know it was a deliberate limit and not an accident.

The EARS patterns: EARS, the Easy Approach to Requirements Syntax, was developed by Alistair Mavin and colleagues at Rolls-Royce and published in 2009. It gives a few simple sentence templates that reduce ambiguity. Ubiquitous (always true): 'The <system> shall <response>.' Example: 'The app shall display amounts in Bangladeshi taka.' Event-driven: 'When <trigger>, the <system> shall <response>.' Example: 'When the user taps Send, the app shall ask for the PIN.' State-driven: 'While <state>, the <system> shall <response>.' Example: 'While the phone is offline, the app shall queue outgoing messages.' Unwanted behaviour: 'If <unwanted condition>, then the <system> shall <response>.' Example: 'If the PIN is entered incorrectly 3 times, then the app shall lock the account for 30 minutes.' Optional feature: 'Where <feature is included>, the <system> shall <response>.' Example: 'Where fingerprint login is enabled, the app shall accept a fingerprint instead of the PIN.' The fixed order forces writers to state the trigger or condition explicitly.

Worked ambiguity hunt: Original: 'The system should respond quickly to user requests and should support many users at the same time and be secure.' Problems: 'should' is weak for a must-have; 'quickly' and 'many' are unmeasurable; 'secure' is vague; three requirements are joined. Rewrite as separate requirements: 'R1. The system shall return search results within 2 seconds for 95 percent of requests, measured at the server, when 500 users are logged in at the same time. R2. The system shall support at least 500 concurrent logged-in users without errors. R3. The system shall store user passwords only as salted hashes.' The security requirement is now one specific, checkable rule; a real project would have several more security requirements, each equally specific.

User stories: Agile teams often express requirements as user stories in the form 'As a <role>, I want <goal>, so that <benefit>.' Example: 'As a student, I want to see my class routine on the home screen, so that I do not have to open the website every morning.' User stories keep the focus on users and value, but they are deliberately short and need more detail before development. A common checklist for good stories is INVEST, proposed by Bill Wake: Independent, Negotiable, Valuable, Estimable, Small and Testable. Software Project Management (deep-cse-6-11) covers how stories are planned and estimated.

Acceptance criteria and Given-When-Then: Each user story needs acceptance criteria: specific conditions that must be true for the story to count as done. A popular format from behaviour-driven development is Given-When-Then. Given a starting situation, When an action happens, Then an expected result occurs. Example: 'Given the student is logged in and has classes today, When they open the app, Then the home screen shows today's classes in time order with room numbers.' Another: 'Given the student has no classes today, When they open the app, Then the home screen shows the message No classes today.' Acceptance criteria turn a short story into testable behaviour, and testers can turn each one into a test case.

Numbering and traceability: Give every requirement a unique, stable identifier, such as FR-12 for functional and NFR-3 for non-functional requirements. Identifiers let teams refer to requirements in discussions, link them to design elements and test cases, and track changes. Do not renumber requirements when one is deleted; mark it as deleted instead, so old references do not point to the wrong item. A traceability matrix, a table linking each requirement to its design element and tests, shows quickly which requirements are not yet tested.

Glossary and assumptions: A requirements document should include a glossary that defines domain terms precisely (lesson 12), such as what counts as an 'active account' or a 'completed order'. It should also list assumptions and constraints explicitly: 'We assume users have Android 8 or later', 'The system must use the university's existing login server'. Unstated assumptions are a major source of misunderstandings; once written, they can be checked and challenged.

Real-life example 1, a hospital queue system: A team builds a token system for a district hospital outpatient department. The first draft said: 'Patients should not wait too long and the display should be clearly visible.' After review, the requirements became: 'FR-4. When a doctor presses Next, the display shall show the next token number within 3 seconds. NFR-2. Token numbers shall be at least 15 cm tall on the waiting room display. NFR-3. The display shall show numbers in both Bangla and English digits.' The testers could now check each one with a stopwatch and a ruler, and the hospital staff could see exactly what they would get.

Real-life example 2, a mobile banking feature: A fintech company in Dhaka writes stories for a bill payment feature. 'As a customer, I want to save my electricity account number, so that I do not have to type it every month.' Acceptance criteria in Given-When-Then form covered saving, editing, deleting and the limit of 10 saved accounts. During review, a tester asked: 'Then what happens when the customer tries to save an 11th account?' Nobody had decided. The team added a criterion with a clear error message. This is the value of precise requirements language: gaps appear on paper, not in production.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Vague adjectives instead of measurable criteria. Several requirements in one sentence. Using 'will' or 'should' for mandatory requirements. Describing the solution instead of the need ('use a red button' when the need is 'make the delete action clearly distinct'). Missing conditions and error cases. Unstated assumptions. Exams often give vague requirements to rewrite, ask for the qualities of good requirements, ask you to write requirements using EARS patterns, ask for user stories with Given-When-Then acceptance criteria, or ask about traceability.

Recap: Requirements are contracts written in sentences, so each sentence must have one meaning and be testable. Write requirements that are necessary, unambiguous, complete, atomic, feasible, verifiable and consistent. Use shall or must consistently for mandatory requirements. Replace vague words with numbers and conditions. Use EARS patterns to make triggers and states explicit. Write user stories with INVEST in mind and add Given-When-Then acceptance criteria. Number every requirement, trace it to tests, define terms in a glossary and write down assumptions. Like the tailor's measurements, precise requirements let everyone check the result against the same tape.
key_points: Requirements are contracts; each sentence must have one meaning and be verifiable.
Good requirements are necessary, unambiguous, complete, atomic, feasible, verifiable and consistent.
Use shall or must consistently for mandatory requirements; should for recommendations, may for options; avoid will.
Replace vague words (fast, user-friendly, many, secure, etc., and/or) with measurable conditions.
EARS patterns: ubiquitous, event-driven (When), state-driven (While), unwanted behaviour (If...then), optional feature (Where).
User stories (As a..., I want..., so that...) need acceptance criteria, often in Given-When-Then form; INVEST checks story quality.
Give each requirement a stable ID, trace it to tests, and include a glossary and explicit assumptions.
lessons.tip: For every requirement you write, ask: 'How exactly would a tester prove this passed or failed?' If you cannot describe the test, rewrite the requirement until you can.
lessons.task: Take this requirement: 'The app should be fast and easy to use and should work offline.' Rewrite it as at least three separate, numbered, testable requirements, using at least one EARS pattern. Then write one user story for the offline feature with two Given-When-Then acceptance criteria.

quiz.q: Which requirement is verifiable?
options: The app shall load the home screen within 2 seconds on a 4G connection for 95 percent of launches.
quiz.explain: It states a measurable condition that a tester can check.

quiz.q: Which EARS pattern is 'If the PIN is entered incorrectly 3 times, then the app shall lock the account for 30 minutes'?
quiz.explain: The If...then pattern handles unwanted conditions and the system's response.

quiz.q: What is wrong with 'The system shall allow users to register and log in and shall send a welcome email'?
options: It joins several requirements, so it cannot be cleanly passed or failed
quiz.explain: Requirements should be atomic; split it into separate testable statements.

quiz.q: What does a Given-When-Then acceptance criterion describe?
options: A starting situation, an action and the expected result
quiz.explain: Given-When-Then turns a story into testable behaviour.

quiz.q: Why should requirement IDs not be renumbered when one is deleted?
options: Renumbering is impossible in word processors
Old references in designs, tests and discussions would point to the wrong requirement
IDs must always be prime numbers
Deleted requirements must be kept as active
quiz.explain: Stable IDs keep traceability intact; mark deleted items instead of reusing their numbers.

lessons.title: Technical Reports: Kinds and Structure
lessons.content:
When a doctor examines a patient, the hospital keeps a file: who the patient is, the complaint, the tests done, the results, the diagnosis and the treatment. Any other doctor can pick up the file and understand the case in minutes, because every file follows the same structure. Technical reports work the same way. A report records what was studied or done, what was found and what should happen next, in a structure readers already know. Engineers write lab reports at university, and progress reports, feasibility studies, incident reports and recommendation reports at work. This lesson maps the kinds of reports and the standard structure they share; lesson 19 then covers how to write each section.

What a technical report is: A technical report is a document that presents technical information gathered through investigation, testing, analysis or work, for a specific reader who needs it to understand a situation or make a decision. Unlike a user manual, it is not mainly about telling readers how to do something. Unlike a research paper (lesson 21), it is not necessarily aimed at publishing new knowledge for the research community; many reports are internal to a company, a client or a course. Reports are judged by whether the reader can find the key findings quickly, trust them and act on them.

Common kinds of reports: Lab reports describe an experiment: aim, method, results and analysis, mostly for teachers at university. Progress or status reports tell a supervisor or client how a project is going: what is done, what is next, what problems exist. Feasibility reports study whether a proposed project is technically, economically and operationally possible. Recommendation reports compare options and recommend one, such as which cloud provider to choose. Incident reports or postmortems analyse a failure, such as a server outage, and what will prevent it next time. Research reports and project reports, including final-year project reports and theses, present an investigation in depth. Test reports summarise testing results against requirements. Many organisations also use trip reports, evaluation reports and audit reports.

Informal and formal reports: Short reports, one to five pages, are often written as memos or emails with headings: a progress report or incident summary sent to a team. Long formal reports, from about ten pages up to a thesis, have full front matter, numbered sections and back matter. The same principles apply to both: purpose and main findings first, clear headings, evidence for claims, and a conclusion or recommendation the reader can act on. The difference is how much apparatus is needed to help the reader navigate.

The three-part structure: A formal report has three parts. Front matter helps readers decide what to read and find it: title page, abstract or executive summary, acknowledgements (optional), table of contents, list of figures, list of tables, and list of abbreviations if needed. The body contains the actual content: introduction, background or literature review if needed, method, results, discussion, conclusion and recommendations. Back matter holds supporting material: references, appendices (raw data, long calculations, code listings, questionnaires) and sometimes a glossary or index. Many universities give a template with exactly these parts; follow it.

The title page: A title page usually has the full title, the author or authors, their IDs or affiliations, the course or organisation, the person the report is submitted to, and the date. The title itself deserves care. 'Report on Network' tells the reader almost nothing. 'Performance of Campus Wi-Fi During Peak Hours: Measurements and Recommendations' tells them the topic, the type of work and that there are recommendations. A good title is specific and contains the key terms someone might search for.

Abstract versus executive summary: Both summarise the whole report at the start, but for different readers. An abstract, common in academic and research reports, is usually one paragraph of about 150 to 250 words summarising the problem, method, main results and conclusion. An executive summary, common in business and professional reports, is written for decision makers who may read nothing else; it can be a page or more, focuses on findings, conclusions, recommendations, costs and impact, and uses less technical detail. Both must stand alone: a reader should understand them without reading the rest. Lesson 19 shows how to write an abstract.

IMRaD: Many technical and scientific reports organise the body as IMRaD: Introduction (what problem, why it matters, what we aimed to do), Methods (how we did it), Results (what we found), and Discussion (what it means, limitations, comparison with expectations). IMRaD became the standard structure of scientific papers during the twentieth century because it matches the questions readers ask, in the order they ask them. Lab reports, project reports and research papers are often IMRaD or close variations, usually with a conclusion added at the end.

Other body structures: Not every report fits IMRaD.
