A recommendation report often follows: introduction, criteria for the decision, options considered, evaluation of each option against the criteria, conclusion and recommendation. A feasibility report covers technical, economic (costs and benefits), operational, legal and schedule feasibility before concluding. A progress report is organised by time or by task. An incident report follows a timeline. Choose the structure that matches the reader's questions, and use headings that reveal it.

Numbering and cross-references: Formal reports usually number sections (1, 1.1, 1.1.1), figures (Figure 1, 2, 3) and tables (Table 1, 2, 3), and sometimes equations. Front matter pages are often numbered with Roman numerals (i, ii, iii) and the body with Arabic numerals starting at 1 on the first page of the introduction. Use your word processor's automatic numbering and cross-reference features, so that inserting a new figure renumbers everything correctly. Manual numbering in a long report almost always ends with 'see Figure 7' pointing to the wrong figure.

Appendices: Appendices hold material that some readers need but that would interrupt the main text: full data tables, detailed derivations, survey questions, long code, circuit diagrams, test logs. Each appendix gets a letter and title (Appendix A: Survey Questionnaire) and must be mentioned in the text. Do not hide essential results in an appendix; the main text should still make sense on its own. And do not use appendices as a dumping ground for everything you produced.

Lab reports, briefly: The lab report is the first formal report most CSE students write. A typical one has: title and experiment number; objective (what the experiment should show or measure); theory in a few paragraphs, only what is needed to understand the results; apparatus or software used, with versions; procedure, written as what you actually did, in past tense; observations and results, with tables and graphs; analysis or discussion, comparing results with theory and explaining errors; and a short conclusion that answers the objective. Many students copy the procedure from the lab sheet and skip the discussion, which is where most marks are.

Progress reports, worked: A progress report answers four questions for a supervisor: what was planned, what is done, what is next, and what problems or risks exist. Example for a final-year project at week 8 of 14: 'Summary: The project is on schedule except for the mobile app, which is one week behind. Completed: literature review, dataset collection (2,400 labelled images), first model training with 84 percent validation accuracy. In progress: improving accuracy with data augmentation, target 90 percent by week 10. Next: mobile app integration, weeks 10 to 12; testing with farmers, week 13. Problems: the app's camera module crashes on two older phones; we are testing a lighter library. Help needed: access to the department GPU server for two days next week.' The supervisor knows the status in one minute and can act on the request.

Incident reports and blameless postmortems: When something important fails, such as an outage of a payment service, teams write an incident report or postmortem. Typical sections: summary; impact (who was affected, how badly, for how long); timeline of detection, response and recovery with exact times; root cause and contributing factors; what went well and what went badly; and action items with owners and deadlines to prevent recurrence. Many software organisations, influenced by Google's site reliability engineering practices, run blameless postmortems: they focus on how the system and process allowed the failure, not on punishing an individual, because people hide mistakes when they fear blame, and hidden mistakes repeat.

Worked incident summary: 'On 12 June, from 10:15 to 10:40 (25 minutes, UTC+6), about 12 percent of Send Money transactions failed with a timeout error. Cause: a database configuration change reduced the maximum number of connections from 200 to 50; under morning peak load, requests waited for connections and timed out. Detection: alert on error rate at 10:19, four minutes after the start. Resolution: the change was rolled back at 10:37; errors stopped by 10:40. No money was lost; failed transactions were not charged. Actions: add connection limits to the configuration review checklist (owner: Nabila, 20 June); add a load test before database configuration changes (owner: Tareq, 30 June).' Readers learn what happened, how bad it was, why, and what will change.

Real-life example 1, a feasibility report for a city college: A college in Khulna asks a student team whether it is feasible to move student records from paper files to a web system. The team's report covers technical feasibility (the college has internet and two staff who can use computers), economic feasibility (estimated cost of hosting and development compared with the time saved by staff), operational feasibility (staff willingness, need for training), and schedule (six months). Its executive summary gives the recommendation in the first paragraph: feasible, if two staff receive training and records are digitised department by department. The principal reads only the executive summary and approves.

Real-life example 2, a recommendation report: A small software company in Dhaka must choose a tool for team communication. The report states the criteria first (cost per user, Bangla support, mobile app quality, file-sharing limits, data location), evaluates three options in a table, explains the trade-offs in a short discussion, and recommends one with a phased rollout. Because the criteria were agreed before the options were judged, the decision is easy to explain to the whole team.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Starting with long background and hiding the findings at the end. Missing executive summary or abstract. Titles that say nothing. Inconsistent or manual numbering. Results without interpretation, or interpretation without data. Appendices never mentioned in the text. Incident reports that blame a person instead of finding causes. Exams often ask you to list the parts of a formal report, distinguish an abstract from an executive summary, explain IMRaD, outline a progress report or feasibility report, or explain the purpose of front matter and back matter.

Recap: Technical reports record investigations and work for readers who need to understand or decide. Kinds include lab, progress, feasibility, recommendation, incident, test and project reports. Formal reports have front matter (title page, abstract or executive summary, contents, lists), a body (often IMRaD, or a structure matching the reader's questions) and back matter (references, appendices). Number sections, figures and tables automatically. Progress reports answer done, next and problems; incident reports give impact, timeline, root cause and actions, ideally blamelessly. Like a patient's file, a well-structured report lets any reader understand the case quickly.
key_points: A technical report presents findings from investigation or work for a reader who must understand or decide.
Kinds: lab, progress, feasibility, recommendation, incident or postmortem, test, project and research reports.
Formal structure: front matter (title page, abstract or executive summary, contents, lists), body, back matter (references, appendices).
An abstract summarises problem, method, results and conclusion in about 150 to 250 words; an executive summary targets decision makers.
IMRaD (Introduction, Methods, Results, Discussion) matches the questions readers ask; other reports follow criteria, options or timelines.
Progress reports state what is done, next, and problems or help needed.
Incident reports give impact, timeline, root cause and owned action items; blameless postmortems focus on systems, not individuals.
lessons.tip: Before writing a report, list the three questions your main reader will ask first. Make sure your summary answers all three in its first paragraph.
lessons.task: Write a one-page progress report on any project you are doing now (a course project, a club event, or even a home repair). Use four headings: Completed, In progress, Next steps, Problems and help needed. Include at least two specific numbers or dates.

quiz.q: Which part of a formal report contains appendices and references?
quiz.explain: Back matter holds supporting material such as references, appendices and glossaries.

quiz.q: How does an executive summary differ from an abstract?
options: It is written for decision makers and focuses on findings, recommendations, costs and impact
It is always shorter than 50 words
It appears only in lab reports
quiz.explain: Executive summaries serve decision makers who may read nothing else.

quiz.q: What does IMRaD stand for?
quiz.explain: IMRaD is the standard structure of many scientific and technical reports.

quiz.q: An outage ran from 10:15 to 10:40. How long was it?
quiz.explain: From 10:15 to 10:40 is 25 minutes.

quiz.q: Why do many teams run blameless postmortems?
options: Because nobody is ever responsible for anything
Because fear of blame makes people hide mistakes, so causes are not fixed
Because postmortems must be anonymous by law
Because blame takes too long to write
quiz.explain: Focusing on system and process causes encourages honest reporting and real fixes.

lessons.title: Writing the Report Sections
lessons.content:
A cricket commentator does not describe every ball of a match in the evening news. The news report starts with the result: 'Bangladesh won by 5 wickets.' Then the key moments, then the details for fans who want more. Yet in the full match record, every ball, run and wicket is there for anyone who needs to check. A good technical report works the same way: each section has a specific job and a specific reader. Lesson 18 gave the structure. This lesson shows how to write each section: the title, abstract, introduction, methods, results, discussion, conclusion and recommendations.

Write in the order that works, not the order of the report: The order you read a report is not the best order to write it. Many experienced writers start with the methods, because they know exactly what they did. Then they write the results, then the discussion, then the conclusion and recommendations, then the introduction, and finally the abstract and title. Writing the introduction and abstract last means they describe what the report actually contains, not what you hoped it would contain when you started.

The title: A title should tell the reader the topic and, if possible, the main type of finding or the context. It should contain the key terms someone would search for. Avoid vague titles ('A Study on Networks'), cute titles that hide the content, and unexplained abbreviations. Compare: 'Wi-Fi Report' with 'Wi-Fi Performance in Three Campus Buildings During Peak Hours'. The second is longer, but the reader knows exactly what they are getting. Titles of around 10 to 15 words are common for reports and papers.

The abstract: An abstract is a miniature version of the whole report. An informative abstract, the kind most technical reports and papers need, includes: the problem and why it matters (one or two sentences); the aim or objective; the method in brief; the main results with numbers; and the main conclusion or recommendation. A descriptive abstract, in contrast, only says what the report covers ('This report discusses Wi-Fi performance') without giving results; it is used mainly for very long documents or reviews, and is much less useful to busy readers. Most abstracts are one paragraph of about 150 to 250 words, though rules vary by university and journal. Avoid citations, undefined abbreviations and references to figures in the abstract, because it must stand alone.

A worked abstract: Here is an informative abstract of 173 words for a student project: 'Students at our university often complain that campus Wi-Fi becomes unusable between classes, but no measurements existed to show when and where the problem occurs. This report measures Wi-Fi performance in three academic buildings over two weeks and identifies the main cause of slowdowns. We ran an automated speed and latency test every 10 minutes from fixed laptops in six locations and recorded the number of connected devices from the access point logs. Median download speed fell from 38 Mbps during class hours to 6 Mbps in the 10 minutes after classes ended, while connected devices per access point rose from about 25 to about 90. Speed was strongly linked to the number of devices and only weakly to the time of day once device count was considered. These results suggest that the access points are overloaded during breaks rather than faulty. We recommend adding access points in the two most crowded corridors and limiting video streaming during peak periods, and we estimate the cost of the first measure at BDT 3.2 lakh.' Notice: problem, aim, method, results with numbers, interpretation and recommendation, all in one paragraph.

The introduction: The introduction tells the reader why the report exists and what it will do. A common pattern moves from general to specific: first the context and problem (what situation, why it matters, who is affected); then what is already known or has been tried, briefly, with citations if relevant; then the gap (what is missing, unknown or unsolved); then the aim and objectives of this report, often as a short list; and finally the scope (what is included and excluded) and a short roadmap of the sections. In a short report this might be three paragraphs; in a thesis it is a full chapter. Lesson 21 introduces the CARS model, a well-known way to structure research introductions.

Objectives: Objectives should be specific and checkable, because your conclusion will answer them. 'To study Wi-Fi' is too vague. 'To measure download speed and latency in three buildings every 10 minutes for two weeks' and 'To identify whether slowdowns are linked to the number of connected devices' are objectives you can clearly meet or not meet. Later, in the conclusion, go back through each objective and state what you found.

The methods section: The methods section, also called methodology, materials and methods, or experimental setup, explains how you did the work in enough detail that a competent reader could repeat it and judge whether your results are trustworthy. Include: what equipment, software and versions you used; the data and where it came from, including sample size and how participants or items were chosen; the procedure, in the order it was done; any measurements and how they were taken; and the analysis method, such as statistical tests or evaluation metrics. Write it mainly in the past tense ('We measured', or 'Speed was measured', depending on the expected style). Do not include results here. Mention limitations of the method briefly, or save them for the discussion.

The results section: The results section presents what you found, as objectively as possible. Use tables and figures for the data, as lesson 10 explained, and use the text to guide the reader to the key findings: 'Median speed dropped from 38 to 6 Mbps after classes ended (Figure 2).' Present results in a logical order, usually the order of your objectives or methods. Report negative and unexpected results too; leaving them out is misleading. Avoid long interpretation here; a sentence linking a result to the objective is fine, but the deeper 'what it means' belongs in the discussion. Some short reports combine results and discussion, which is acceptable if the difference between data and interpretation stays clear.

Results versus discussion: The results answer 'What did we find?' The discussion answers 'What does it mean?' A useful test: a result can be checked against the data ('Speed fell to 6 Mbps'); a discussion statement is an interpretation that could be argued ('This suggests the access points are overloaded'). Mixing them makes it hard for readers to separate evidence from opinion. Keeping them apart shows you know the difference, which teachers and reviewers notice.

The discussion section: In the discussion, you interpret the results and connect them to the problem. Typical moves: restate the main finding briefly; explain why it happened, with evidence; compare with expectations, theory or other studies (agreeing or disagreeing, and why); acknowledge limitations honestly, such as small sample, short time period or measurement errors, and say how they might affect the conclusions; and state implications, meaning what the results mean for practice or for future work. Use hedging appropriately (lesson 05): 'suggests', 'is likely', 'appears' when evidence is limited, and firmer words when it is strong.

The conclusion: The conclusion closes the report. It should answer the objectives from the introduction, summarise the key findings and their significance, and avoid introducing new data or new arguments. It is not a copy of the abstract, though they overlap. A good conclusion is short, often one to three paragraphs, and confident within the limits of the evidence. If the reader read only the introduction and the conclusion, they should know what was asked and what was answered.

Recommendations: Many reports end with recommendations: specific actions the reader should take based on the findings. Good recommendations are numbered, actionable, specific about who should do what, and linked to findings. 'Improve the Wi-Fi' is not a recommendation. 'Install two additional access points in the second-floor corridor of Building B before the next semester (estimated cost BDT 1.6 lakh), because this location had the highest device count and lowest speed' is. Order recommendations by priority or by cost and effort. In some reports, especially recommendation reports and executive summaries, the recommendations appear at the very start as well.

References and appendices: Every source used must appear in the reference list in a consistent citation style (lesson 22), and every reference in the list should be cited in the text. Appendices hold raw data, full questionnaires and long code, each labelled and referred to in the text. A quick check before submission: count your citations in the text and entries in the reference list, and make sure each figure, table and appendix is mentioned at least once.

Real-life example 1, a networking lab report: Farhan's lab report on TCP and UDP throughput had a results section that only contained the raw table and a discussion that said 'TCP is reliable and UDP is fast'. His teacher marked it low. In the revision, his results text pointed to the key comparison ('UDP throughput averaged 94 Mbps versus 89 Mbps for TCP over 10 runs'), and his discussion explained the difference using TCP's acknowledgement and congestion control overhead, noted that UDP lost 0.4 percent of packets while TCP lost none, and admitted that the test used only one cable length. The grade rose because the analysis now showed understanding, not just measurement.

Real-life example 2, a final-year project report: A team building a Bangla handwritten digit recognizer wrote their introduction last. Their first draft introduction promised a mobile app and real-time recognition, but the final project delivered a desktop prototype. Writing it last, they rewrote the objectives to match what they actually did and moved the mobile app to the 'future work' part of the conclusion. The external examiner later commented that the report was refreshingly honest and consistent, which made the viva go smoothly.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Abstracts without results or numbers. Introductions that never state an aim. Methods too vague to repeat. Results sections full of interpretation, or discussions that only repeat results. Conclusions with new information. Recommendations that are vague or not linked to findings. Exams often ask you to write an abstract for a given study, to distinguish results from discussion, to list what a methods section must include, to distinguish informative from descriptive abstracts, or to write recommendations from given findings.

Recap: Write the methods and results first, the introduction and abstract last. Give a specific title. Write an informative abstract with problem, aim, method, results with numbers and conclusion, about 150 to 250 words. Build the introduction from context to gap to aim and scope, with checkable objectives. Make methods repeatable. Present results objectively with figures and tables. Interpret in the discussion, including limitations. Conclude by answering the objectives, and give numbered, specific, linked recommendations. Like the match report and the scorecard, each section serves its reader and its purpose.
key_points: Write methods and results first, then discussion and conclusion, and the introduction and abstract last.
Titles should be specific and include searchable key terms.
An informative abstract gives problem, aim, method, results with numbers and conclusion in about 150 to 250 words; a descriptive abstract only lists topics.
Introductions move from context and problem to gap, aim, checkable objectives and scope.
Methods must be detailed enough to repeat: equipment, versions, data, sample, procedure and analysis.
Results present findings objectively; the discussion interprets them, compares, and states limitations.
Conclusions answer the objectives without new data; recommendations are numbered, specific, actionable and linked to findings.
lessons.tip: After writing your discussion, mark each sentence R (result, checkable against data) or I (interpretation). If a section labelled Results is full of I, or the Discussion is full of R, move sentences to where they belong.
lessons.task: Take a lab experiment or project you have done. Write an informative abstract of 150 to 200 words with problem, aim, method, at least two numerical results and a conclusion. Count the words, then ask a friend who did not do the work to explain your findings back to you from the abstract alone.

quiz.q: Which section is usually best written last?
quiz.explain: The abstract summarises the whole report, so it is easiest to write accurately once everything else is done.

quiz.q: What makes an abstract 'informative' rather than 'descriptive'?
options: It includes the main results and conclusions, not just the topics covered
It is longer than two pages
It lists the table of contents
quiz.explain: Informative abstracts give findings with numbers; descriptive ones only say what the report discusses.

quiz.q: Which sentence belongs in the discussion rather than the results?
options: Median speed fell from 38 to 6 Mbps after classes ended.
Devices per access point rose from 25 to 90.
Table 2 lists latency for each location.
This suggests the access points are overloaded during breaks rather than faulty.
quiz.explain: It is an interpretation of the data, which belongs in the discussion.

quiz.q: What is the main goal of a methods section?
options: To give enough detail that a competent reader could repeat the work and judge its reliability
quiz.explain: Repeatability and credibility depend on a clear, complete methods section.

quiz.q: Which is a good recommendation?
options: Install two access points in Building B's second-floor corridor before next semester (about BDT 1.6 lakh), where speed was lowest.
quiz.explain: It is specific, actionable, costed and linked to a finding.

lessons.title: Writing Proposals
lessons.content:
Imagine you want your parents to let you join a two-week robotics camp in Dhaka. If you just say 'Please, it will be fun', the answer is probably no. But if you explain what you will learn, how it will help your studies, how much it costs, how you will travel safely, and how you will keep up with schoolwork, you have a much better chance. You have just written a proposal. In technical work, a proposal asks a reader to approve, fund or choose your plan. Students write project and thesis proposals; companies write proposals to win clients; researchers write grant proposals to get funding. This lesson shows how to write a proposal that persuades with clear, honest, specific information.

What a proposal is: A proposal is a document that offers to do specific work, explains why it is needed and how it will be done, and asks the reader for a decision: approval, money, time or a contract. Unlike a report, which describes work already done, a proposal describes work that has not happened yet. It must therefore convince the reader that the problem is real, the plan is sound, the team is capable, the cost is reasonable and the result will be worth it. A proposal is also a promise: once approved, it becomes the plan you will be held to.

Solicited and unsolicited proposals: A solicited proposal answers a request from the reader. Organisations publish a request for proposals (RFP), a call for proposals, or a tender, describing what they need and how proposals will be judged. Universities ask students for thesis proposals in a set format. In these cases, follow the instructions exactly: required sections, page limits, fonts, deadlines and evaluation criteria. Many proposals are rejected without being read because they ignored a formatting rule or missed a deadline. An unsolicited proposal is one you send without being asked, such as offering a school a free attendance app. It must work harder to show that the problem exists and that the reader should care.

Internal and external proposals: Internal proposals go to people in your own organisation, such as asking your manager for time to rebuild the testing system or asking the department for lab equipment. External proposals go to other organisations: clients, government agencies, funding bodies. External proposals usually need more background about your team and more formal language, while internal ones can assume shared context. Both need the same core: problem, plan, cost and benefit.

The standard parts of a proposal: Most proposals contain these parts, though names vary: title page; summary or abstract; introduction and problem statement, sometimes called background or statement of need; objectives; proposed approach or methodology; timeline or work plan; budget and justification; team or qualifications; expected outcomes, deliverables and evaluation plan; risks; and references and appendices. A research or thesis proposal adds a literature review showing what is already known. A business proposal adds pricing options, terms and sometimes case studies of earlier projects.

The problem statement: This is the foundation. The reader must agree there is a problem worth solving before they care about your solution. Describe the situation, who is affected and how badly, using evidence: numbers, sources, observations. 'Many students miss classes' is weak. 'At our college, 22 percent of first-year students missed more than a quarter of classes last semester, according to the academic office, and attendance is still recorded on paper and reported to guardians only at the end of the term' is strong. Keep the problem focused on the reader's interests: what it costs them, risks for them, or opportunities they could miss.

SMART objectives: Objectives state what the project will achieve. A widely used checklist says objectives should be SMART: Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant and Time-bound. 'Improve attendance' is not SMART. 'Reduce the share of first-year students missing more than a quarter of classes from 22 percent to 15 percent within one academic year, by sending guardians weekly SMS attendance summaries' is. SMART objectives make the proposal credible and give a clear way to judge success later.

The approach or methodology: Explain how you will achieve each objective: what you will build or do, in which steps, with what tools, and why this approach is suitable. Show that you have thought about alternatives and chosen sensibly. Link each step to an objective, so the reader sees nothing is missing and nothing is extra. If the work involves people, explain how you will get consent and protect privacy, which Ethics and Cyber Law (deep-cse-6-6) covers in more detail. Be specific enough that the reader believes you, but do not drown them in technical detail; put long technical specifications in an appendix.

The timeline: A timeline shows when each task will happen and when deliverables will be ready. For short projects, a table with tasks, start week, end week and deliverables works. For longer projects, a Gantt chart, a horizontal bar chart with tasks down the side and time along the top, shows overlaps and dependencies at a glance. Include milestones, such as 'prototype ready, week 8', and leave some buffer time. Reviewers distrust timelines where every task finishes exactly on the last day. Software Project Management (deep-cse-6-11) explains scheduling methods in depth.

The budget: A budget lists every cost, how it was calculated, and the total. Group costs into categories such as equipment, personnel, services, travel, training and contingency. Show the calculation for each line, so reviewers can check it. Then write a short budget justification explaining why each item is needed. Make sure the numbers add up exactly; reviewers do check, and an arithmetic error damages trust in everything else. Do not inflate costs, and do not hide costs that will appear later.

A worked budget: Here is a one-year budget for the college attendance project. Equipment: 10 tablets for taking attendance at BDT 18,000 each, 10 times 18,000 = BDT 180,000. SMS service: about BDT 60,000 for weekly messages to guardians for one year. Cloud hosting: BDT 3,600 per month for 12 months = BDT 43,200. Field travel to collect requirements and support teachers: BDT 40,000. Teacher training sessions: BDT 25,000. Subtotal: 180,000 + 60,000 + 43,200 + 40,000 + 25,000 = BDT 348,200. Contingency at 10 percent of the subtotal: BDT 34,820. Total requested: BDT 383,020. Each line shows quantity times unit price where possible, and the contingency is stated openly instead of being hidden inside other lines.

Team and qualifications: Readers fund people as much as ideas. Briefly describe who will do the work and why they can: relevant skills, past projects, publications or similar systems built. For a student proposal, this may be one paragraph about the student's coursework and the supervisor's expertise. For a company proposal, it may include short biographies and examples of earlier clients. Match qualifications to the tasks in your plan.

Deliverables, evaluation and risks: State exactly what the reader will receive: software, a report, a trained model, training sessions, source code, documentation. Explain how success will be measured, linking back to the SMART objectives: 'We will compare attendance rates before and after using the academic office's records.' Finally, list the main risks and how you will reduce them: 'Risk: teachers may not use the tablets regularly. Mitigation: short training, a two-minute attendance process, and a weekly reminder from the department head.' Honest risk analysis increases trust; pretending there are no risks reduces it.

The summary: Like an executive summary, the proposal summary is often the only part busy reviewers read closely before deciding whether to read on. In one or two short paragraphs, state the problem, the proposed solution, the main objectives, the cost and duration, and the expected benefit. Write it last, and make it able to stand alone.

Format and presentation: Reviewers judge a proposal partly by how easy it is to read. Use the headings the reader expects, in the order they expect. Put the most important number in each section where the eye lands first, such as the total cost at the start of the budget section, not buried at the bottom. Use one table for the budget and one chart or table for the timeline rather than long paragraphs of numbers. Keep page limits strictly; a proposal that is two pages over a ten-page limit tells the reviewer you cannot follow simple rules. Finally, proofread names and numbers carefully: a wrong organisation name copied from an earlier proposal is a common and embarrassing mistake.

Persuasion without exaggeration: A proposal is persuasive writing, but the persuasion should come from evidence and clarity, not hype. Avoid 'revolutionary', 'cutting-edge' and 'world-class' unless you can prove them. Use the reader's language and criteria: if the call for proposals lists 'impact on rural communities' as a criterion, address that clearly under a heading using the same words. Make reviewers' jobs easy: they often have dozens of proposals and a scoring sheet.

Real-life example 1, a thesis proposal: Sumaiya proposes a thesis on detecting fake news in Bangla social media posts. Her first draft had a long history of fake news and only a vague plan. Her supervisor asked: 'What exactly will you produce, and how will you know it works?' The revision had a one-paragraph problem statement with evidence, three SMART objectives (build a labelled dataset of 5,000 posts, train and compare three models, reach at least 85 percent F1 score on a held-out test set), a 16-week timeline with milestones, the data ethics plan, and a short risk section. The committee approved it in one meeting. Final Year Project and Thesis (deep-cse-6-7) covers the full thesis proposal process in more detail.

Real-life example 2, a software company proposal: A Chattogram software firm answers an RFP from an NGO that wants a mobile app for community health workers. The firm's proposal mirrors the RFP's section headings, answers each evaluation criterion explicitly, shows a Gantt chart of 20 weeks with three milestones, gives an itemised budget with a contingency line, and includes screenshots of a similar app they built earlier. A competitor's proposal was more impressive visually but had a budget that did not add up. The NGO chose the first firm because it was clearer and easier to trust.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Ignoring the RFP's instructions. Weak problem statements without evidence. Vague objectives. Approaches not linked to objectives. Unrealistic timelines with no buffer. Budgets with arithmetic errors, hidden costs or no justification. Missing evaluation plan or risks. Exaggerated claims. Exams often ask you to list the parts of a proposal, distinguish solicited and unsolicited proposals, write SMART objectives, prepare a simple budget, or write a problem statement for a given situation.

Recap: A proposal asks the reader to approve or fund work that has not yet been done. Solicited proposals must follow the request exactly; unsolicited ones must first prove the need. Include a summary, evidence-based problem statement, SMART objectives, an approach linked to objectives, a realistic timeline with milestones, an exact, justified budget, team qualifications, deliverables, an evaluation plan and risks. Persuade with evidence and clarity, not hype. Like asking your parents about the robotics camp, a good proposal answers the reader's questions before they ask them.
key_points: A proposal offers to do specific future work and asks the reader to approve, fund or choose it.
Solicited proposals answer an RFP or call and must follow its instructions exactly; unsolicited ones must first prove the need.
Common parts: summary, problem statement, objectives, approach, timeline, budget, team, deliverables, evaluation and risks.
A strong problem statement uses evidence and focuses on the reader's interests.
Objectives should be SMART: Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant and Time-bound.
Budgets show each line's calculation, group costs, state contingency openly and must add up exactly.
Persuade with evidence, clear structure and honest risks rather than hype.
lessons.tip: Before submitting a proposal, give it to someone outside the project with the evaluation criteria. Ask them to score it. Every criterion they cannot find quickly is a heading you need to add or rewrite.
lessons.task: Write a one-page internal proposal asking your department or school for something specific, such as a new printer for the lab or a weekly coding club. Include a problem statement with at least one number, two SMART objectives, a timeline of at least three steps, and an itemised budget. Check the budget total with a calculator.

quiz.q: What is a solicited proposal?
options: A proposal sent without any request
A proposal written in response to a request such as an RFP or call for proposals
A proposal that has already been approved
quiz.explain: Solicited proposals answer a request and must follow its instructions.

quiz.q: Which objective is SMART?
options: Reduce first-year students missing over a quarter of classes from 22 percent to 15 percent within one academic year.
quiz.explain: It is specific, measurable, achievable, relevant and time-bound.

quiz.q: In the worked budget, the subtotal is BDT 348,200. What is a 10 percent contingency?
quiz.explain: 10 percent of 348,200 is 34,820.

quiz.q: What does a Gantt chart show?
options: Tasks as bars along a time axis, showing overlaps and milestones
quiz.explain: A Gantt chart is a horizontal bar chart of tasks over time.

quiz.q: Why should a proposal include a risk section?
options: Because honest risks with mitigations increase trust in the plan
quiz.explain: Reviewers trust proposals that recognise risks and plan for them.

lessons.title: Research Papers and Thesis Writing
lessons.content:
Think of a science fair. Dozens of students stand beside posters, and visitors walk past quickly. The visitors stop only where the poster tells them in one glance what new thing was discovered and why it matters. Research papers live in a much bigger science fair: thousands of papers are published every week, and readers decide in seconds whether to read further. A thesis is your own long exhibit, read carefully by a few examiners who must decide whether you deserve a degree. This lesson explains how research papers and theses are organised, how to state contributions, how to write related work and introductions, how peer review works, and how to respond to reviewers.

Where this fits: Research Methodology (deep-cse-7-7) covers how to plan and run research: choosing questions, designing experiments, statistics and validity. Lessons 18 and 19 covered reports and their sections. Here we focus on the writing conventions specific to research papers and theses, which build on IMRaD but add their own expectations.

What makes a research paper different: A research paper reports original work that adds something new to knowledge: a new algorithm, a better result, a new dataset, a careful measurement, or a new explanation. Its readers are other researchers who know the field. They want to know quickly what is new, whether it is correct, and how it compares with earlier work. Unlike a report written for one client, a research paper is written for a community and becomes part of the permanent public record, where it may be cited for decades.

The typical structure: Most computer science papers follow a variation of IMRaD: title; abstract; introduction; background or related work; the approach, method, system design or model; experimental setup; results; discussion, sometimes combined with results; related work, if not earlier; conclusion and future work; acknowledgements; and references. Some fields, especially theory, organise papers around definitions, theorems and proofs instead of experiments. Each conference or journal publishes an author guide and a template, often in LaTeX or Word, with strict page limits.

The contributions list: A strong habit in computer science papers is to end the introduction with an explicit list of contributions. For example: 'This paper makes three contributions. First, we release a dataset of 12,000 labelled Bangla product reviews. Second, we propose a lightweight model that reaches accuracy comparable to large models while running on low-end phones. Third, we show through experiments that most remaining errors come from reviews that mix Bangla and English.' Each contribution should be specific and checkable, and the rest of the paper should provide evidence for each one. Reviewers often judge a paper first by this list.

The CARS model for introductions: In 1990, the linguist John Swales described a pattern found in many research introductions, called CARS: Create A Research Space. It has three moves. Move 1, establishing a territory: show that the research area is important and summarise relevant earlier work. Move 2, establishing a niche: point out a gap, a problem, a limitation or an unanswered question in that earlier work. Move 3, occupying the niche: state what this paper does to fill the gap, its contributions, and how the paper is organised. Following these moves makes the reader feel the need for your work before you describe it.

A worked CARS introduction, in brief: Move 1: 'Online shopping in Bangladesh has grown rapidly, and customer reviews strongly influence buying decisions. Sentiment analysis can summarise thousands of reviews automatically, and many models achieve high accuracy in English.' Move 2: 'However, few public datasets exist for Bangla reviews, and existing models are too large to run on the low-cost phones most local sellers use.' Move 3: 'In this paper, we build a 12,000-review Bangla dataset and a lightweight model, and we make three contributions, listed below. Section 2 reviews related work; Section 3 describes the dataset.' Three short paragraphs, and the reader knows why the paper exists.

Related work: The related work section shows that you know the field and explains how your work differs. It should not be a list of summaries, one paper per paragraph ('Rahman et al. did X. Ahmed et al. did Y.'). Instead, group earlier work by theme or approach, explain what each group achieved and what it left open, and position your work in relation to it: 'Earlier Bangla sentiment studies used small datasets of under 3,000 reviews [4, 7, 9]; we provide a dataset four times larger.' Be fair to other authors: describe their work accurately and respectfully, even when pointing out limitations. Placing related work early helps readers who are new to the area; placing it near the end, as some papers do, keeps the focus on your contributions.

Writing the method and evaluation: The method or approach section describes what you built or did, in enough detail to be reproduced, often with diagrams, pseudocode and equations. The evaluation describes datasets, baselines (the earlier methods you compare against), metrics, and the experimental setup, including hardware and software versions. Strong papers compare against strong, recent baselines, not weak ones chosen to make results look good. Many venues now encourage or require sharing code and data so that others can reproduce the results; say where they are available.

Results, limitations and honesty: Present results clearly in tables and graphs, as lesson 10 explained, and explain what they show. Report variation, such as averages over several runs with standard deviations, not just the single best run. Include a limitations or threats to validity section: what might make your conclusions wrong or less general. Reviewers trust authors who discuss weaknesses openly. Never fabricate, select or manipulate data to fit a story; this is research misconduct, discussed in lesson 23 and in Ethics and Cyber Law (deep-cse-6-6).

Conference papers and journal papers: In computer science, many important results are published at conferences, unlike many other sciences where journals dominate. Conference papers have fixed deadlines, strict page limits (often 8 to 12 pages, sometimes fewer), one round of review, and are presented in a talk. Journal papers have no fixed deadline, are usually longer and more complete, and often go through several rounds of review and revision over months. A common path is to publish a conference version first and later an extended journal version with substantial new material, clearly stating the overlap.

Peer review: Before publication, papers go through peer review: the editor or programme committee sends the paper to usually two to four experts in the field. They evaluate originality, correctness, significance, clarity and relation to earlier work, and recommend acceptance, revision or rejection, with detailed comments. Reviewing is often single-blind (authors do not know reviewers' names) or double-blind (neither side knows the other's names, so authors must remove identifying information from the paper). Rejection is normal: many top venues accept only a fraction of submissions. The comments, even harsh ones, are free expert advice to make the paper better.

Responding to reviewers: When a journal asks for revisions, or a conference allows a rebuttal, you must respond. The standard approach: thank the reviewers briefly; then copy each comment and reply to it point by point; for each, say what you changed and where (section, page, line), or politely explain with evidence why you did not change it. Example: 'Reviewer 2, Comment 3: The baseline is outdated. Response: We agree. We added a comparison with two models published in 2023 (Section 5.2, Table 4). Our model remains more accurate on low-resource phones, although one new model is slightly more accurate on desktop hardware; we now discuss this in Section 6.' Never argue emotionally or ignore a comment. Make it easy for the editor to see that every point was handled.

The thesis: A thesis (also called a dissertation in some countries) is a long document presenting a student's research for a degree: often 40 to 100 pages for a bachelor's or master's thesis and more for a PhD, depending on the university. A typical CSE thesis has: front matter (title page, declaration of originality, certificate of approval, acknowledgements, abstract, contents, lists of figures, tables and abbreviations); Chapter 1 Introduction (motivation, problem, objectives, contributions, organisation); Chapter 2 Background and literature review; Chapter 3 Methodology or proposed system; Chapter 4 Implementation or experimental setup; Chapter 5 Results and discussion; Chapter 6 Conclusion, limitations and future work; references; and appendices. Always follow your department's template and rules exactly.

Thesis writing habits: Start writing early; do not wait until all experiments finish. Write the literature review as you read, and the methods as you build. Keep a single reference manager library (lesson 22) from day one. Agree on a chapter outline with your supervisor before drafting, and send chapters for feedback one at a time rather than the whole thesis at the end. Each chapter should open with a short paragraph saying what it covers and close with a short summary linking to the next. Leave at least two weeks for editing, formatting and checking references.

Real-life example 1, a first conference paper: Two final-year students in Rajshahi submitted their Bangla sentiment paper to an international conference. The reviewers said the contributions were unclear and the baselines were weak. The students rewrote the introduction with a three-item contributions list, added two recent baselines, and released their dataset publicly. The revised paper was accepted at a different conference six months later, and the dataset was later used by other researchers, who cited their work.

Real-life example 2, a thesis defence that went smoothly: Arif's thesis on traffic sign detection followed the department template exactly, had a clear objective-to-result mapping in Chapter 6, and an honest limitations section noting poor performance at night. During the viva, an examiner asked about night-time accuracy. Arif pointed to the limitations section and his proposed future work. The examiner said this was exactly what a good thesis should do: know and state its boundaries.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Contributions not stated or too vague. Related work as a list of summaries. Weak or missing baselines. Reporting only the best run. Ignoring the venue's page limit or template. Emotional or incomplete responses to reviewers. Starting thesis writing too late. Exams often ask about the structure of a research paper, the CARS model, the purpose of related work, single- versus double-blind review, conference versus journal publication, or how to respond to reviewer comments.

Recap: Research papers report original contributions to a community of experts, usually in an IMRaD-like structure with an explicit contributions list. Use the CARS moves to build the introduction: territory, niche, occupation. Group related work by theme and position your work fairly. Describe methods reproducibly, compare with strong baselines, report variation and limitations honestly. Know the difference between conference and journal publication, expect peer review and treat comments as advice, and respond point by point. Write a thesis chapter by chapter, early, following the department template. At the science fair of research, clear writing is what makes readers stop at your poster.
key_points: Research papers report original contributions for expert readers and become part of the permanent public record.
End the introduction with an explicit, specific list of contributions, each supported later in the paper.
The CARS model (Swales, 1990): establish a territory, establish a niche (gap), occupy the niche (your work).
Related work should group earlier studies by theme and position your work fairly, not list summaries.
Compare with strong, recent baselines; report variation and limitations; never fabricate or manipulate data.
CS conference papers have deadlines, page limits and one review round; journal papers are longer with several rounds.
Respond to reviewers point by point, stating what changed and where; write a thesis early, chapter by chapter, following the template.
lessons.tip: Write your contributions list on the first day of a paper project, even if it changes later. If you cannot write three specific contribution sentences, you are not yet ready to write the paper.
lessons.task: Pick a research topic you find interesting. Write a three-paragraph introduction using the CARS moves: territory, niche and occupying the niche. End it with a list of two or three specific contributions. Then underline the sentence that states the gap.

quiz.q: What are the three moves of the CARS model?
options: Establish a territory, establish a niche, occupy the niche
quiz.explain: Swales's CARS model builds an introduction that creates space for the new research.

quiz.q: What is the best way to write a related work section?
options: One paragraph per paper, summarised in order of publication
Copy the abstracts of earlier papers
Group earlier work by theme and explain how your work differs
Mention only papers that agree with you
quiz.explain: Thematic grouping shows understanding and positions the new work clearly.

quiz.q: In double-blind review, who knows whose names?
options: Neither authors nor reviewers know each other's names
Reviewers know the authors' names only
Only the authors know the reviewers' names
quiz.explain: In double-blind review both sides are anonymous to each other.

quiz.q: How should you respond to a reviewer's comment you disagree with?
options: Argue that the reviewer did not understand the paper
Delete the section the reviewer commented on
Politely explain with evidence why you did not change it
quiz.explain: Point-by-point, polite, evidence-based replies make the editor's decision easier.

quiz.q: Why should papers report results over several runs rather than only the best run?
options: Because conferences require exactly five runs
Because the best run may be luck; averages and variation show how reliable results are
Because more numbers make the paper longer
Because the best run is always wrong
quiz.explain: Reporting variation gives an honest picture of performance.

lessons.title: Citing and Referencing
lessons.content:
When your friend tells you 'the exam has been moved to Sunday', your first question is: 'Who said so?' If the answer is 'the department notice board', you trust it. If it is 'someone in the canteen', you check. Citations do the same job in technical writing. Every time you use someone else's idea, data, words, figure or code, a citation tells the reader where it came from, so they can check it, learn more, and give credit to the person who did the work. This lesson explains why and when to cite, how quoting, paraphrasing and summarising differ, how the two most common styles in computer science work, IEEE and APA, and how to manage references with tools.

What a citation and a reference are: A citation is a short marker in the text that points to a source, such as [3] or (Rahman, 2021). A reference is the full description of that source in the reference list at the end, with enough detail for anyone to find it: authors, title, where it was published, year, pages, and a DOI or URL. Together they form a chain from your sentence to the original work. Some styles call the list 'References' (only works cited), while a 'Bibliography' can also include works you read but did not cite; most technical documents use a reference list.

Why citing matters: Citations give credit to the people whose work you used, which is both fair and expected. They let readers verify your claims and find the original evidence. They show that you know the field and that your work builds on solid foundations. They separate your own contribution from others', which is exactly what examiners and reviewers want to see. And they protect you from plagiarism, which lesson 23 covers in detail. Good citing makes your writing more credible, not less original.

What to cite and what not to cite: Cite any idea, theory, method, finding, data, figure, table, quotation, code or design that comes from someone else, whether from a paper, book, website, video, lecture, dataset or conversation. Cite even when you rewrite it in your own words. You do not need to cite common knowledge: facts widely known in the field and easily found in many sources without dispute, such as 'binary search runs in O(log n) time' or 'Dhaka is the capital of Bangladesh'. When unsure whether something is common knowledge for your readers, cite it; an extra citation never hurts.

Quoting, paraphrasing and summarising: There are three ways to use a source. A quotation copies the exact words, inside quotation marks, with a citation and, in some styles, a page number. Use quotations rarely in technical writing: only when the exact wording matters, such as a definition from a standard or a famous statement. A paraphrase restates a specific passage in your own words and sentence structure, at about the same length, with a citation. A summary condenses a larger part, such as a whole paper's main idea, into a few sentences of your own, with a citation. Paraphrases and summaries are the most common in technical writing because they let you integrate sources smoothly.

A worked paraphrase: Original idea, from a classic 1968 letter by Edsger Dijkstra: the go to statement makes programs hard to understand, because the reader can no longer easily follow how the program reached a given point. Poor paraphrase, too close to the original wording: 'The go to statement makes programs hard to understand, since readers cannot easily follow how they reached a point [1].' Good paraphrase: 'Dijkstra argued that unrestricted jumps make it difficult to reason about a program, because the path that led to any line becomes hard to trace [1].' The good paraphrase changes both words and structure, keeps the meaning, and still cites the source. Changing a few words in someone else's sentence is not a paraphrase; it is called patchwriting, and it counts as plagiarism.

Citation styles: A citation style is a set of rules for how citations and references look. Different fields and publishers prefer different styles. In computer science and engineering, IEEE style is very common, and ACM has its own similar style. In social sciences, education and many human-computer interaction venues, APA style is common. Other styles include Harvard (an author-date family), Chicago, MLA and Vancouver. The golden rules: use the style your teacher, department, journal or conference requires, and be consistent throughout. Mixing styles looks careless.

IEEE style: IEEE is a numbered style. In the text, sources are numbered in the order they are first cited, in square brackets: 'Earlier work used small datasets [1], [2].' The same source keeps the same number every time. The reference list is ordered by number, not alphabetically. Authors are written with initials first. A journal article example: [1] E. W. Dijkstra, 'Go to statement considered harmful,' Commun. ACM, vol. 11, no. 3, pp. 147-148, Mar. 1968. A book example: [2] D. E. Knuth, The Art of Computer Programming, vol. 1, Fundamental Algorithms, 3rd ed. Reading, MA, USA: Addison-Wesley, 1997. In real IEEE references, the article title is in double quotation marks and the journal and book titles are in italics; here we show them in plain text.

APA style: APA, from the American Psychological Association, is an author-date style, currently in its 7th edition (2019). In the text, you cite the author's surname and year: (Dijkstra, 1968), or 'Dijkstra (1968) argued that...'. For two authors, use both names: (Rahman & Ahmed, 2021). For three or more authors, APA 7 uses the first author and 'et al.': (Hossain et al., 2022). The reference list is alphabetical by first author's surname. Journal article: Dijkstra, E. W. (1968). Go to statement considered harmful. Communications of the ACM, 11(3), 147-148. Book: Knuth, D. E. (1997). The art of computer programming: Vol. 1. Fundamental algorithms (3rd ed.). Addison-Wesley. In APA, the journal name and volume number and the book title are in italics.

IEEE versus APA at a glance: IEEE uses numbers in brackets in the text and a list in citation order; APA uses author and year in the text and an alphabetical list. IEEE puts initials before surnames; APA puts surnames first. IEEE places the year near the end of the reference; APA places it right after the authors. Numbered styles save space and suit technical papers with many citations. Author-date styles let readers see who and when without flipping to the list.

Placing citations in sentences: Put the citation right after the claim it supports, not only at the end of a long paragraph, so readers know which sentence comes from which source. 'Earlier models reached 80 percent accuracy [4], but none ran on phones [5], [6]' is clearer than one bracket of numbers at the end. When you only read about a study in another paper, cite what you actually read: in APA, '(Karim, 2015, as cited in Islam, 2020)'. Cite the original only if you have checked it yourself.

DOIs and URLs: A DOI, or Digital Object Identifier, is a permanent identifier for a published item, such as a journal article, that keeps working even if the publisher's website changes. It looks like 10.1000/xyz123 and can be written as a link starting with https://doi.org/. Include a DOI whenever one exists; both IEEE and APA recommend it. For web sources without a DOI, include the URL and, for pages that change, the date you accessed it.

Citing web pages, software and datasets: Web pages need an author or organisation, the page title, the site name, the date published or updated, and the URL. APA example: Bangladesh Bureau of Statistics. (2023). Title of the page. URL. If no date is given, write n.d. for 'no date'. Software should be cited when it was important to your work, with the author or organisation, name, version and URL or DOI, such as a specific version of a deep learning library. Datasets need their creator, title, version, publisher or repository and DOI or URL. Many datasets and libraries include a 'How to cite' file; use it. Generative AI tools are a special case covered in lesson 23.

Reference managers: Collecting references by hand becomes painful beyond a few sources. Reference managers store your sources, often with their PDFs and notes, and insert citations and reference lists in any style automatically. Zotero is free and open-source; Mendeley is free and owned by the publisher Elsevier; EndNote is commercial. They add a plugin to Word or LibreOffice, and they can capture a reference from a web page or database with one click. Always check imported references, because metadata from websites is sometimes wrong: missing authors, wrong year, title in all capitals.

BibTeX: If you write in LaTeX, as many CS researchers do, references are kept in a .bib file using BibTeX format. Each entry has a type, a key and fields, for example: @article{dijkstra1968, author = {Edsger W. Dijkstra}, title = {Go To Statement Considered Harmful}, journal = {Communications of the ACM}, volume = {11}, number = {3}, pages = {147--148}, year = {1968}}. In the text you write \cite{dijkstra1968}, and LaTeX produces the citation and the reference list in whatever style the template uses. Reference managers and Google Scholar can export BibTeX, but check the entries for errors.

Real-life example 1, a lab report: A student's lab report on sorting algorithms copied a complexity table from a website without citing it. The teacher recognised the table and asked where it came from. The student had not meant to cheat, but the report lost marks for missing attribution. In the next report, she added '(adapted from [3])' under the table and included the website in the reference list with an access date. The same table, properly cited, was now perfectly acceptable.

Real-life example 2, a thesis with a reference manager: Tanvir started his thesis with Zotero on the first day, saving each paper with tags such as 'dataset', 'baseline' and 'survey'. Three months later, his supervisor asked him to switch from APA to IEEE style because of the university template. With Zotero, this took one click. His friend, who had typed 85 references by hand, spent a whole weekend reformatting them and still had inconsistent author initials.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Not citing paraphrased ideas. Patchwriting instead of real paraphrasing. Citing a source you never read, only saw cited elsewhere; cite what you actually read, or say 'as cited in'. Mixing citation styles. References in the list that are never cited in the text, or citations with no reference. Missing DOIs or access dates. Exams often ask you to distinguish quotation, paraphrase and summary, to format a reference in IEEE or APA, to explain common knowledge, or to compare numbered and author-date styles.

Recap: Citations point from your text to sources, and references describe those sources fully. Cite ideas, data, figures, quotations and code from others, even when paraphrased; common knowledge needs no citation. Quote rarely, paraphrase and summarise in your own words and structure, and always cite. IEEE uses numbered citations in order of appearance; APA uses author and year with an alphabetical list. Include DOIs, cite software and datasets, and use a reference manager or BibTeX to stay consistent. Like checking who announced the exam change, citations let every reader trace each claim to its source.
key_points: A citation is a short marker in the text; a reference is the full description of the source in the list.
Cite others' ideas, data, figures, quotations and code even when paraphrased; common knowledge needs no citation.
Quotations copy exact words; paraphrases restate a passage in your own words and structure; summaries condense larger parts.
Changing a few words of a source sentence (patchwriting) is still plagiarism.
IEEE: numbered citations [1] in order of first appearance, list by number, initials before surnames.
APA 7: (Author, Year) in text, et al. for three or more authors, alphabetical list, year after authors.
Use DOIs, cite software and datasets, and use reference managers (Zotero, Mendeley) or BibTeX, checking imported data.
lessons.tip: Save the full reference the moment you read a useful source, not when you write. Finding a half-remembered article again weeks later can take longer than writing the paragraph that uses it.
lessons.task: Choose two sources you have used recently: one book or article and one web page. Write their references in both IEEE and APA style. Then pick one paragraph from one source and write a paraphrase and a two-sentence summary, each with a citation.

A 2021 study found 37 percent of users skip onboarding screens.
A figure copied from a website
A paraphrase of an argument from a paper

lessons.title: Plagiarism, Integrity and AI Writing Tools
lessons.content:
Imagine you spend a whole week building a model of a bridge for the school science fair, and on the day another student shows your model with their name on it. You would feel cheated, and the judges would be misled about who can actually build bridges. Plagiarism does exactly this with ideas and words. It takes credit for someone else's work and misleads the reader about who did what. In technical writing, honesty is not an extra rule on top of good writing; it is the foundation. Readers trust your report, paper or documentation only if they trust that the words, data and ideas are what you say they are. This lesson explains what plagiarism is, how similarity checkers work, how to use AI writing tools honestly, how licences such as Creative Commons work, and why honest data matters.

What plagiarism is: Plagiarism is presenting someone else's words, ideas, data, images, code or other work as your own, without proper acknowledgement. It does not matter whether the source is a published paper, a website, a friend's assignment, a lecture slide or a generated text. It also does not matter whether it was deliberate: careless copying without citation is still plagiarism, though institutions may treat intentional and accidental cases differently. The cure is simple: acknowledge every source clearly, as lesson 22 explained, and make sure your own contribution is genuinely yours.

Types of plagiarism: Direct or verbatim plagiarism copies text word for word without quotation marks and citation. Mosaic plagiarism or patchwriting mixes copied phrases with your own words, or changes a few words while keeping the original structure. Paraphrasing without citation restates someone's ideas in new words but hides where they came from. Idea plagiarism uses someone's original argument, method or design without credit. Self-plagiarism reuses large parts of your own earlier submitted or published work without permission or disclosure, such as submitting the same report for two courses. Contract cheating means getting someone else, a friend, a paid service or a tool, to do the work you submit as your own. Code plagiarism copies code from classmates, websites or repositories without attribution or against the licence.

Why plagiarism is serious: For students, plagiarism can lead to zero marks, failing a course, suspension, or a degree being cancelled even years later. For researchers, it can lead to retracted papers and damaged careers. Beyond rules, plagiarism hurts real people: the original authors lose credit, honest classmates are graded unfairly, and readers are misled. It also robs you of learning: the skills an assignment is meant to build only develop if you do the work. Employers and examiners can usually tell when someone cannot explain work they claim to have written.

Research misconduct beyond plagiarism: In research, the three most serious forms of misconduct are often called FFP: fabrication, falsification and plagiarism. Fabrication means making up data or results that were never obtained. Falsification means changing data, results, images or methods so that the record no longer reflects what happened, such as deleting inconvenient data points without reason or editing an image to hide a flaw. Both destroy the trust that makes research and engineering work. If an experiment fails or data are messy, report it honestly and explain; that is far better than a perfect-looking lie.

How similarity checkers work: Universities and publishers use similarity checking software, such as Turnitin or iThenticate, to compare a submitted document with a large database of web pages, published papers and earlier student submissions. The software highlights matching passages and shows a similarity percentage. Many universities in Bangladesh, as elsewhere, require a similarity report for theses and journal submissions, often with a maximum allowed percentage set by the institution.

A percentage is not a verdict: The similarity percentage only measures matching text, not plagiarism. A report can show 15 percent similarity because of properly quoted definitions, standard phrases ('the results show that'), the reference list, a template's headings or your own earlier proposal. Equally, a paper with a low percentage can still be plagiarised, for example if ideas were taken and fully rewritten without credit, or if text was translated from another language. Teachers and editors therefore read the highlighted matches and judge each one. As a writer, check your own report if your institution allows it, and fix any unquoted or uncited matches before submission, not by disguising them, but by quoting, paraphrasing properly and citing.

Code and plagiarism: Copying code is common in software work, and much of it is legal and encouraged, but it still needs honesty. In assignments, follow the course rules: if collaboration is not allowed, do not share or copy solutions, even partly. When you use code from a website, a forum answer or an open-source project, keep or add a comment that says where it came from, and check its licence. Many forum and open-source licences require attribution. Code similarity checkers such as MOSS (Measure Of Software Similarity), developed at Stanford, compare programs structurally, so renaming variables and reordering functions usually does not hide copying.

AI writing tools: Generative AI tools, such as chatbots that write text or code, are now widely available. They can help with legitimate tasks: brainstorming, explaining a concept, checking grammar, suggesting a clearer sentence, or finding bugs. But they also raise integrity issues. Text produced by a tool is not your own work; submitting it as if you wrote it can count as plagiarism or contract cheating under many institutions' rules. Policies differ widely: some courses ban AI tools, some allow them for specific tasks, and some require full disclosure. Always read and follow the policy of your course, university, journal or employer.

Accuracy risks with AI tools: AI tools can produce fluent text that is wrong. They may state false facts confidently, misunderstand technical details, or invent references that look real but do not exist. In technical writing, where accuracy matters, every claim, number, code snippet and citation from an AI tool must be checked against reliable sources. Never cite a source you have not found and read yourself. And remember that you, not the tool, are responsible for everything in your document.

Disclosing AI use: Where AI tools are allowed, transparency is the rule. Many journals and universities ask authors to describe how they used AI tools, for example in the methods or acknowledgements: 'We used a generative AI tool to improve grammar in Sections 1 and 2; all content was reviewed and edited by the authors.' Major publishers do not allow an AI tool to be listed as an author, because a tool cannot take responsibility for the work. Keeping a short record of how you used a tool, such as the prompts and what you changed, makes honest disclosure easy.

Copyright and licences: Even when you cite a source, you may not be allowed to reuse it freely. Copyright gives creators rights over copying and adapting their work. Short quotations with citation are generally acceptable for study, criticism and research under fair use or fair dealing rules, which differ by country, but copying whole figures, long passages, photos or code may need permission or a licence. Always check the licence of images, datasets, fonts and code before including them in a public report, documentation or product.

Creative Commons: Creative Commons is a non-profit organisation, founded in 2001, that provides free, standard licences that creators can use to allow others to reuse their work under certain conditions. Its licences combine four elements. BY (Attribution): you must credit the creator. SA (ShareAlike): if you adapt the work, you must share your version under the same licence. NC (NonCommercial): you may not use the work for commercial purposes. ND (NoDerivatives): you may share the work but not change it. For example, CC BY allows any use with credit; CC BY-NC-SA allows non-commercial use and adaptation with credit, as long as adaptations use the same licence. CC0 is a separate tool by which creators give up their rights as far as the law allows, placing the work effectively in the public domain. When you use a CC-licensed image, credit it with title, creator, source and licence, for example: 'Photo: Dhaka skyline by A. Rahman, from Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 4.0.'

Ethics and law in context: Ethics and Cyber Law (deep-cse-6-6) covers intellectual property, copyright law, software licences and professional codes of conduct in depth, including Bangladesh's legal framework. Here the focus is on writing practice: credit sources, use only what you are allowed to use, and present data and results truthfully.

Real-life example 1, a group report: In a group project, one member wrote the literature review by pasting paragraphs from three papers and changing a few words. The similarity report flagged 31 percent, mostly in that section. The group leader caught it before submission, and the team rewrote the section: they read the papers, summarised the key ideas in their own words, compared them, and cited each one. The new similarity was 9 percent, mostly from the reference list and quoted definitions. The section also became better, because it now compared the papers instead of listing them.

Real-life example 2, AI tool in a software team: A junior developer at a Dhaka company used an AI tool to draft the README for an internal library. The draft looked polished but described a configuration option that did not exist and gave the wrong default port. A reviewer tested the steps, found the errors and fixed them. The team then agreed on a simple rule: AI-assisted documentation is allowed, but every command and example must be run before merging, and the commit message says that a tool was used. The rule kept the speed benefit and removed the accuracy risk.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Thinking that citing makes copying entire paragraphs acceptable; long copying still needs quotation marks or a summary. Patchwriting. Reusing your own old report without permission. Trusting a low similarity percentage as proof of originality. Using AI-generated text or references without checking or disclosure. Using images from search results without checking licences. Exams often ask you to define plagiarism and list its types, to explain what similarity percentages mean, to describe Creative Commons licence elements, to discuss responsible use of AI tools, or to define fabrication and falsification.

Recap: Plagiarism is presenting others' words, ideas, data, images or code as your own, deliberately or carelessly. Its types include direct, mosaic, uncited paraphrase, idea, self-plagiarism, contract cheating and code plagiarism. Fabrication and falsification, together with plagiarism, are the most serious research misconduct. Similarity checkers measure matching text; the percentage is not a verdict. Use AI tools only as allowed, check everything they produce, disclose their use, and remember you are responsible. Respect copyright and licences, and understand Creative Commons elements BY, SA, NC and ND. Like the bridge model at the science fair, your work should carry your name only when it is truly yours.

Types: direct, mosaic or patchwriting, uncited paraphrase, idea, self-plagiarism, contract cheating and code plagiarism.
Fabrication, falsification and plagiarism (FFP) are the most serious forms of research misconduct.
Similarity checkers such as Turnitin show matching text; the percentage is not a verdict and must be interpreted.
AI tools must be used only as policies allow, their output checked for errors and invented references, and their use disclosed.
Citing a source does not grant permission to reuse it; check copyright and licences.

lessons.tip: Keep your own notes in your own words, with the source next to each note. When you write from notes rather than from the open source, plagiarism becomes almost impossible and your understanding becomes much deeper.

Write a proper credit line with title, creator, source and licence, and explain in two sentences what the licence lets you do and not do. Then write a one-sentence AI-use disclosure for an imaginary report where you used a tool to check grammar.
