quiz.explain: Patchwriting stays too close to the source and counts as plagiarism even with a citation.

quiz.q: What does a 15 percent similarity score from a checker mean?
options: 15 percent of the document is plagiarised
15 percent of the text matches other sources, which a person must examine
The document is 85 percent original research
quiz.explain: Matches may include quotations, references or standard phrases; the percentage is not a verdict.

quiz.q: What does the Creative Commons NC element mean?
options: The work may not be used for commercial purposes
The work may not be shared at all
Adaptations must use the same licence
quiz.explain: NC means NonCommercial; SA is the share-alike requirement.

quiz.q: Which is falsification?
options: Quoting a definition with quotation marks
Deleting inconvenient data points without reason so results look better
quiz.explain: Falsification changes data or results so the record no longer reflects what happened.

quiz.q: Why should every reference suggested by an AI tool be checked?
options: Because AI tools can invent references that look real but do not exist
Because AI tools always use APA style
Because checking makes the document longer
quiz.explain: Generated text can include fabricated sources; only cite what you have found and read.

lessons.title: Technical Presentations and Posters
lessons.content:
A tour guide at Lalbagh Fort does not read a history book aloud to visitors. She points at the gate, tells one striking story about it, lets people look, and moves on. The building is the evidence; her sentences make it meaningful. A good technical presentation works the same way: the speaker gives the message, and the slides show the evidence. Engineers present constantly: project demos, thesis defences, conference talks, sprint reviews, client pitches. Many careful writers turn into poor presenters by pasting their report onto slides and reading it. This lesson shows how to plan a talk, design slides using the assertion-evidence approach, time your talk, handle questions, defend a thesis and design a poster.

Why presentations are different from documents: A reader controls the pace: they can skim, reread and skip. A listener cannot. They hear each sentence once, at your speed, and must remember it. So a presentation must carry fewer ideas than a report, repeat the main message, make structure obvious ('Second, the results'), and use visuals that can be understood in seconds. The audience also judges you, not just the content: confidence, clarity and respect for their time matter. A presentation is not a report read aloud; it is a guided tour of the report's most important ideas.

Planning: audience, purpose and one message: Start with the same questions as for writing (lesson 02): who is in the audience, what do they know, and what should they think or do afterwards? Then write your main message in one sentence, such as 'Our app cuts bus waiting time by showing live locations, and we need approval for a three-month pilot.' Everything in the talk should support that sentence. A common structure: opening (problem and why it matters), roadmap, two to four main points with evidence, conclusion restating the message, and next steps or a request.

The trouble with bullet-point slides: Many slides use a short topic title, such as 'Results', and a list of bullet points. This encourages speakers to read text the audience is also reading, splits attention, and hides the logical connection between ideas. Research on slide design has repeatedly found that audiences remember more when slides use meaningful sentence headlines and visual evidence instead of bullet lists. Bullets are not forbidden, but they should be the exception, not the template.

The assertion-evidence approach: Michael Alley, an engineering communication professor at Pennsylvania State University, promotes the assertion-evidence slide design. Each slide has a headline that is a complete sentence stating the slide's main message, the assertion, usually no more than two lines. The body of the slide is visual evidence supporting that assertion: a graph, photo, diagram, equation, short demo or table, with minimal text labels. Example: instead of the title 'Results' and five bullets, the headline says 'Waiting time fell from 18 to 7 minutes on the pilot route', and the body shows a simple bar chart of before and after. The audience gets the message from the headline in two seconds, and the speaker explains the evidence.

Designing readable slides: Use large fonts: commonly recommended minimums are around 28 points for headlines and 18 to 24 points for body text in a normal room. Use high contrast, such as dark text on a light background, following the contrast ideas from lesson 10. Keep one idea per slide. Label graph axes in large text and remove gridlines and decoration that do not help. Use colour to highlight the one thing you want people to look at. Avoid long sentences, code blocks larger than a few lines, and tables with dozens of numbers; show the key row and put the full table in a backup slide or handout.

Timing, worked: Suppose you have a 15-minute slot that includes 5 minutes for questions. Then your talk is 15 - 5 = 10 minutes. A common rule of thumb for technical talks is about one content slide per minute, so plan around 10 content slides plus a title slide; complex slides with data may need two minutes each, so use fewer. Many people speak about 120 to 150 words per minute when presenting; at about 130 words per minute, 10 minutes is roughly 10 x 130 = 1,300 spoken words. That is about the length of a short essay, far less than your report, which is why you must choose only the most important points. Rehearse with a timer at least twice, and know which slides you will skip if you run late.

Openings, signposts and endings: The first 30 seconds decide whether people listen. Do not open with 'Today I will talk about my project' or a long list of acknowledgements. Open with the problem in a concrete form: a number, a picture or a short story the audience recognises. Then give a one-sentence roadmap: 'I will show the problem, our design, and results from a two-week pilot.' During the talk, signpost each move ('That was the design; now, does it work?') so listeners always know where they are. End with a slide that restates the main message and the request or next step, not a slide that says only 'Thank you' or 'Questions?'. The last slide often stays on screen during the whole question period, so make it work hard: the message, two or three key numbers, and your contact details.

Speaking and delivery: Face the audience, not the screen. Speak slowly and clearly, slower than in conversation, especially if the audience is mixed or the room is large. Pause after important points. Use the headline as a cue, then explain the evidence in your own words; do not read the slide. Point to specific parts of a graph ('this tall bar is the morning peak'). Use speaker notes or small cards for key numbers, not a full script. Bangla, English or a mix may be appropriate depending on the audience; whichever you use, keep technical terms consistent with your slides.

Demos: Live demos can be powerful but risky. Prepare a demo script, use test data, close other applications and notifications, increase font size, and check the projector and internet beforehand. Always have a backup: a short recorded video or screenshots on slides. If the demo fails, switch calmly to the backup instead of debugging in front of the audience.

Handling questions: Questions show interest, not attack. Listen to the whole question, repeat or rephrase it so everyone hears it, then answer briefly and directly. If you do not know, say so honestly and offer to follow up: 'I have not measured that yet; it is a good point, and I will check it.' If a question is outside the scope, acknowledge it and connect it to your work briefly. Prepare backup slides for likely questions, such as detailed results, cost breakdowns or limitations. Never argue with or belittle a questioner.

The thesis defence or viva: A thesis defence usually has a presentation of 15 to 30 minutes followed by questions from examiners, though rules vary by university. Examiners want to see that you did the work, understand it deeply, know its limitations and can explain choices. Prepare by rereading your thesis, listing likely questions (why this method, why these baselines, what if the data were different, what are the limitations, what would you do next), and practising answers with friends or your supervisor. Bring a copy of your thesis. It is fine to pause and think before answering. Referring to your own limitations section, as in lesson 21's example, is a strong answer.

Posters: Posters are common at conferences, project shows and university fairs. Visitors walk by and decide in a few seconds whether to stop, so a poster must work at two distances. From several metres away, a large title and one strong visual should show what the work is about. Up close, a viewer should be able to understand the problem, approach, key results and conclusion in about two to three minutes. Common sizes include A0 (841 by 1189 millimetres) and A1 (594 by 841 millimetres); always check the event's required size and orientation.

Poster design: Use a clear grid of two to four columns, read from top left to bottom right. Keep text short: many guides suggest roughly 300 to 800 words for the whole poster. Use large fonts: commonly recommended sizes are around 72 points or more for the title and at least 24 points for body text, so it is readable from about 1 to 2 metres. Let figures carry the results, with headline-style captions that state the finding. Leave white space. Include names, affiliations, a QR code linking to the paper or demo, and contact details. Stand beside your poster and prepare a 30-second and a 2-minute explanation.

Real-life example 1, a project showcase: A student team presented a crop disease detection app at a university project show. Their first deck had 28 slides with long bullet lists for a 10-minute slot. After a practice run went 19 minutes, they rebuilt it with 10 assertion-evidence slides, such as 'The model identifies 4 common rice diseases with 91 percent accuracy' over a confusion matrix, and 'Farmers in our test used the app without training' over a photo of a field test. They finished in 9 minutes, and the judges spent the remaining time asking about deployment, which is exactly the discussion the team wanted.

Real-life example 2, a client pitch: A small Sylhet software firm pitched a delivery-tracking system to a local courier company. Instead of starting with technology, they opened with one slide headed 'Customers call your office 300 times a day asking where their parcel is', with a photo of the busy call desk. Every later slide supported the message that live tracking would reduce calls. The courier company's manager later said the first slide was the reason they listened carefully to the rest.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Too many slides and too much text. Reading slides aloud. Topic titles instead of assertion headlines. Tiny fonts and unreadable graphs. No rehearsal, running out of time. Live demos without backup. Defensive answers to questions. Posters with walls of text. Exams often ask about principles of effective slide design, the assertion-evidence approach, how to plan the timing of a talk, how to handle questions, or what makes a good poster.

Recap: Presentations guide listeners through a few key ideas at your pace, so plan around one main message for a specific audience. Use assertion-evidence slides: a sentence headline stating the point and visual evidence below. Make slides readable with large fonts, high contrast and one idea each. Plan timing: subtract question time, about one slide per minute, and rehearse with a timer. Speak to the audience, prepare backups for demos, handle questions calmly and honestly, prepare thoroughly for a thesis defence, and design posters that work from a distance and up close. Like the guide at Lalbagh Fort, let the evidence show and let your words give it meaning.
key_points: Listeners cannot reread, so talks carry fewer ideas, repeat the main message and make structure obvious.
Plan around one main message for a specific audience, with two to four main points and a clear ending.
Assertion-evidence slides (Michael Alley): a full-sentence headline stating the point, with visual evidence below.
Readable slides: large fonts, high contrast, one idea per slide, labelled graphs, minimal text.
Timing: subtract question time, plan about one content slide per minute, and rehearse with a timer.
Answer questions by listening, rephrasing, answering briefly and admitting what you do not know; always have demo backups.
Posters must work from a distance (title and one strong visual) and up close (2-3 minute read), with large fonts and short text.
lessons.tip: Read only your slide headlines aloud, in order, without the bodies. If they tell the whole story of your talk, your slides are well built. If they sound like 'Introduction, Method, Results', rewrite them as sentences.
lessons.task: Take a report or project you have done and plan a 7-minute talk with 2 minutes for questions. Write the headline sentences for each content slide, describe the visual evidence for each, and calculate how many slides fit. Then rehearse once with a timer and note your actual time.

quiz.q: What is the headline of an assertion-evidence slide?
options: A complete sentence stating the slide's main message
quiz.explain: The headline is the assertion; the slide body provides visual evidence.

quiz.q: You have a 15-minute slot including 5 minutes of questions. About how many content slides should you plan at one per minute?
quiz.explain: 15 - 5 = 10 minutes of talk, so about 10 content slides.

quiz.q: What should you do if you do not know the answer to a question?
options: Say honestly that you do not know and offer to follow up
Change the subject to your demo
quiz.explain: Honest answers maintain credibility; guessing can damage it.

quiz.q: Why should a live demo have a backup?
options: Because demos are not allowed at conferences
Because backups make the talk longer
Because equipment, internet or software can fail, and a video or screenshots keep the talk going
Because audiences prefer videos to demos
quiz.explain: A recorded backup avoids debugging in front of the audience.

quiz.q: What should a poster communicate from several metres away?
options: What the work is about, through a large title and one strong visual
Every number in the results table
quiz.explain: Visitors decide in seconds whether to stop, so the title and main visual must be readable from a distance.

lessons.title: Editing, Reviewing and Capstone Documentation
lessons.content:
A cricket team does not end practice after the batters hit a few balls. The coach watches, points out a dropped elbow, and the batter tries again. Writing works the same way: the first draft is batting practice, and editing is the coaching that turns it into a match-winning innings. Professional writers spend as much time revising as drafting, and the best technical documents in the world, from aircraft manuals to programming language references, have been reviewed many times. This final lesson explains the levels of editing, how to give and receive feedback, how to use checklists, style guides and tools, how to manage documents with version control, and then brings the whole course together in a capstone: a complete documentation set for an invented app called BusKoi.

Why editing matters: First drafts are for getting ideas down; they almost always contain unclear sentences, missing steps, repeated points and errors. Editing makes the document correct, clear and usable for its readers. In technical writing, an editing slip can have real costs: a wrong command deletes data, a missing warning causes injury, a confusing requirement creates months of rework. Editing is also where the advice from earlier lessons, plain language, structure, consistent terms, good visuals and honest citations, is actually applied.

Levels of edit: It helps to edit in passes, from big to small, because there is no point polishing a sentence in a section you will delete. Substantive or structural editing checks the whole: Is the purpose clear? Is the audience right? Is anything important missing or unnecessary? Is the order logical? Do headings reveal the structure? Line or stylistic editing works on paragraphs and sentences: clarity, conciseness, active voice where useful, plain words, consistent terms, smooth transitions. Copyediting checks correctness and consistency in detail: grammar, spelling, punctuation, numbers, units, abbreviations, capitalisation, cross-references and citation format. Proofreading is the final check of the finished version for small errors such as typos, broken links, wrong page numbers and layout problems. Many teams also add a technical review, in which an expert checks that every fact, command and number is correct.

Editing your own writing: Self-editing is hard because you read what you meant, not what you wrote. Useful techniques: take a break, ideally a day, before editing; read on paper or in a different font or device; read aloud, which reveals long sentences and missing words; follow your own instructions exactly, step by step, on a clean machine; search for your known weaknesses, such as 'very', 'in order to', passive verbs or inconsistent terms; and check one thing at a time, such as all numbers and units in one pass and all headings in another.

Giving feedback: When reviewing others' documents, start with the big picture, not commas. Say what works, then what to improve, with reasons and examples: not 'This section is bad' but 'The setup steps assume Node is installed; a new developer would get stuck at step 3. Could you add a prerequisites list?' Comment on the writing, not the person. Separate must-fix problems (wrong facts, missing safety warnings, broken steps) from suggestions (word choice, style). Be specific about location, and keep the number of comments manageable; ten important comments help more than eighty tiny ones.

Receiving feedback: Feedback is information, not an attack. Read all comments before reacting, ask questions if something is unclear, and thank reviewers for their time. Fix factual errors and clarity problems even when you think the reader 'should have understood'; if one reviewer was confused, real readers will be too. For style suggestions, you may decide, but follow your team's style guide. Keep track of which comments you addressed, as in responding to journal reviewers in lesson 21.

A worked line edit: Original sentence from a draft user guide: 'In order to be able to make use of the application, it is necessary for the user to first of all perform the installation of the latest version.' That is 28 words. Line edit: 'To use the app, first install the latest version.' That is 9 words, with the same meaning. What changed: 'in order to be able to make use of' became 'to use'; the weak construction 'it is necessary for the user to' became a direct instruction; 'perform the installation of' became the verb 'install'; and 'first of all' became 'first'. In a copyedit pass, the editor would then check that the guide calls it 'the app' everywhere, not 'the application' in some places, and that 'latest version' matches the version number given on the download page.

Checklists: A checklist makes sure important checks are not forgotten, especially under time pressure. A short pre-publication checklist for technical documents might be: purpose and audience stated; summary or main point first; headings in parallel form; procedures tested on a clean setup; warnings before dangerous steps; terms consistent and defined; numbers, units and dates in a consistent format; figures and tables numbered, captioned and referred to; accessibility checked (alt text, contrast); all sources cited; spelling and links checked. Adapt the list to your document type and keep it with your templates.

Style guides: A style guide is a set of rules for writing in an organisation: voice and tone, word choices, capitalisation, number formats, how to write UI labels and code, and more. Large technology companies publish theirs, and many teams adopt one instead of writing their own. Two widely used examples are the Google developer documentation style guide and the Microsoft Writing Style Guide. Both recommend a friendly, conversational but professional tone, second person ('you'), active voice, present tense, sentence-case headings and plain words. A team style guide or a short list of house rules prevents endless debates and makes documents written by many people read as one voice.

Tools: Spell checkers and grammar checkers, such as those built into word processors, LanguageTool or Grammarly, catch many surface errors but miss errors of meaning and sometimes suggest wrong changes, especially for technical terms. Prose linters such as Vale can check a docs-as-code repository against a style guide's rules automatically, flagging banned words, passive voice or inconsistent terms in every pull request. Link checkers find broken links. Readability formulas (lesson 04) give a rough signal but not a verdict. Tools support editing; they do not replace a careful human reader.

Version control for documents: Documents change, and you need to know what changed, when and why. For word-processor documents, use track changes and comments during review, and save named versions, such as v1.0, v1.1, v2.0, rather than 'final', 'final2' and 'final-really'. For docs-as-code (lesson 15), use Git: each change is a commit with a message, reviews happen in pull requests, and you can see or undo any change. A document's front page or a change history table often records version, date, author and summary of changes, which is especially important for specifications, manuals and policies.

The capstone: documenting BusKoi: Now put the course together. Imagine a student team building BusKoi ('Where is the bus?'), a mobile app that shows live locations of buses on a few Dhaka routes, using GPS devices on buses and a server that sends positions to the app. Over one semester, the team must produce a set of documents, each for a different reader and purpose.

Capstone part 1, the proposal: For the transport company and their supervisor, the team writes a proposal (lesson 20): a problem statement with evidence (passengers in a short survey reported waiting an average of 20 minutes without knowing when the bus would come), SMART objectives (show bus positions updated at least every 30 seconds on two routes within four months), the approach, a timeline with milestones, an itemised budget with contingency, risks and an evaluation plan.

Capstone part 2, requirements and design: For developers and testers, they write requirements (lesson 17) using EARS patterns, such as 'When a bus's GPS position is more than 2 minutes old, the app shall show the bus icon in grey with the label Last seen 2 min ago', user stories with Given-When-Then acceptance criteria, a short design document with goals and non-goals, and ADRs for key decisions, such as choosing a map provider. They document the server's API (lesson 16) with an OpenAPI file, examples and error codes.

Capstone part 3, user-facing documentation: For passengers, they write in-app microcopy and a short help page in Bangla and English (lessons 13 and 14), with a task-based structure: find your route, read arrival times, report a problem. For bus company staff, they write a procedure for installing and checking the GPS device, with numbered steps, a caution before connecting power, and a troubleshooting table. For new developers, they write a README and a contributing guide (lesson 15).

Capstone part 4, reports and presentation: During the project, the team sends short progress reports (lesson 18). After a server outage during testing, they write a blameless incident report with a timeline and action items. At the end, they write a final project report with an informative abstract, IMRaD body, honest limitations (accuracy drops in narrow streets with tall buildings) and recommendations (lesson 19), with every source cited in IEEE style (lesson 22) and a statement of how they used AI tools (lesson 23). They present it with assertion-evidence slides and a poster for the department project show (lesson 24). Every document goes through structural, line and copy edits, peer review and a final checklist before release.

What next: Technical writing connects to many other courses. Ethics and Cyber Law (deep-cse-6-6) covers intellectual property, privacy and professional responsibility. Final Year Project and Thesis (deep-cse-6-7) is where you will write a full proposal, report and defence of your own. Software Project Management (deep-cse-6-11) covers planning, estimation and reporting in software projects. Research Methodology (deep-cse-7-7) prepares you for theses and research papers. Above all, keep writing: every lab report, README, commit message and email is practice.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Editing only for typos and skipping structural editing. Editing everything in one pass. Not testing procedures. Vague or harsh feedback. Ignoring a style guide. Trusting tools blindly. Unclear version names. Exams often ask you to explain levels of editing, list items for a review checklist, describe how to give constructive feedback, explain the purpose of a style guide, or plan a documentation set for a given project.

Recap: Editing turns a draft into a usable document. Edit in passes: structural, line, copyediting and proofreading, plus technical review. Self-edit with breaks, reading aloud and testing. Give specific, kind, prioritised feedback, and receive feedback as information. Use checklists, a style guide and tools, but keep a human reader in charge. Track versions clearly. And as the BusKoi capstone shows, a real project needs many documents, each designed for its reader and purpose: proposal, requirements, design, API docs, user help, procedures, reports and presentations. Like a batter after many coached practice sessions, a writer who revises with care is ready for the real match.
key_points: Edit in passes from big to small: structural, line or stylistic, copyediting and proofreading, plus technical review.
Self-edit after a break, read aloud, check one thing per pass and test every procedure.
Good feedback is specific, explains why, separates must-fix from suggestions and comments on the writing, not the person.
Checklists make sure key checks (purpose, tested steps, warnings, terms, numbers, citations, accessibility) are not forgotten.
Style guides such as Google's developer documentation guide and Microsoft's Writing Style Guide keep many writers consistent.
Tools (spell checkers, Vale, link checkers) support editing but do not replace a human reader; track versions with clear names or Git.
A real project like BusKoi needs a full documentation set: proposal, requirements, design, API docs, user help, procedures, reports and presentations.
lessons.tip: Keep a personal 'mistakes I make' list. Each time a reviewer catches a pattern in your writing, add it. Before submitting anything, search your draft for every item on the list.
lessons.task: Choose a document you wrote earlier in this course. Edit it in three separate passes: structural (purpose, order, missing parts), line (sentences and words), and copy (numbers, terms, citations). Note at least three changes from each pass. Then list the documents you would need for a project like BusKoi, with the reader and purpose of each.

quiz.q: Which level of edit checks purpose, audience, missing content and the order of sections?
quiz.explain: Structural editing deals with the big picture before sentences and typos.

quiz.q: Which is the most useful review comment?
options: The setup steps assume Node is installed; a new developer would get stuck at step 3. Could you add a prerequisites list?
I would have written this differently.
quiz.explain: It is specific, explains the problem's impact and suggests a fix.

quiz.q: What is the main purpose of a style guide?
options: To keep writing by many people consistent in tone, terms and formats
quiz.explain: Style guides settle recurring choices so documents read as one voice.

quiz.q: Why is self-editing difficult?
options: Because spell checkers do not work on your own text
Because it is always faster than drafting
Because you tend to read what you meant rather than what you wrote
quiz.explain: Breaks, reading aloud and testing help you see the text as a reader does.

quiz.q: In the BusKoi capstone, which document is written mainly for bus company staff installing GPS devices?
options: A procedure with numbered steps, a caution and a troubleshooting table
quiz.explain: Staff installing devices need task-based instructions with safety notices.
